en: The *Lishi Apitan Lun* (Abhidharmakośa-śāstra on the Establishment of the World), Volume One, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Western India during the Chen Dynasty. Chapter One: On Earthquakes. **Chapter One: On Earthquakes** [The Buddha said: "There are eight causes and conditions for the occurrence of earthquakes. What are these eight? First, when the great earth rests upon water, and the great water rests upon wind, if a strong wind arises and stirs up the great water, the great earth consequently shakes. This is the first cause and condition for an earthquake. Second, when a Bodhisattva descends from Tuṣita Heaven to enter his mother’s womb, at that time the great earth shakes in six ways. This is the second cause and condition for an earthquake. Third, when a Bodhisattva emerges from his mother’s womb, at that time the great earth shakes in six ways. This is the third cause and condition for an earthquake. Fourth, when a Bodhisattva attains supreme, perfect enlightenment, at that time the great earth shakes in six ways. This is the fourth cause and condition for an earthquake. Fifth, when a Tathāgata turns the wheel of the Dharma, at that time the great earth shakes in six ways. This is the fifth cause and condition for an earthquake. Sixth, when a Tathāgata manifests the great miracle, at that time the great earth shakes in six ways. This is the sixth cause and condition for an earthquake. Seventh, when a Tathāgata enters the parinirvāṇa, at that time the great earth shakes in six ways. This is the seventh cause and condition for an earthquake. Eighth, when a great Arhat enters the parinirvāṇa, at that time the great earth shakes in six ways. This is the eighth cause and condition for an earthquake. Thus spoke the Buddha. The venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. As spoken by the Buddha, the Blessed One, and the Arhats:
Thus have I heard.

At one time the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying in the great city of Śrāvastī, at the Puṣpakūṭāgāra on the Lotus Double-Storied Pavilion in the monastery of the laywoman Viśākhā, Mother of Mṛgāra, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus—all of whom were arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who had attained their own benefit, who had destroyed all fetters of existence, whose minds had attained mastery, who had accomplished what was to be done, who had laid down the heavy burden, and who were liberated through right knowledge—with the sole exception of Ānanda.
At that time, the great earth shook.

Then Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, who was among the great assembly, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and for what reason does the great earth tremble?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu Pūrṇa:
"Now listen attentively with a single mind and reflect well upon it; I shall analyze and explain it for you."
"There are two causes and conditions that cause the great earth to quake. What are these two? Monks!"
This earth element rests upon the water element; this water element rests upon the wind element; and this wind element rests in space. Bhikṣus!
There comes a time when a great wind blows and stirs the water element; when the water element is stirred, it in turn stirs the earth element.
For this reason, the great earth shakes. Bhikṣus!
Furthermore, there are gods of great supernormal power and majesty who, if they wish to cause the great earth to tremble, are able to make it shake.

If there are bhikṣus who possess great supernormal powers and great majestic virtue, they can contemplate the characteristic of earth as small and the characteristic of water as large; if they wish to cause the earth to move, they are also able to shake it.
"This is called the second causal condition by which the earth is made to tremble.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The water element is moved by wind; The earth trembles because the water moves."
This is the first cause and condition for movement; it is what is described by the term "reality.
When gods and bhikṣus, possessing great majestic power, are able to move [the earth], this is the second cause and condition for movement; it is spoken of as the taming of wicked people.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
“There is a wind named Vairambha; this wind blows constantly, and everything it encounters moves together with it, never ceasing.”

As the wind-force increases, there are winds blowing downward and winds moving sideways; these winds rotate equally and sustain one another in a circle, with a thickness of nine hundred and sixty million *yojanas*, a width of one billion two hundred and thirty-four million five hundred thousand *yojanas*, and a circumference of three billion six hundred and one million three hundred and fifty thousand *yojanas*.
The upper limit of this wind is precisely the water element.

This water remains level and stable throughout its upper and lower reaches, without dispersing or overflowing; it is forty-eight thousand *yojanas* in thickness, twelve billion three hundred and fifty million *yojanas* in breadth, and thirty-six billion one hundred and three thousand five hundred *yojanas* in circumference.

The upper limit of this water is precisely the boundary of the earth; its upper and lower limits are entirely equal, abiding immovably. It is two hundred and forty-four thousand *yojanas* in thickness, twelve billion three hundred and forty-five thousand *yojanas* in breadth, and thirty-six billion one thousand three hundred and fifty *yojanas* in circumference.
Thus the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, said:
"Monks! There is a great hell named Andhakāra (Darkness)."
On the outer boundaries of each respective world-system there are [such forms], all of which are without any covering.
Within this space, sentient beings cannot see them even by raising their own hands.
Although the sun and moon possess great majestic power and spiritual authority, their radiance does not illuminate those forms.
The Buddha said:
"Regarding these dark hells, where do they reside?
Beyond the iron wheels of two adjacent worlds, in what is called the 'beyond-the-boundary' region, lie these cold hells."
First is named Arbuda; second, Nirarbuda; third, Aṭaṭa; fourth, Hahava; fifth, Huhuva; sixth, Utpala; seventh, Kumuda; eighth, Saugandhika; ninth, Puṇḍarīka; and tenth, Padma.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, including Pūrṇa:
“Suppose there were ten *vāha* measures of sesame seeds in the kingdom of Magadha—one *vāha* being twenty *khalī*—and this amount of sesame were gathered together in one place.”
Suppose there were a person who, for a full hundred years, came once every day to remove a single sesame seed; Bhikṣus!
Such a heap of sesame seeds might yet be exhausted, but I have not said that the lifespan in the Arbuda hell has reached its end.
"Monks! Ten times the lifespan in the Arbuda hell is the lifespan in the Nirarbuda hell;
ten times the lifespan in the Nirarbuda hell is the lifespan in the Aṭaṭa hell."
It is the same even for the Padma Hell.
Bhikṣus! This bhikṣu Kokālika gave rise to a heart of distrust and malice toward Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana; because of that mind, he fell into the Padma Hell.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"When a person dwells in the world, An axe is born within their mouth;
Because of uttering evil words, They thus hack at their own body."
To praise those who deserve censure, and to revile those who deserve praise—through such verbal transgressions one meets with ruin; because of that ruin, one finds no joy.
If one’s own household loses its wealth, exhausting both possessions and oneself, [one suffers].
That person’s sin is still light;
but if one conceives a mind of malice and lack of faith toward the Sugata, that sin is heavier than that.
[It exceeds] a hundred thousand *nirarbuda* hells and three hundred million *arbuda* hells.
Sixty thousand and five thousand; if one slanders the noble ones with evil speech and an evil mind, one falls into hell according to the measure of that offense.
The bhikṣu Kokālika fell into the Padma Hell.
"They slander the great śrāvakas, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
"The beings therein move horizontally, yet they perceive it as being upward, just like a gecko."
On the outer edge of the Iron Wheel, they constantly move horizontally.
Their bodies are as large as a *nyagrodha* tree; when touched by cold winds, their bodies split open like a ripe melon.
Just as a grove of bamboo thickets, when struck by a great fire, emits a crackling sound of "ta-ta," so too do these beings,
when touched by the cold wind, experience their bones shatter with a crackling sound of "ta-ta" that resounds far and wide.
Because of these sounds, they mutually come to know that there are sentient beings taking birth therein.
At times, as they go and come, they encounter one another; because of this contact, they mutually come to know that there are sentient beings taking birth therein.

At that time, when the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world, a great light surpassing the great majestic spiritual power of all devas shines throughout that realm. By means of this radiance, they are able to see one another and reflect:
"There are sentient beings who have taken birth here."
If there are sentient beings who die here in this world, they mostly take rebirth here.

As for the Cold Ice Hell (Himāra), which lies outside the Iron Wheel, if sentient beings from other worlds die and are reborn in the Cold Ice Hell, they mostly take rebirth outside the Iron Wheel of those respective worlds.
Between the two realms, its narrowest point is eighty thousand yojanas; it has no bottom below and no covering above, while its widest point is one hundred and sixty thousand yojanas.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, being among the great assembly, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have heard these verses of the Dharma from the World-Honored One; I have received and upheld this true meaning directly from the mouth of the World-Honored One.
In the past, there was a Buddha named Śikhin, who had a disciple foremost in great supernormal powers named Abhiyu.

This bhikṣu, seated in the Brahma-abode of the fourth dhyāna, illuminates a thousand worlds with the light of a single finger and preaches the Dharma with a single voice, such that all within the thousand worlds simultaneously understand the true meaning.
“World-Honored One!
If the majestic spiritual power of the disciples of the Buddhas is already such as this, what then can be said of the measure of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas?
After Ānanda had asked this, the Buddha replied:
“Ānanda! This bhikṣu Abhihū is at the stage of a disciple; such matters as these cannot be fathomed even by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Second, the Venerable Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have heard these verses of the Dharma from the Buddha’s own mouth; I have received and upheld this true meaning from the World-Honored One.
In the past, there was a Buddha named Śikhin, who had a disciple foremost in supernatural powers named Abhihaṃsa.”

This bhikṣu sits in the Brahma-abode of the fourth dhyāna; with the light from a single finger, he illuminates a thousand worlds, and with a single voice, he preaches the Dharma, so that all within those thousand worlds simultaneously understand the true meaning.
“World-Honored One!
If the majestic spiritual power of the disciples of the Buddhas is already such as this, what can be said of the measure of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas?
After Ānanda had asked this, the Buddha replied:
“Ānanda! This bhikṣu Abhihūṃ is at the stage of a disciple; such matters as these cannot be fathomed by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
This was repeated three times, with the same answer each time.
After the fourth question had been asked, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"Wherever there is a place surrounded by one sun and one moon, it is called a single world-system (*lokadhātu*).

From one up to a thousand, within these there are a thousand suns and moons, a thousand Sumeru Kings of Mountains, a thousand Four Great Heavenly Kings, a thousand Trāyastriṃśa heavens, a thousand Yāma heavens, a thousand Tuṣita heavens, a thousand Nirmāṇarati heavens, a thousand Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens, a thousand Brahmā-purohita heavens, and a thousand Brahmakāyika heavens."
In this place, the Great Brahmā King is the sovereign of a thousand worlds; he rules with mastery, is not dependent on others, and knows how to accomplish the affairs of others.
Because his first dhyāna is of the highest grade, he attains such sovereignty.
The Great Brahmā King dwells in this place and is thus called the foremost. Ānanda!

This realm governed by Brahmā contains four thousand great continents, four thousand great trees, four thousand great dragon palaces, and the dwelling places of four thousand garuḍa kings; it includes seven thousand great rivers, nine thousand great mountains, eight thousand great forests, eight thousand great hells, one thousand hells of Yama, two thousand great oceans, and sixteen thousand hell-gardens. This is called a small chiliocosm.
Again, a thousand times that is called a medium chiliocosm.
Again, a thousand times that is called a great trichiliocosm, Ānanda!
If the Tathāgata intends to illuminate and intends to speak, the light of his radiance fills this great trichiliocosm;
all beings simultaneously understand the phrases of the Dharma he teaches.

If he further wishes to transcend the great trichiliocosm according to the Tathāgata’s intention, none among the sentient beings therein shall fail to see or hear him emitting light and preaching the Dharma. Ānanda!

If the Tathāgata wishes to emit light and preach the Dharma, he sits in the Brahma-abode of Akaniṣṭha Heaven; whether it be a great trichiliocosm or beyond a great trichiliocosm, his light shines everywhere, and he preaches the words and meanings of the Dharma with the eightfold Brahma-voice, so that all may fully understand and comprehend them.

Ānanda! Regarding this radiance of the Tathāgata and the sound of his preaching of the Dharma, there is not a single sentient being who does not see it or hear it; at that time, there is no sentient being whose faculties are incomplete.
Ānanda! While the Tathāgata was in the Akaniṣṭha heaven, he uttered these sounds and proclaimed these words and phrases:
"Receive the Buddha's teaching, And arouse respectful, right diligence."
Abiding in the cultivation of contemplation, one escapes the perils of the three realms of existence and destroys the army of the King of Death, as an elephant breaks through a reed hut.
If one dwells with heedfulness within the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya, [one shall attain liberation].
"This person abandons birth and death, even unto the ultimate end of suffering.

At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I have now obtained rare offerings; I have now well attained rare benefit; I have gained a Great Teacher endowed with supernormal powers and vast majesty.
At that time, the one named Udāyin, whose original name was Viśuddhanāman, was in the great assembly, not far from the Buddha.
Then the bhikṣu Udāyin said to Ānanda:
"If your Great Teacher possesses all majestic virtues and great supernormal powers, what have you attained?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣu Udāyin:
"Do not harbor thoughts that contradict Ānanda’s intention.

Had I not previously prophesied that Ānanda would attain the fruit of Arhatship in this very life, then by the karmic retribution born of this faith, he would have become the king of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven thirty-six times, and likewise the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven thirty-six times; how much more so would he have become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, a Kṣatriya king consecrated with the royal office, or even a king over the four continents?"
"Udāyin! Regarding the bhikṣu Ānanda, I have already given him a prediction in the past.
I have said that among the sentient beings within the desire realm, those born from water are most numerous, while those born from earth are few."
Those born in that land are mostly in the realm of animals, while those in the human realm are few.
Among those in the human realm, those who break the precepts are many, while those who uphold the precepts are few.
Among those who uphold the precepts, ordinary worldlings are many and noble disciples are few.
Among noble disciples, those still in training are many and those beyond training are few.
Among those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), those liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) are many, while those liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*) are few.
Such Arhats liberated at any time are rare in the world; I have prophesied that Ānanda shall attain this state.
There are certain non-Buddhists who assert:
"This great earth-element moves constantly without ceasing.
To this statement, one should respond:
"This is not so. If it were truly as you say, then when a person throws something forward, the object should fall behind.
Furthermore, the various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) speak thus:
Regarding the statement, "This great earth-element constantly falls downward," one should answer: "This is not so."
"If it were truly so, then like an object thrown upward, it should not reach the ground.
Furthermore, the various non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthikas) say this:
"The sun, moon, and stars remain fixed and do not move; it is the great earth itself that rotates, which people mistakenly perceive as the sky turning."
To this, one should reply: "This is not so.
If it were as you say, the arrow would not reach the target."
Furthermore, when various non-Buddhists (tīrthika) assert:
"The great earth is constantly floating, coming and going with the wind," one should answer as follows:
"This is not so. If it were truly thus, the earth would always tremble together [with the mountains].
If it were not so, what would be the characteristic of the earth?"
"The earth abides immovably.
This meaning has been taught by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Thus have I heard.
Chapter Two: Jambudvīpa. The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus!
There is a tree named Jambu; because of this tree, the name of this continent is established as Jambudvīpa."
This tree grows on the northern edge of Jambudvīpa, on the southern bank of the Narmadā River.
The base of the tree stands precisely at the center of the continent; from the center of the tree's trunk to either the eastern or western corner is one thousand yojanas.

This tree grows to full maturity, possessing a beautiful form; its branches and leaves overlap one another, being dense, thick, and abundant with foliage. It remains for a long time without withering, such that no wind or rain can penetrate it.
"O Bhikṣus!
It is as if a master garland-maker were to fashion a flower garland and an ear ornament; such is the lovely form of that tree.
At its summit it is like a floral canopy, with successive layers covering one another, reaching a height of one hundred yojanas."
The lower trunk is vast and straight, entirely free of knots or joints; it is only after fifty yojanas that branches and twigs appear.
The diameter of the tree’s trunk is five yojanas, and its circumference is fifteen yojanas.
Each individual branch extends horizontally for fifty yojanas; the distance between them spans one hundred yojanas, and their circumference is three hundred yojanas.
When the fruit ripens, its sweetness is beyond compare, like fine honey; its flavor is so sweet that one can never tire of it—such is the taste of the fruit.
The fruit is as large as a basin, and its seed is about the size of a jambu fruit found in the world.
Upon it dwell two birds, shaped like great palace monkeys or sixty-year-old elephants; these two birds and beasts constantly eat its fruit.
The fruits on the eastern branch mostly fall upon the land of Jambudvīpa, while few fall into the water;
the fruits on the western branch mostly fall upon the land of Jambudvīpa, while few fall into the water;
the fruits on the southern branch all fall upon the land of Jambudvīpa.
The fruits from the northern branches all fall into the river and are eaten by fish.
The roots of the tree are entirely covered with golden sand; during the spring rains, they do not leak or become damp; in summer, it is not hot; and in winter, there is no wind or cold.
"There are gandharvas and yakṣas who dwell beneath this tree.
How is such a matter known?
Formerly, in the city of Rājagṛha, there were two bhikṣus who possessed supernatural powers and were friends with one another.
Having heard from the Buddha’s own mouth that the characteristics of the Jambū tree were such as these, the two bhikṣus said to one another:
"We should go to see that Jambū tree."
Each saying, "I shall go," they proceeded to the tree.
Seeing that the fruits were ripe and had fallen to the ground, breaking of their own accord, one bhikṣu inserted his hand through a hole in the stalk until it reached his forearm;

yet even his longest finger did not reach the pit. As he pulled his hand out, it was stained by the fruit, his arm and hand becoming entirely red, just like those in the world who are defiled by the juice of precious red sandalwood.
The fragrance of those fruits was able to captivate the hearts of people.
At that time, as a bhikṣu smelled the scent of the fruit, a second bhikṣu asked him,
"Do you wish to eat it?"
“Elder! I do not delight in eating.
This matter is rare and inconceivable.”
This freedom from the fetter of desire is most vast and great. Why is this?
If a person who has not yet abandoned desire smells such a fragrance, their mental vapors will immediately arise and they will fall into madness.
"There are certain non-Buddhist practitioners who have attained freedom from desire; if they smell this fragrance, they will fall away from their state of detachment.
These two bhikṣus returned to Rājagṛha and recounted the matter as described above.

At that time, there was a man named Dīrghajaṅgha (Long Shanks), who was originally of royal lineage and belonged to the Kauṇḍinya clan. He had attained supernatural powers as the karmic fruit of his past deeds.
This man possessed such majestic and divine features that when he walked upon water, his front foot had not yet sunk before his back foot had already shifted;
when he walked upon grass, although the grass had not yet been crushed, he was able to take his next step.
When walking upon tree leaves, even before the leaves have bent down, his hind foot has already passed over them; the places trodden by his shoes present no difficulty whatsoever.
This person with long calves heard from the Buddha that the Jambū trees are such and such.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If I were to go now, would I reach the Jambū tree?"
He replied,
“I have arrived.
The man prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and facing directly north, set out from there.
The mountain ranges that must be crossed are:

first, the Lesser Black Mountain; second, the Greater Black Mountain; third, the Mountain of Many Yak-cows; fourth, the Mountain of Sunlight; fifth, the Silver Mountain; sixth, the Fragrant Water Mountain; and seventh, the Golden Rim Mountain.
This man ascended the summit of Mount Suvarṇapārśva, turned his face northward, and gazing far into the distance with his body erect, saw only darkness; terrified, he turned back.
The Buddha asked him, "Did you reach the Jambū tree?"
He replied, "It has not reached it.
The Buddha asked:
"What do you see? The man replied,
"I see only darkness."
The Buddha said,
"This dark-colored [mass] is the Jambu tree.
The man prostrated again at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and proceeded further north, crossing seven great mountains.
The first is named Cūḍakāra, the second Mahākāra, the third Ghoṣaṇa Mountain, the fourth Śūra Mountain, the fifth Kīla Mountain, the sixth Gandha Mountain, and the seventh Subhājika Mountain.
Furthermore, he crossed over six great kingdoms:
first, the kingdom of Kuru; second, the kingdom of Kaurava; third, the kingdom of Videha; fourth, the kingdom of Mahāvideha; fifth, the kingdom of Uttaramantra; and sixth, the kingdom of Sāṭimbara.
These are called the six great lands.
Furthermore, one crosses seven great groves of trees; between these groves there are rivers, which one must cross.
One also crosses the Āmalaka grove and the Harītakī grove, up to the southern branch of the Jambū tree in Jambudvīpa.
Moving from the southern branch, he proceeded to the northern branch of the tree.
Looking down, he observed that the water below was different from the usual water; it was exceptionally clear and pure, transparent through to the bottom with no obstructions whatsoever.
Having observed this, the person reflects:
"Will my supernormal powers be accomplished here?
Thereupon, he steps upon the water with his feet and grasps a tree branch with his hands; yet his feet sink into the water like stones, and thus he does not accomplish these supernormal powers.

Why is this so? Because this water is the lightest and most subtle; if that water were poured into this mountain stream, it would float upon the surface like ghee or oil, but if this water were poured into that water, it would sink like a stone.
This person took a fruit from a Jambu tree and returned to Rājagṛha to present it to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha accepted the fruit, broke it into many pieces, and distributed them to the great assembly; the juice of the fruit stained the Buddha’s hand.
At that time, the Buddha struck the mountain rock with this hand; to this day it remains red just as it was then, neither damp nor dry, with the imprint of the palm clearly visible.
Because he previously divided the fruit into pieces, this rock was named Pippala Rock (the "Piece-by-Piece" Rock).
At that time, the Buddha transformed himself into Uruvilvā Kāśyapa and took a fruit from this Jambū tree, sending it to Kāśyapa, saying: "Kāśyapa!..."
"Eat this fruit," [the Buddha said].
Kāśyapa asked the Buddha,
"Great Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"How can such fruit be obtained?
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"This tree is called Jambu; this fruit is obtained from that tree."
Kāśyapa said, “I cannot eat these fruits; Śramaṇa, simply take them for yourself.
At that time, various devas again sent jambu-tree fruits as offerings to the Buddha, whether he was in Śrāvastī, Rājagṛha, or the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
After the Buddha had accepted [the offering], he distributed it as alms to the great assembly.
Furthermore, other bhikṣus who had resided in Jambudvīpa returned to this land and recounted it.
The bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana also once resided there; having returned here, he related it in turn to the bhikṣus.
By these causes and conditions, this matter may be understood.
Chapter Three: The Six Great Kingdoms. Outside the Jambū tree there are two groves, shaped like half-moons, which encircle this tree.
Within it is a grove named Harītakī, and outside it is one named Āmalaka.
When the fruit of the Āmalaka ripens, its flavor is most excellent; it is neither pungent nor bitter, like fine honey.
The fruit is shaped like a vessel with a capacity of two *shu*; its seed is like the seed of a natural *āmalaka* fruit.
As for the *harītakī* fruit, when its seeds ripen, its flavor is most exquisite—neither pungent nor bitter, like fine honey.
The fruits are twice as large as those before, and their kernels are likewise so.
To the south of the Āmalaka forest, there are another seven forests, with seven rivers interspersed between them.

The forest furthest to the north is named Āmra; the next is named Jambu; the third is named Sāla; the fourth is named Tāla; the fifth is named Manuṣya-vana (Human Forest); the sixth is named Dāḍima-vana (Pomegranate Forest); and the seventh is named Kapiṭtha-vana.
When the seeds of these various fruits ripen, they are neither pungent nor bitter, but as sweet as honey.
Among the people in this grove, the shape of their bodies resembles that of humans; they are like the noble kṣatriya lineage of Jambudvīpa, and their clan name is Kauri.
If a man is sixteen years old and a woman is fifteen years old, they are fully adorned and appear as if they were about to be married;
such are the lovely forest fruits for these people.
The shape of its stem is like a human topknot.
When those who have not yet abandoned desire see this fruit, they immediately give rise to thoughts of attachment.
Even those among the various non-Buddhists who have abandoned desire will, upon seeing this fruit, fall away from their meditative concentration, and the mind of desire will arise once more.
When its fruit ripens, only birds compete to eat it.
What remains after the birds have eaten falls scattered upon the ground like a śītavana cemetery, utterly loathsome.
When those who have regressed from meditative concentration see these signs, they develop a profound sense of weary detachment and regain their original state of concentration.
These two forests are fifty yojanas wide and extend east and west to the sea.
Each of these rivers is fifty yojanas wide and flows from east to west to reach the ocean.
Forests and rivers alternate and intermingle across the land of Jambudvīpa;
together, they cover seven hundred yojanas.

To the south of the Kīṭāda Forest, there are six great kingdoms. The southernmost kingdom is named Go-lo (Gaula); the next is named Ku-la-po (Kulapa); the third is named Pi-ti-ho (Videha); the fourth is named Mo-ho-pi-ti-ho (Mahāvideha); the fifth is named Yü-t'o-lo-man-to (Uttaramantra); and the northernmost is named She-hsi-mo-lo-ye (Śikhimālaya).
Within these six kingdoms, the people are all upright and virtuous; they uphold the ten wholesome dharmas, personally refraining from killing and not instructing others to kill.
When a beast is about to die, it goes of its own accord to where people are; once it has died, they then consume its flesh.
In this place, there are the greatest number of wild oxen (*gavaya*); their hair-tufts and tails are used to thatch houses.
The land produces wheat without the need for plowing or cultivation; when this wheat forms grains, they are devoid of husks or chaff.
The people of that country grind and steam it to make rice;
this wheat-rice has a sweet and pleasant flavor, like fine honey.
How is this known?
In the distant past, there was a king who renounced the household life; his queen also renounced the world, as did the royal preceptor, a brahmin.
Having all gone forth, they separated from one another and entered the mountains to study the Way.
At one time, when the king’s consort had her menses and they were purified, she went to the king’s presence to see him and addressed him, saying:
“Great King!”
"I am currently in my menses; moreover, people of antiquity have held children in high esteem.
Although the King wished to reject her and did not comply with the Queen's wishes, he reflected that the matter was grave and feared it might be improper, and so they eventually united in harmony.
Then there were two children of great merit, a son and a daughter, who both entered the womb at the same time.

Having abandoned the king and departed, after some time had passed, her belly grew large; traveling from village to village, then to district and county, and eventually through the various provinces, everyone reviled her, saying:
"This woman has no heart for the Way; she has left the household life and broken the precepts."
Upon hearing these words, the queen felt deep remorse and regret.
At that time, the state preceptor, a great brahmin who had already become a rishi and attained the five supernormal powers, was dwelling in dependence upon a certain mountain forest.
At that time, when the queen heard that the brahmin was dwelling on that mountain, she went there to seek him out.
Having seen the teacher, she asked him,
"Who caused this pregnancy?"
The queen replied, "This was done by the king.
At that time, the rishi, mindful of the king’s past kindness, built a leaf hut for him in another location and spoke to the queen:
"Stay here. I shall now gather tree roots and fruits to provide for you.
Following these words, the Queen Mother remained there.
Thereupon, the rishi gathered tree roots and fruits according to the Dharma to provide for the consort.
When her months of pregnancy were complete, she gave birth to two children, one male and one female.
When they had reached weaning age, he drove out the consort, saying: "Depart now;
I shall provide for my two children with whatever roots and fruits I obtain."
The queen abandoned her two sons and departed according to his words.
The rishi subsequently gathered roots and fruits to nourish and raise the children.

When the two boys had grown somewhat and reached the stage of conscious awareness, the rishi tested them by giving them a mixture of ripe and unripe fruits; thereupon, the two boys were able to distinguish between them on their own, eating the ripe ones and discarding the unripe ones.
The seer reflected thus:
"This child’s body has already grown large, and his mind has reached the stage of consciousness; he is now able to distinguish between the ripeness of fruits.
In which kingdom should I establish him, so that he may dwell in abundance, joy, and peace?"

By means of his five supernatural powers, he saw this field of barley; immediately employing his spiritual power, he took the two young children, flew through the air, and placed them upon that ground.
The teacher instructed the boy,
saying, "This grass is called wheat. Thereupon,
the rishi himself harvested it, ground it into flour for food, and provided various instructions.
“From this day forward, you should rely upon this Dharma as your sustenance.
Abiding within this, do not give rise to sorrow or distress; I shall come to visit and look after you from time to time.”
These two children remained there, and from time to time, the rishi went to visit them.

As the two children grew with the passing months and years, their male and female organs respectively matured; they subsequently became husband and wife, and as their descendants multiplied, they divided into six kingdoms.
At that time, having already studied the Way, the Great King relinquished his human body and was reborn in the heavens.
After relinquishing his celestial body, he again received a human body.
Having received a human body, he followed the unsurpassed True Dharma as taught by the Buddha, left the household life to study the Way, and attained the six kinds of unimpeded supernormal powers.
By means of the six supernormal powers, he observed his own past lives and saw six great kingdoms, whereupon he reflected:
"These six great kingdoms are all my descendants."
Out of compassion for the people of those six countries, he went there to beg for alms and returned with barley rice.
Without asking the other bhikṣus, he ate it alone before the others had eaten.
At that time, the bhikṣus called out the name of this bhikṣu and reviled him greatly, saying:
"O Elder! You are exceedingly stingy and envious!"
"Hey! You wicked man, having obtained this rice porridge, you eat it all by yourself without asking the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣu replied:
"I do not now refuse to give alms to you out of envy. Why is this?
Such food and drink cannot be consumed by those who have not yet abandoned desire."
At that time, the bhikṣu washed the bowl three times and discarded the water twice; then, taking a small portion of the final rinse, he offered it to the other bhikṣus.
In all of Jambudvīpa, there was not a single flavor equal to this one.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu explained to the bhikṣus the sequence of causes and conditions regarding the flavors of this food:
"Those six great kingdoms were originally my own descendants; therefore, for the sake of benefiting the people of those lands, I go there to beg for alms."
Other bhikṣus went there to beg for alms, and Mahāmaudgalyāyana also went to beg for alms.
The Blessed One, the World-Honored One, explained to the bhikṣus the causal conditions regarding the sequence of these six kingdoms; thus, one comes to know the affairs of the six great nations.
The Chapter on the Six Great Kingdoms is concluded.

4. The Chapter on Yakṣa Deities. Fourth: At that time, within Jambudvīpa there were two pairs of mountain ranges; to the south of the Ganges was the mountain named Sataśīrṣa, and to the north of the Ganges was the mountain named Himavat.
Among the Sata-karī mountains, this mountain range is the greatest;
its six peaks are named: first, Sajja; second, Pinha; third, Mace; fourth, Acyava; fifth, Antara-karī; and sixth, Pāriyātra.
Among the mountains of Himavat, this mountain range is the greatest:
first is named Cūḍakāra, second Mahākā, third Ghoṇa, fourth Śūrpa-ketu, fifth Kīla, sixth Gandhamādana, and seventh Suparṇabhava.
If all the deities dwelling on the southern mountains are called the Satakr̥ti deities;
if they dwell on the northern mountains, they are all called the Haimavata deities.
This deity Sātāgira presides over all the deities south of the river, and is therefore called a king;
this deity Haimavata presides over all the deities north of the river, and is therefore called a king.
How is this known?
There was a divine king named Haimavata who dwelt on Mount Haimavata.
This divine king was the eldest of all, having reached the pinnacle of age, and he was afflicted by a grave and painful illness.
When this deity was approaching death, he had a crown prince named Himavanta. He summoned him and instructed him, saying to his son:

"My son, I have already heard that among the yakṣas from of old, there is one who is most venerable. He has seen past Buddhas and once encountered Kāśyapa Buddha, who told him that Śākyamuni Buddha would soon appear in the world."
"Based on the signs I perceive and the causal conditions of my views regarding 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' it will not be long before Śākyamuni Buddha descends.
Father, if I should pass away in the interim and fail to reach the Buddha, you must certainly go so that he may see the Buddha; if you see the Buddha, it will surely bring great benefit."
The Prince asked,
"How may I know that a Buddha has appeared in the world?
His father replied to his son:
“Since a treasure never before seen has appeared within your dwelling, you should know that at this time a Tathāgata has appeared in the world.
Furthermore, there is a divine king named Sātāgira who dwells within the borders of the kingdom of Magadha; you should become friends with him and together establish a vow:
‘In whatever place either of us resides, if a rare and extraordinary treasure should appear, we shall not fail to inform one another.’”
At that time, after the father king had thus instructed his son, he passed away.
Thereupon, the prince made offerings to his father’s remains and, bearing in mind the weighty bequest of his father, crossed the river to seek out the divine king Śatagiri.
Having arrived at the abode of the deity, they conversed face-to-face, exchanging words with mutual courtesy and respect, and sat together in one place.
The deity Haimavata addressed King Sādhīra, saying: "My Lord!
My father spoke these words as mentioned above when he was on the verge of death, and thereupon passed away.
For this reason, I now tell you of this matter:
if extraordinary treasures appear within your house, you must certainly inform me.
Sājīrī replied, "So it is, so it is. Thereupon,
having both made their vows, the two returned to their respective abodes.
Later, a miraculous treasure appeared in the palace of King Haimavata: a thousand-petaled lotus, as large as a chariot wheel, with petals of gold and a stem of various jewels.
At that time, there was a deity who, seeing these lotuses, hurried to inform the king:
"Does Your Majesty not know?
These jewels are rare and extraordinary, never before seen in this world; they have now appeared."
There are lotus flowers as large as chariot wheels, with petals of pure gold and stalks of various jewels.
These are celestial objects; I pray that Your Majesty will go to behold them.

At that time, having heard these words, the divine king went to the site of the pond and saw this lotus flower, complete with a thousand petals, as large as a chariot wheel, composed of various jewels, and wonderfully adorned.
Having seen this, his heart was filled with wonder and alarm, and the hairs on his body all stood on end.
He descended into the pond, joined his palms in reverence, prostrated three times, and circumambulated it three times.
He reflected thus:
"In the past, I encountered a virtuous friend who instructed me, saying:
'If there be any extraordinary treasure in the place where you dwell, you must send word to inform me.'"
Thereupon, he dispatched a messenger to inform the divine king Sātāgira, saying: "Lord!
A rare treasure has now appeared at my dwelling place."
He related the matter of the Jewel Sign in detail:
"You should now come with me to behold it.

At that time, the World-Honored One had already appeared in the world; the True Dharma had been proclaimed, which is exclusively tranquil; and he was now approaching parinirvāṇa, proceeding toward Bodhi according to the teachings of the Sugata.
At that time, King Sotthiyo awoke and recalled this matter, reflecting thus:
"In the past, I had a good friend who came and told me:
'The place where you dwell is where the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, attained the Way.'"

"If a Buddha has already appeared, you should inform me. This was what he desired; therefore, I ought to inform him. King Satāgirī then dispatched a messenger, saying to that king: [The messenger said: "O Great King, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, one endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Bhagavān, has appeared in the world. He dwells in the city of Kapilavastu, in the Śākya realm, at the Nyagrodha Park. O Great King, this is the time; this is the occasion. You should go yourself to pay homage to that Blessed One. The king replied: "I am unable to go myself. However, I shall send my son, Prince Mahādeva, to go and pay homage to that Blessed One. The messenger returned and informed King Satāgirī: "O Great King, the king of the Śākyas has sent his son, Prince Mahādeva, to go and pay homage to that Blessed One. King Satāgirī then sent a messenger to say to Prince Mahādeva: "O Prince, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha... [as above] ...has appeared in the world. He dwells in the city of Kapilavastu, in the Śākya realm, at the Nyagrodha Park. O Prince, this is the time; this is the occasion. You should go yourself to pay homage to that Blessed One. The prince replied: "I am unable to go myself. However, I shall send my younger brother, Prince Mahāsudarśana, to go and pay homage to that Blessed One. The messenger returned and informed King Satāgirī: "O Great King, Prince Mahādeva has sent his younger brother, Prince Mahāsudarśana, to go and pay homage to that Blessed One. He dwells in the city of Kapilavastu, in the Śākya realm, at the Nyagrodha Park. O Prince, this is the time; this is the occasion. You should go yourself to pay homage to that Blessed One. The messenger returned and informed King Satāgirī: "O Great King, Prince Sudarśana has sent his younger brother, Prince Ānanda, to go and pay homage to that Blessed One. King Satāgirī then sent a messenger to say to Prince Ānanda: "O Prince, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha... [as above] ...has appeared in the world. He dwells in the city of Kapilavastu, in the Śākya realm, at the Nyagrodha Park. O Prince, this is the time; this is the occasion. You should go yourself to pay homage to that Blessed One. The prince replied: "I am able to go myself. The messenger returned and informed King Satāgirī: "O Great King, Prince Ānanda has said, 'I am able to go myself. King Satāgirī then sent a messenger to say to Prince Ānanda: "O Prince, please go yourself to pay homage to that Blessed One. The prince then set out for the city of Kapilavastu. On the way, he met the Elder Mahākāśyapa. Seeing him, the prince asked: "Venerable Sir, where are you going? The Elder replied: "Prince, I am going to the city of Kapilavastu to see the Blessed One. The prince said: "Venerable Sir, please wait for a moment while I return to inform my parents. Having received the Elder's permission, he went back to inform his parents. His father said: "Son, you may go yourself to pay homage to that Blessed One. The prince then departed from the city of Rājagṛha and arrived at the city of Kapilavastu. At that time, the Blessed One was dwelling in the Nyagrodha Park, surrounded by a great assembly of monks. The prince approached the Blessed One, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and sat down to one side. Then the Blessed One, knowing the prince’s thoughts, preached the Dharma to him, exhorting, inspiring, and delighting him. Having heard the Dharma, the prince attained the fruit of stream-entry. He then rose from his seat, paid homage at the Blessed One’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. He went to his parents and said: "Father and Mother, I have seen the Blessed One. I have heard the Dharma and attained the fruit of stream-entry. Father and Mother, please go yourselves to pay homage to that Blessed One. His parents replied: "Son, we are old and infirm. We are unable to go ourselves. However, we shall send our daughter-in-law, Queen Mṛgajā, to go and pay homage to that Blessed One. The prince returned and informed the Elder Mahākāśyapa: "Venerable Sir, my parents have said, 'We are old and infirm. We are unable to go ourselves. However, we shall send our daughter-in-law, Queen Mṛgajā, to go and pay homage to that Blessed One. Venerable Sir, please wait for a moment while I return to inform her. Having received the Elder's permission, he went back to inform Queen Mṛgajā: "Mother, I have seen the Blessed One. I have heard the Dharma and attained the fruit of stream-entry. Mother, please go yourself to pay homage to that Blessed One. The queen replied: "Son, I am unable to go myself. However, I shall send my daughter-in-law, Queen Padumāvatī, to go and pay homage to that Blessed One. The prince returned and informed the Elder Mahākāśyapa: "Venerable Sir, my mother-in-law has said, 'I am unable to go myself. However, I shall send my daughter-in-law, Queen Padumāvatī, to go and pay homage to that Blessed One. Venerable Sir, please wait for a moment while I return to inform her. Mother, please go yourself to pay homage to that Blessed One. The queen replied: "Son, I am unable to go myself. However, I shall send my daughter-in-law, Queen Amitā, to go and pay homage to that Blessed One. The prince returned and informed the Elder Mahākāśyapa: "Venerable Sir, my mother-in-law has said, 'I am unable to go myself. However, I shall send my daughter-in-law, Queen Amitā, to go and pay homage to that Blessed One. Venerable Sir, please wait for a moment while I return to inform her. Having received the Elder's permission, he went back to inform Queen Amitā: "Mother, I have seen the Blessed One. I have heard the Dharma and attained the fruit of stream-entry. Mother, please go yourself to pay homage to that Blessed One. The queen replied: "Son, I
“Lord! What benefit does a single lotus flower provide?
And what benefit do even a hundred or a thousand provide?”
Within my land, there has never before been such a treasure, yet now it has appeared.
What is called this treasure?
It is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who has now emerged in the world.
"You should now come and serve this treasure together with me.

On the fifteenth day of the ninth month, during the time of the *poṣadha*, Hemavata was surrounded by five hundred deities; taking various lotus flowers, he traveled through the air facing south toward King Sātāgira.
That king, moreover, leading a retinue of five hundred deities and surrounded by them, came to welcome this king on the southern bank of the Ganges, where they gathered together.
Having met one another, King Haimavata spoke a verse, asking those deities:
“Today is the fifteenth day of purity, The time when the Four Kings assemble.”
"Whom do we serve as our teacher?
You believe in the Arhat.
At that time, King Satāgira replied with a verse:
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, dwelt in the city of Magadha;
for the sake of extinguishing all suffering, he taught the Dharma of omniscience:
"All sufferings and the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and its non-arising."
The eightfold path leading to the cessation of suffering, free from affliction and directed toward Nirvana—
therefore you and I should attend upon such a person;
none can compare to him, for this is my faith in Rāhula.
At that time, having heard these verses, Haimavata was greatly terrified; the hair on his body stood on end, and he harbored doubts and remained unconvinced.
He deliberated three times and said: "My Lord!..."
"You have now said that the World-Honored One has appeared in the world? He replied,
"Lord Prefect!"
"I say that the Buddha Jewel has appeared in the world.
The second and third questions and answers were likewise.

At that time, the King of Spirits of the Northern Mountain immediately contemplated, according to his power, the four dharmas of the Buddhas' conduct, deportment, majestic bearing, and spheres of activity, and questioned the King of Spirits of the Southern Mountain, speaking in verse as he asked:
"Does the Buddha’s mind dwell in peace toward sentient beings?
Have the two thoughts of hatred and attachment already been extinguished?
At that time, the Spirit-King of the Southern Mountains replied in verse:
“The Buddha-mind toward sentient beings Is truly established;
The two thoughts of hatred and love Are extinguished forever without remainder.
The King of the Northern Mountains repeated his verse and asked:
“Does the Buddha speak falsely?
Does he utter words that cause distress to others?
Does he engage in divisive speech?”
"Is there any speech that is meaningless?
The King of the Southern Mountains replied in verse:
"The Buddha does not speak false words, Nor does he utter harsh or bitter speech."
"I do not speak divisive words; I speak words that accord with the true measure of reality.
The King of the Northern Mountains repeated his verse and asked:
"Does the Buddha not steal from others?"
Do you not harm the lives of others?
Are you far removed from negligence?
Do you not impair meditative concentration?
The divine king of the Southern Mountains replied with a verse:
“The Buddha does not steal the wealth of others; Therefore, he protects the lives of others.
He remains far removed from all negligence And does not harm profound meditative concentration.”
The King of the Northern Mountains again asked in verse:
“The Buddha is free from attachment and desire; Is his mind pure and without turbidity?
Having crossed over the stream of ignorance, Has he attained the pure Dharma-eye?”
The King of the Southern Mountains replied:
“Unattached to the dust of desire, his mind-ground is most pure;
having transcended ignorance, he has attained the pure eye regarding all phenomena.”
The King of the Northern Mountains again asked:
"Is the Buddha’s wisdom complete?
Is the Dharma pure?"
"Have the four floods been severed?
Has rebirth been brought to an end?
The King of the Southern Mountains replied again:
“The Buddha’s insight is fully perfected; The Dharma-foot is long purified.
The four currents have been severed and extinguished; Therefore, there is no further rebirth.
At that time, having heard this, the King of the Northern Mountain Devas felt joy arise in his heart and spoke a verse in praise:
“The wise one’s intention is fulfilled; all tasks are already accomplished.
With body and speech purified, he praises the one endowed with clarity and sufficiency.
The King of the Southern Mountains, his heart and mouth filled with joy, spoke this verse in praise:
“The Buddha’s mind is tranquil and pure; his body and speech can benefit others.
With the ten powers, there is none equal to him; I now rejoice in your praise.
The wise one has accomplished his mind, as well as his physical and vocal actions.”
Endowed with the feet of clear knowledge,
I shall go with you to behold it.
Today is the fifteenth day of the *poṣadha*, the time when the Four Great Kings patrol the world.
"With hearts liberated and free from attachment, I shall prostrate together with you.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying beneath the Nyagrodha tree in Rājagṛha; these two divine kings, surrounded by a thousand deities, went to where the Buddha was.

Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Then the King of the Northern Mountain asked in verse:
"Able to speak and able to practice, Crossing the stream forever free from outflows,
Walking alone like a lion, The Buddha is unstained by worldly dharmas."
Having crossed to the further shore of all phenomena, you have come with earnest intent to ask: "Where do sentient beings arise?
Where do they repeatedly practice existence?"
"What is it that you grasp? Where do you suffer?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the divine king Haimavata in verse:
"Sentient beings are born into the six sense bases; repeatedly they practice the six sense bases;
grasping at these six kinds of dharmas, they undergo suffering and affliction within the six sense bases.
Thus the King of the Northern Mountains repeated his verse and questioned the Buddha.
“What is this grasping that one takes up, which causes sentient beings to suffer?
I pray you answer my question on renunciation: how is one liberated from suffering?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the divine king Haimavata in verse:
“There are five objects of the world; I say the mind is the sixth.
By becoming free from desire and attachment toward them, one is liberated from such suffering.
When sentient beings attain deliverance, I have already explained it according to the measure of reality.”
Since you have now asked this question, I shall therefore answer concerning renunciation.
The King of the Northern Mountains again addressed the Buddha in verse:
“Who is able to cross the swift current, never wearying day or night?”
"Without bottom and without a foothold, who would not sink into such depths?
Then the World-Honored One replied to the divine king Haimavata in verse:
"Always maintaining pure precepts, With diligence and an undistracted mind,"
Discerning internal right mindfulness, which is difficult to master even through the perfection of wisdom;
perceiving desire as being without desire, subduing and extinguishing the fetters of form,
and forever eradicating the craving for existence— such a person shall never sink.
At that time, the two mountain kings, the Southern and the Northern, simultaneously spoke these verses in praise of the Buddha:
"We have now seen him well; Welcome, O Well-Come One, you who are now so luminous!
We behold the Perfectly Awakened One, Who proclaims the path of ambrosia."
Named "Without Extinction," he perceives the true meaning; Always delighting in inquiry and debate, he is free from attachment.
Having reached the limit of wisdom, he is fully liberated; He walks the noble path, a great seer.
"More than a thousand yakṣas, whose fame and majestic power are renowned, have all taken refuge in the Buddha; he is my unsurpassed teacher.
These three yakṣas sat in a triangular formation, and for this reason, the road is named "The Rhombus" (Lingjiao) to this day.
At that time, the World-Honored One dwelt beneath a tree; therefore, this tree is named Gūḍhaka-gupta.
From these two matters concerning the yakṣas, one knows of the two mountains to the south and north.
The *Yakṣadeva-parivarta* is concluded.
*Lishi apitan lun* (Treatise on the Abhidharma of the Establishment of the World), Fascicle One.
*Buddhabhāṣita-lishi-apitan-lun* (The Treatise on the Abhidharma of the Establishment of the World Spoken by the Buddha), Fascicle Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha from Western India.
Chapter Five: The Elephant King Laṭṭhikāra. Chapter Five: The Elephant King Laṭṭhikāra.
Mount Cūḷakāla is one and a half *gavyūti* in height; its breadth is likewise, and its circumference is the same.
Mount Mahākāla is three *gavyūta* high, and its breadth and middle [circumference] are likewise.
Mount Gohana is one and a half *yojana* high, and its breadth and middle [circumference] are likewise as well.
Mount Āṣāḍha is three yojanas high, and its width and intermediate dimensions are likewise the same.
Mount Kīlapa is six yojanas high, and its width and intermediate dimensions are likewise the same.
Mount Gandhamādana is twelve yojanas high, and its width and intermediate dimensions are likewise the same.
Mount Vipula is twenty-four yojanas high, and its width and intermediate dimensions are likewise the same.
On Mount Uṣṇīṣa-parvata, during the autumn months when the sky is clear and rainless, it radiates the most brilliant light.
Furthermore, there are people dwelling near the Snowy Mountains who, during the four-month highland assembly, call out to one another and go to gaze upon the heavens.
Upon reaching the summit of Mount Mahākāla, they looked northward and saw from afar that mountain, its radiance shining brilliantly;
thereupon they said to one another, "This is Mount Sumeru."
"I have now seen the heavens.

On the northern side of Mount Uṣaṇabhaṃsa, there is a most excellent place, and further there is a great lake named Mandākinī, fifty yojanas long and ten yojanas wide; its waters are pure, cool, sweet, light, and soft, and it is fully provided with lotus roots, stalks, and stems.

The bottom and banks of that pond were all constructed as embankments from bricks made of four treasures—silver, gold, crystal, and lapis lazuli—with silver situated on the outermost layer, surrounding it in successive order.
Wherever it is moistened by the water, it takes on the same color as the jewels.

On the four sides of the pond are four stairways leading down to the bottom of the water, all composed of the four precious substances. From the southeast corner of the pond, one proceeds directly to the mountain; on that mountain is a rock formation named Nanda, fifty yojanas long and ten yojanas wide.

The cliffs are entirely made of lapis lazuli, smooth and lovely, resembling palatial chambers. Their jewel-tones vary, displaying diverse appearances with natural carvings and paintings like those on a northern woolen carpet; among them, humans, beasts, grasses, trees, and plants are all fully represented.
The colors of these cliffs are likewise so.
Just as a person’s earrings are adorned with the seven precious gems, so too are the colors and forms of this ground.

All of it is made of smooth and lovely lapis lazuli, possessing the colors of various jewels; when one’s foot treads upon it, it immediately sinks in, and when the foot is lifted, it returns to its original state, being as soft as a cluster of fine cotton or *tūla* cotton. Thus, the softness of that ground is likewise.
This is the Nanda Rock; when one treads upon it, it sinks to the ankle, and as soon as the foot is lifted, it rises again.
Within it are numerous palaces, some made of gold, some of silver, and others likewise of crystal or lapis lazuli, while some are composed of all four precious substances combined.
All these palaces are the dwellings of the elephant kings and their like.
In the midst of the rocky pools is a most excellent place, where stands the king of trees, Nyagrodha, named Suvyavasthita.
Its roots, stems, branches, and trunk are all fully developed, and its form is lovely to behold.
Its leaves are dense and thick, remaining long without withering and unharmed by wind or rain.
Just as a finely crafted floral garland or various precious earrings, or like a parasol with its layers of canopy overlapping one another, the form of this tree is likewise so.

Each is one yojana high, with branches hanging down like pillars; numbering eight thousand in total, they all extend downward into the earth, and for this reason it is named "Well-Established" (Susthitā).

Outside the southwest corner of the pond is a most excellent place where stands a king of śāla trees named Sudarśana; its roots, trunk, and branches are all fully developed, and its appearance is lovely.

Its leaves are dense and thick, remaining for a long time without withering, and it is impervious to wind and rain; like exquisite flower garlands and various jeweled earrings adorned by the world, or like parasols layered one above another, the form and appearance of that tree are likewise so.
It is one yojana in height; its trunk is thick and straight for half a yojana before branches and leaves appear.
The diameter of this tree’s trunk is five *vyāma*, and its circumference is fifteen *vyāma*; its lateral branches extend four ways, each reaching half a yojana.

Furthermore, outside that tree there was a grove of śāla trees, arranged in high and low tiers in seven concentric rows; their branches and leaves overlapped one another so that from the outside they appeared as a single uniform mass.

Its innermost enclosure of trees has a circumference of thirteen *vyāmas*; in this manner, each successive outer enclosure is reduced by one *vyāma*, until the outermost enclosure of trees has a circumference of seven *vyāmas*.
The innermost enclosure is the highest, and those of the successive outer enclosures gradually decrease in height.

The form and characteristics of that tree were such that its roots, trunk, branches, and twigs were all fully developed; its appearance was lovely, its foliage was dense, it remained long without withering, and it was unassailed by wind or rain. Like exquisite flower garlands and various jeweled earrings adorned in the world, or like parasols layered one above the other, the form and characteristics of that tree were likewise.
When withered leaves and dry branches fall, because the trees are so dense, they drop outside the forest.
The outer perimeter of that forest protrudes on all four sides, resembling gate-houses.

The ground beneath that tree was covered with golden sand, sprinkled with fragrant water, perfumed with various famous incenses, strewn with diverse flowers, and hung with many precious garments beneath the tree.
These sāla flowers and various other blossoms completely covered the ground, making it exceedingly delightful.

The elephant king Lūśagiri constantly dwelt there; his body was pure white, his seven limbs touched the earth, and he was endowed with six tusks. He could manifest transformations at will, possessing great supernatural powers and great majestic virtue.
Each successive tier contained eight thousand elephants:

the first tier consisted of white male elephants; the next, white female elephants; the third, yellow male elephants; the fourth, yellow female elephants; the fifth, red male elephants; the sixth, red female elephants; the seventh, blue male elephants; and the eighth, blue female elephants.
The black male and female elephants outside were not included in the count.
Whenever this elephant king wished to go to the Mandākinī pond to bathe, the black elephants from outside would immediately lead their herds there to guard the paths and the riverbanks.
Having thus provided protection, the elephant king, surrounded by his herd, proceeded to the site of the pond.

The white female elephants surrounded the elephant king as he entered the pond to bathe; they took the water of this pond to wash and rub the king’s body—some came to wash his face, some to wash his ears—and they did likewise for every part of his body.

When the king was bathing, these elephants gathered various kinds of flowers to form floral garlands and presented them to the king; whether as ear-ornaments or as necklaces, these diverse decorations adorned the king’s body.
Having finished bathing, he ascended from the pool to the bank and went beneath a Nyagrodha tree to dry his body.

In the past, at this very spot, a hunter shot and killed an elephant king; it was on account of this that the *Pūrvajanma-sūtra* (Sutra of the Bodhisattva’s Former Births) was extensively expounded therein.
At that time, the elephants entered the pond one after another according to their color to bathe. Having finished bathing, they went beneath the trees and gathered around the elephant king.
The black elephant was the last to enter the water; he pulled up lotus roots, scrubbed them clean, and returned to the base of the tree.

The black male elephant gave it to the black female elephant; the black female elephant gave it to the blue male elephant; the blue male elephant gave it to the blue female elephant; the blue female elephant gave it to the red male elephant; the red male elephant gave it to the red female elephant; the red female elephant gave it to the yellow male elephant; the yellow male elephant gave it to the yellow female elephant; the yellow female elephant gave it to the white male elephant; the white male elephant gave it to the white female elephant; and the white female elephant gave it to the Great Elephant King, so that the Elephant King might eat it.
After the Elephant King had finished eating, he distributed the remaining lotus roots to the other elephants in their proper order, leaving only the black elephant.
If there was not enough for him to eat, he would send the black elephant back to the pond to gather more, ensuring that his needs were fully satisfied.
As for this black elephant, it feeds exclusively in the pond.
When these various elephants have eaten this lotus root, their bodies become composed of seven parts.
If they eat grass, trees, or leaves, they produce excrement and urine.
Whenever these elephants void excrement or urine, they all have the black elephant remove it for them;
the same applies when food is sent to them.
This White Elephant King dwells on Mount Nanda during the four months of the rainy season, and dwells beneath the auspicious tree of the Śāla King during the eight months of spring and winter.

Thereafter, the Elephant King also constantly resided at this Nanda Rock; during the day he would move to stay beneath the Sāla king tree named Sudarśana, and after bathing, at the time of eating, he was always beneath the Nyagrodha tree.
How is this known?
Formerly, the Venerable Śāriputra, who was of great wisdom and lived a pure life, suffered from a wind-related ailment.
A physician said to him:
“Venerable One!
This lotus root can cure this illness.
At that time, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana, who possessed the life of purity and supernormal powers, had already seen this lotus root in the past.
Then this Venerable One spoke these words:
"I shall go, take this lotus root, and bring it here.
Maudgalyāyana immediately traveled by means of his supernormal powers to the edge of the Golden Mountain and reflected thus:
"This elephant king possesses great supernatural powers, great majestic virtue, and a mind of arrogance.
Therefore, he resolved to cause the elephant king to be struck with terror, and immediately manifested himself as being as tall and large as the elephant's body.

Maudgalyāyana transformed himself into a great elephant twice the size of that one, and further manifested a retinue of elephants, each with twice the number of bodies and heads; they completely surrounded the elephant king and descended from the air.
At that time, having witnessed this event, the White Elephant King was seized with terror; the hair on his body stood on end, and he thought to himself:
"Another elephant king has come from another place, whose supernatural powers, majestic virtue, physical form, and number of heads all surpass mine."
"Now they shall expel me and seize this dwelling place.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, perceiving his fear and observing his unusual demeanor, immediately withdrew the miraculous manifestations produced by his supernormal powers and sat cross-legged in another location.
When the White Elephant King saw this, he reflected:
"This is not some other elephant king; it is a great bhikṣu.

At that time, the elephant king transformed his own body into that of a celestial youth, adorning his arms and hands with celestial gold and jewels, and his body with a celestial crown, earrings, and various precious necklaces.

At that time, as Maudgalyāyana sat upright in meditation, the celestial youth silently joined his palms, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, and paid homage to the Venerable One.
Then Maudgalyāyana spoke to the Elephant King:
"O Elder Elephant King!
"Your great supernormal powers and majestic virtue are difficult to equal.
The Elephant King replied,
"Virtuous One!"
"I am a beast; what supernatural power or majestic virtue do I possess?
Why has the Holy Master come here, and what do you intend to do?"
Maudgalyāyana replied,
“I wish to have some lotus roots. Thereupon,
the elephant king immediately commanded the black elephant:
"Go and fetch lotus roots, according to the Venerable One's wish.

At that time, the black elephant immediately entered the pond, gathered bundles of lotus roots, and loaded them at will upon its back for the elephant to carry. Then, it followed Mahāmaudgalyāyana as he flew through the air.
When Maudgalyāyana arrived, the bhikṣus there immediately accepted the lotus roots.
From that time until the present, this place has been called the Elephant’s Descent Caitya, also known as the Lotus-Root-Sending Caitya, and further named the Lotus-Root-Receiving Caitya.
After the Venerable Śāriputra had eaten this lotus root, his illness was immediately cured.
Once Śāriputra had recovered from that illness, he remained free from any physical ailment until his final parinirvāṇa.
Those bhikṣus all ate this lotus root.
Such a lotus root was lovely in form, with thick and abundant juice; it was sweet without any bitterness or pungency, like fine honey.
Whether square, round, long, or short, each measuring one foot in length and breadth, every joint is like this.
The juice from a single joint fills a bowl of the lowest grade.

A certain bhikṣu, having traveled by supernatural power to the side of Mount Kāñcanapārśva, witnessed these things and returned here to recount them. Then the Buddha, the World-Honored One, explained these causes and conditions for the sake of the bhikṣus; thus, such matters as these came to be known.
Chapter Six: The Four Continents. At that time, the Buddha said:
“There are four continents in the world:
first, Jambudvīpa; second, Aparagoyānī; third, Pūrvavideha; and fourth, Uttarakuru.”
At that time, a bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How vast is the land of this Jambudvīpa?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Jambudvīpa is large; its eastern boundary is two thousand yojanas, and its western and northern boundaries are likewise each two thousand yojanas. Its southern boundary is only three yojanas, making its total circumference six thousand and three yojanas; its shape is like a chariot."
All sentient beings born upon this earth have faces that resemble the shape of the land.
This Jambudvīpa possesses both mountains and rivers, with various countries interspersed among these mountains and rivers.
At that time, a bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How large is the form of Aparagoyānī?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Aparagoyānī is large, measuring two thousand three hundred and thirty-three yojanas plus one-third of a yojana in breadth, and seven thousand yojanas in circumference.”

The terrain is circular, with no mountains but with rivers; in the midst of these rivers stand various kingdoms. The people are wealthy and happy, free from thieves and bandits, and it is entirely filled with many who are virtuous and good.
At that time, the bhikṣu again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How large is the land of Pūrvavideha in the east?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Pūrvavideha in the east is large, measuring two thousand three hundred and thirty-three yojanas plus one-third of a yojana in width, and seven thousand yojanas in circumference."
The terrain is circular like the full moon; it contains many mountains and but a single river.
Within these mountains are situated various kingdoms where the people are wealthy and happy, free from bandits and thieves, and entirely filled with the virtuous and the good.
All the mountains are composed of gold and jewels; the plows, hoes, axes, and all other implements are made of pure gold.
There is a river named Saṭha, whose banks and shores are all delightful; there, the venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja established a saṃghārāma on its bank.
How is it known that such matters occurred?
Long ago, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a bhikṣu and a śrāmaṇera who both possessed supernatural powers; they traveled from Vārāṇasī down to Pūrvavideha in the east.

At that time, this śrāmaṇera took a pebble, intending to sharpen his needle upon it; he then carried this stone back to Vārāṇasī and placed it within the monastery, whereupon that very night it emitted a great radiance.
At that time, the bhikṣu asked the śrāmaṇera:
"Will you take those objects and bring them back here?
[The śrāmaṇera replied: "Venerable Sir!"
"I have brought this pebble back here with the intention of using it to sharpen my razor, needle,
and other tools. The bhikṣu then said to the śrāmaṇera,
"Take this stone and send it back to that country."
At that time, following the words of the bhikṣu, the śrāmaṇera took up the stone and threw it into the deep waters of the river at Vārāṇasī.

At once, this river emitted a great radiance, and all the turtles, fish, and other aquatic creatures became clearly visible. The people of the country vied with one another to go and witness the sight; the streets and alleys were so crowded that there was no longer room for doorways, and everyone said that a dragon had manifested great supernatural power.

At that time, the bhikṣu and this śrāmaṇera entered the city for alms in the early morning and saw a vast, countless multitude of people gathered by the riverbank; the city gates were so congested that it was difficult even to pass through them.
The bhikṣu asked the śrāmaṇera, "Where did you previously throw that stone?"
The śrāmaṇera replied,
"Venerable sir!
I shall throw this stone into the deep part of the river."
The bhikṣu spoke again to the śrāmaṇera:
"Take this stone and return it to its original place.

At that time, the śrāmaṇera followed his instructions; in the presence of the assembly, he entered the deep waters of the river to retrieve the stone, yet his body and robes remained dry. He leaped up into the air, flew away, and returned the stone to its original place.
At that time, countless bhikṣus traveled to and from that country, all of whom spoke in this manner.
Then the Buddha, the World-Honored One, explained these causes and conditions for the sake of the bhikṣus; thus it was known.
At that time, a bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How vast is the land of Uttarakuru in the north?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“To the north lies Uttarakuru; its eastern boundary is two thousand yojanas long, its western boundary is two thousand yojanas long, and it is the same from south to north; its four sides total eight thousand yojanas.”
Surrounded by a city of golden mountains, with ground made of gold, it is perpetually bright day and night.
This land of Uttarakuru possesses four virtues:
first, evenness; second, tranquility; third, purity; and fourth, freedom from thorns.

That which is called "level" means that within that land there are no pits or ravines, nor are there burrows; it is neither sloping nor uneven, and it is free from mud and slickness; therefore, it is named "level."
As for its tranquility: within that land, there are no lions, tigers, leopards, bears, brown bears, venomous snakes, bees, or wasps capable of harming people; therefore, it is called "tranquil."
As for its purity: within that land, there are no impure things such as corpses, dead snakes, or dead dogs;
whenever the people, whether great or small, relieve themselves, the earth opens to receive them, and having received them, it closes back up again—therefore, it is called pure.
Regarding its being "thornless": within that land, there are no trees with sharp thorns and no trees with foul odors; therefore, it is called "thornless.
There is a grass there named Cāpī, which is deep blue in color and its form is exceedingly lovely, like the neck of a peacock; when touched, it is as soft as kācilindika cloth.
The kācilindika garment cannot be soiled; it is cool in summer and warm in winter.
Furthermore, just as the āśīna garment does not burn when set on fire, its touch is likewise soft and supple.
This land is completely covered by śābbi grass, which does not wither throughout the four seasons and grows to a height of only four inches.

The various rivers of that country possess the eight qualities of meritorious water; their banks, islets, and beds are all strewn with golden sand. The waters flow constantly without increase or decrease, and the golden embankments are so firm and solid that they never collapse.
Thus the Buddha spoke.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“The garuḍa bird dwells upon the four continents:”

Between the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha and the southern continent of Jambudvīpa, there is a Garuḍa island; between the southern continent of Jambudvīpa and the western continent of Aparagoyānī, there is a Garuḍa island; between the western continent of Aparagoyānī and the northern continent of Uttarakuru, there is a Garuḍa island; and between the northern continent of Uttarakuru and the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha, there is a Garuḍa island.
This island of birds is one thousand yojanas in circumference and is circular in shape; it is entirely composed of deep *śāla* groves.
*Garuḍa* birds dwell within these forests, while beneath the waters outside the island is the abode of the nāgas.
The nāgas dwell in this place just as those birds gather and store food and drink, taking it whenever they are hungry.
There are four kinds of garuḍas:
first, those born by transformation; second, those born from moisture; third, those born from eggs; and fourth, those born from a womb.
All dragons are likewise born through the four modes of birth.
A *kālūla* born by transformation can eat all four kinds of dragons;
a *kālūla* born from moisture can eat three kinds, excluding those born by transformation.
The egg-born *kālīras* eat two kinds [of beings] after their meal;
the womb-born *kālīras* eat one kind after their meal.
