When these birds eat, they fan the water with both wings, causing it to part for fifty *yojanas*; they then seize the nāgas and return to their trees to eat them.
The remains left over from what the birds have eaten lie scattered upon the ground like the bones of elephants; for this reason, the four continents are constantly filled with a foul odor.

Between the two continents of Pūrvavideha in the east and Jambudvīpa in the south lies the continent where the Garuḍa birds dwell; there is a tree named Kuśāmbu that possesses complete roots, trunks, branches, and twigs, and its appearance is lovely.

Its leaves are dense and thick, remaining for a long time without withering; wind and rain cannot penetrate them. Like exquisite flower garlands and various jeweled earrings crafted by worldly artisans, or like parasols layered one above another, the form and appearance of that tree are likewise.

It is one hundred yojanas in height; at its base it is thick and straight for fifty yojanas before branches and leaves appear. These branches and leaves spread out in the four directions for a distance of one hundred yojanas.
At its base, the trunk is five yojanas in diameter, with a circumference of fifteen yojanas.
The king of the *garuḍas* is named Vainateya, who dwells upon this tree.
When the great nāga king named Mānasvin wishes to sport with the bird king, he emerges and makes himself manifest.
At that time, the bird king seized this dragon and placed him upon a tree branch.
This dragon king was already large by his very nature, yet he further manifested transformations such that his body became even longer.

Thus the bird-king seized the dragon and returned to the tree; as the dragon’s body grew longer, it filled the entirety of the tree. In this manner, the dragon’s body gradually covered the tree, and because of the dragon's great weight, the tree was bent and crushed.
At that time, having realized this matter, the king of birds released the dragon and thought to himself:
"This Mānasī dragon has destroyed my dwelling place."
Then the king of birds, Vinatāya, gave rise to a heart of regret and remorse; withdrawing to one side, he remained there in silence, brooding with sorrow and distress:
"This dragon Maṇas has indeed been able to stretch me out."

At that time, the dragon king again transformed himself into a celestial youth, his arms and hands adorned with celestial gold and jewels, and his body decorated with a celestial crown, earrings, and various precious necklaces. He went to where the bird king was and spoke these words:
"Good friend!
"What trouble, distress, or suffering do you have that you remain silent and alone, unable to find peace of mind when rising?
The bird king replied, "I am now being tormented;
the dragon Mānasa has destroyed my dwelling place."
The youth replied,
"Good friend!
Will you take the dragon again for food and drink?"
If you are already distressed by the loss of your dwelling, how much more suffering must a dragon endure when deprived of its kin?
If you take the dragon again, your residence will certainly no longer stand.
Thereupon, the two kings, the nāga and the bird, together made a vow not to harm one another and to be friends forever.
For this reason, this tree is named Kuśaṃbaluva.
These four continents and the four bird-islands have the largest landmasses; therefore, they are discussed now.
Each individual island is surrounded by eight islands:
Ox Island, Sheep Island, Coconut Island, Jewel Island, Deity Island, Monkey Island, Elephant Island, and Woman Island.
"The same applies to the other seven continents.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Buddha; thus have I heard.
Chapter Seven: On Quantities. At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣu Pūrṇa:
“The ground of this world is circular in shape, like a bronze candle-stand or a potter’s wheel; the ground of this world is likewise so.”
Just as the rim of a candle-stand rises up, so too are the Cakravāḍa Mountains;
just as the center of a candle-stand rises up, so too is Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, within that world-system.
This Mount Sumeru is composed of the seven precious jewels; its color and form are lovely, and its four corners are perfectly straight.
It is like a skilled craftsman who, using a line and ink, carves planks and pillars so that their shapes are square and regular; Mount Sumeru is just like this.

Half of its form enters the water to a depth of eighty thousand yojanas, and half of its form emerges above the water to a height of eighty thousand yojanas; each of the mountain’s four sides is eighty thousand yojanas long, making its total circumference three hundred and twenty thousand yojanas.

The innermost great ocean is named the Sumeru Sea; it is eighty thousand yojanas deep and forty thousand yojanas wide, with each side measuring one hundred and sixty thousand yojanas, and its circumference being six hundred and forty thousand yojanas.

Beyond the sea there is a mountain named Yugandhara; this mountain enters the water forty thousand yojanas, and its emergence above the water is likewise the same, while its breadth is also forty thousand yojanas.
This mountain is twenty-four thousand yojanas long on one side, with a circumference of nine hundred and sixty thousand yojanas.

The ocean outside this mountain is also named Yugandhara; it is forty thousand yojanas deep and its breadth is likewise. It is three hundred and twenty thousand yojanas long on one side, with a circumference of one million two hundred and eighty thousand yojanas.

Beyond the sea there is a mountain named Īṣādhara; it enters the water for twenty thousand yojanas and likewise rises above the water for that same distance. Its breadth is also thus, measuring thirty-six thousand yojanas on each side, with a circumference of one million four hundred and forty thousand yojanas.

Beyond the mountains lies an ocean also named Īṣādhara; it is twenty thousand yojanas deep and its breadth is likewise. One side measures four hundred thousand yojanas, and its circumference is one million six hundred thousand yojanas.

Beyond the sea there is a mountain named Haraṇyaka; it enters the water for ten thousand yojanas and likewise emerges from the water for ten thousand yojanas. Its breadth is the same: forty-four hundred thousand yojanas on each side, with a circumference of one million seven hundred and sixty thousand yojanas.

Beyond the mountains lies an ocean also named Haraṇyavatī; it is ten thousand yojanas deep and likewise wide, measuring four hundred and sixty thousand yojanas on one side and one million eight hundred and forty thousand yojanas in circumference.

Beyond the sea there is a mountain named Kūṭaśaila (or Xiu-teng-sa), which extends five thousand yojanas into the water and rises above it by the same amount; its width is likewise. One side is forty-seven thousand yojanas long, and its circumference is one million eight hundred and eighty thousand yojanas.

Beyond the mountains there is an ocean also named Sītā; it is five thousand yojanas deep and its breadth is likewise. One side is forty-eight thousand yojanas long, and its circumference is one million nine hundred and twenty thousand yojanas.

Beyond the sea there is a mountain named Aśvakarṇa; it enters the water for two thousand five hundred yojanas, and likewise rises above the water for the same distance. Its breadth is also thus; one side is four hundred and eighty-five thousand yojanas long, and its circumference is one million nine hundred and forty thousand yojanas.

Beyond the mountains there is an ocean also named Aṣāḍhānā; it is two thousand five hundred yojanas deep and its breadth is likewise. One side is four million nine hundred thousand yojanas long, and its circumference is one million nine hundred and sixty thousand yojanas.

Beyond the sea there is a mountain named Vinataka; it enters the water for one thousand two hundred and fifty yojanas, and likewise rises above the water for the same distance. Its breadth is also thus. One side is forty-nine thousand two hundred and fifty yojanas long, and its circumference is one million nine hundred and seventy thousand yojanas.

Beyond the mountains lies an ocean also named Vinata; it is one thousand two hundred and fifty yojanas deep, and its width is likewise. One side is forty-nine thousand five hundred yojanas long, and its circumference is one million nine hundred and eighty thousand yojanas.

Beyond the sea there is a mountain named Nimindhara; it enters the water to a depth of six hundred and twenty-five yojanas, and rises above the water by the same amount. Its breadth is likewise the same; one side is forty-nine thousand six hundred and twenty-five yojanas long, and its circumference is one million nine hundred and eighty-five thousand yojanas.

Beyond the mountains lies an ocean also named Nimindhara; it is six hundred and twenty-five yojanas deep and as wide as well. One side measures four hundred and ninety-seven thousand five hundred yojanas, and its circumference is one million nine hundred and ninety thousand yojanas.

Beyond the Salt Ocean there is a mountain called Cakravāḍa (Iron Ring). It enters the water to a depth of three hundred and twelve yojanas and a half, and its emergence above the water is likewise; its breadth is also thus, and it encircles the world for thirty-six billion, ten thousand, three hundred and fifty yojanas.
From the edge of Mount Nimindhara to the edge of the Cakravāḍa mountains, it is three hundred and sixty million, sixty thousand, three hundred and eighty-eight yojanas.
From the edge of the Nimindhara Ocean to the edge of the Cakravāḍa mountains, it is three hundred and sixty million, twenty-six thousand, six hundred and sixty-three yojanas.
From the southern limit of Jambudvīpa to the Cakravāḍa Mountains is three hundred and sixty million, six thousand, six hundred and sixty-three yojanas.
From the center of Jambudvīpa to the center of Aparagoyānī is three hundred and sixty-six thousand yojanas.
From the northern limit of Jambudvīpa in the south to the northern limit of Uttarakuru, it is four hundred and seven million seven thousand five hundred yojanas.

From the westernmost edge of the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa) to the opposite edge of the Iron Ring Mountains, the diameter is twelve billion two hundred and eight million two hundred and twenty-five yojanas; the circumference of the Iron Ring Mountains is forty-six billion eight hundred and forty-seven million five hundred yojanas.
From the edge of this Mount Sumeru to the edge of that Mount Sumeru, it is twelve billion three hundred and forty-five million yojanas.
From the center of this Mount Sumeru to the center of that Mount Sumeru, it is twelve billion eighty-three thousand four hundred and fifty million yojanas.
"From the base of this Mount Sumeru to the base of that Mount Sumeru, it is twelve billion, three thousand, and fifteen yojanas.
Such was the meaning taught by the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Thus have I heard. Chapter Eight: The Abodes of the Gods. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“This King of Mountains, Sumeru, has four sides—east, west, south, and north. Its eastern side is composed of pure gold; its western side is composed of white silver; its northern side is of lapis lazuli; and its southern side is of crystal. All its sides are composed of various jewels.”
This Mount Sumeru is preeminent in seven qualities.
At its very summit, in the central, level, and most excellent location, lies the Great City of Sudarśana belonging to the Trāyastriṃśa devas, measuring ten thousand yojanas on each of its four sides.

It is surrounded by a city made of pure gold, one yojana in height; the battlements atop the city walls are half a yojana high, and the gates are two yojanas high. Beyond these are secondary gates one and a half yojanas high, with one gate for every ten yojanas.
The four sides of the city have a thousand gate-towers.

These city gates are composed of various jewels and adorned with diverse mani-gems; they are like exquisite carpets from the northern lands, wherein no features of humans, non-humans, dragons, beasts, plants, trees, or miscellaneous flowers are lacking. They are also like earrings, fully filled and complete with adornments of many jewels;
these city gates are likewise so adorned, their exteriors decorated with the forms of all sentient beings, various trees, and diverse flowers.
At the gates of this city, the elephant army, the cavalry, and the chariot army stand arrayed at the gates.
These sons of the gods gather there, adorned with armor and weapons, for the sake of protecting the land, for the purpose of wandering and observing, and for the sake of adornment.

On all four sides outside the city, sevenfold jeweled railings encircle it completely; the innermost is made of pure gold, the next of white silver, the third of lapis lazuli, and the fourth of crystal, while the outer three layers are composed of various miscellaneous jewels.

Beyond the sevenfold [enclosure], there are seven rows of *tāla* trees surrounding it; the innermost row has trees with trunks of pure gold, the next of white silver, the third of lapis lazuli, and the fourth of crystal, while the three outer rows have trunks made of various precious gems.
As for the *jintuoluo* (kanakadāra) tree, its flowers and leaves are made of various jewels such as white silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal; its fruit is likewise.
As for the *yinduoluo* (rūpyadāra) tree, its flowers and leaves are made of gold, lapis lazuli, and *pōlījiā* (sphāṭika) jewels; its fruit is likewise.
The *vīratara* trees have flowers and leaves made of gold, silver, and crystal;
the *sphāṭika* trees have flowers and leaves made of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli.
Its outer three layers of flower petals and fruit are all composed of various jewels.
These tāla trees, stirred by a gentle breeze, produce wondrous sounds that cause sentient beings to give rise to five kinds of fetters:
first, the arising of craving; second, the arising of bondage; third, the arising of delusion and confusion; fourth, the arising of attachment; and fifth, the absence of wearying detachment.

Just as a five-part musical ensemble, or a master musician skillfully performing the five notes in a complex composition, can arouse the five kinds of sensual desires in sentient beings, so too is the sound of this tree.

Between each of its seven tiers of trees, there are everywhere various jeweled lotus ponds, each one hundred celestial *dhanus* in length and breadth, filled with celestial water. Their bases and banks are constructed from bricks of four kinds of jewels, being composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
The four sides of those ponds also have stairways made of bricks of the four precious substances.
Within each pond are immeasurable flowers composed of five jewels, namely: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and musaragalva.
Within these ponds, there are boats made of the four treasures—namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—floating and drifting amidst them.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds of water-play implements: first, towers for plunging into the water;

second, caskets of the seven treasures used to pour water over the body; third, instruments for striking the water to produce music; fourth, splashing water as a form of play; fifth, water-wheels and carts; sixth, floating houses; seventh, jeweled wheels and *pāṭikā* birds; and eighth, ropes and cords for descending, whirling around, and tossing about.
Among them, men and women among the devas travel by boat for recreation; at that time, the precious boat moves at a speed according to their will.
If the men and women among the devas form this thought:
"We wish to go toward that place," [the boat proceeds accordingly].
The boat arrived at that place immediately.
Then those devas formed this thought:
"May you take those flowers and bring them to my abode."
The flowers then arrived spontaneously.
Within them, a natural wind arose as a result of their karmic retribution, blowing various famous flowers and scattering them everywhere among the devas.
Furthermore, there was another distinct wind that blew various flower garlands to adorn their bodies and heads; these became crowns, necklaces, armlets, and even waist-bands, or anklets for the feet.
On the four sides of the pond’s banks there are trees made of five kinds of jewels:
first, gold; second, silver; third, lapis lazuli; fourth, crystal; and fifth, emerald.
Between the rows of those trees are various jeweled halls and palaces formed of the five precious substances, wherein male and female devas dwell.
Outside these cities, many devas fill the entire land.
Outside the tala trees are three tiers of precious moats; each individual moat is two yojanas wide and one and a half yojanas deep, being wider at the bottom than at the top, like the mouth of a jar.

The moats are filled with celestial waters and are likewise constructed of bricks made of the four precious substances—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. Along the four sides of these moats, there are stairways also fashioned from bricks of the four precious substances. Within each moat, moreover, are immeasurable flowers made of the four precious substances, and there float boats made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds of water-play apparatus: first, towers for plunging into the water;

second, caskets made of the seven precious gems used to pour water over the body; third, instruments for striking the water to produce music; fourth, splashing water as a form of amusement; fifth, water-wheels and chariots; sixth, floating houses; seventh, jewel-wheels and *pūtika* birds; eighth, swinging on ropes and cords to whirl and toss about.
Among them, male and female devas travel by boat for recreation; these precious boats move at speeds according to their will.
If the male and female devas form this thought:
"We wish to go to that place," [the boat arrives there immediately].
The boat immediately arrived there;
then those devas formed this thought:
"May he take those flowers and come to where I am."
The flowers then arrive of their own accord.
Within them, as a natural result of their karmic retribution, winds arise that blow various famous flowers, scattering them everywhere among the devas.

Furthermore, there are distinct winds that blow various flower garlands to adorn their bodies and heads; these may become jeweled crowns, necklaces, or armlets, and the same applies to waist-bands and anklets.
In the midst of the moat are various jeweled halls and palaces, the dwelling places of the celestial maidens.
Within these halls are arranged jeweled cauldrons; in each cauldron are planted flowers and grasses, arrayed in rows with five colors and diverse forms.
Beyond its threefold moats, it is surrounded by trees made of the seven precious substances—namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, lotus-colored gems, conch-stone, and harītakī.

Within these groves, there are everywhere ponds of the seven treasures, filled with celestial waters, even including jeweled boats for recreation; as well as various palaces where the male and female celestial hosts dwell.
Numerous devas filled the land, as described above.

At that time, the trees made of the seven precious substances outside the moat blossomed with flowers of the seven jewels—namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and so forth, up to *hari-tāla* and the rest.
Within that grove, the goddesses sing and play music, while immeasurable sons of gods enter and exit the great city to go and listen;
within that city, the sons of gods sing and play music, while the goddesses from outside enter the city to go and listen.
By means of these expedient means for coming and going and for pleasure, one-quarter of the great city was divided [for them].
In the center is a golden wall, the dwelling place of Śakra.
It has twelve *yojanas* and possesses one gate on each of its four sides, totaling four hundred and ninety-nine gates; with one additional small gate, there are five hundred gates in all.
The layout of this city was likewise guarded by the fourfold army;
it featured palisades, moats, trees, ponds, groves, and palaces, where musicians performed songs and instrumental music, as well as various outdoor spectacles.
Its various adornments were all as previously described.

In the center of this city was the residence of Śakra Devānām Indra, a multi-storied jeweled tower named Piṣṭāpura. It was five hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty yojanas in width, and one thousand five hundred yojanas in circumference. Its pillars were nine yojanas high and composed of four kinds of jewels: first, gold; second, silver; third, lapis lazuli; and fourth, crystal. Four types of precious bricks served as the bases for these pillars.
The tower has four stairways on its four sides, and all its walls are composed of the four precious substances.
It is surrounded by three tiers of leather enclosures: the first tier is made of pure gold, the second of white silver, and the third of lapis lazuli.

On each of these tiers, there are threefold rows of precious bells which, stirred by a gentle breeze, produce exquisite sounds like those of the fivefold musical ensemble, or as previously described regarding the sound of the tala trees, capable of causing sentient beings to give rise to the fetters of the five desires.
On the four sides of that pavilion were defensive watchtowers made of jewels: twenty-six on the eastern side and twenty-five on each of the other three sides, totaling one hundred and one.
Each individual watchtower was two yojanas square, making a total circumference of eight yojanas.
Upon each of those bastions there is a jeweled pavilion, half a yojana in height, serving as a lookout.
On each bastion dwell seven goddesses of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, and each goddess has seven female attendants.
Within the pavilions there were seventy-seven thousand chambers; in each chamber there were seven celestial maidens, and for each celestial maiden there were likewise seven handmaidens.
As for those celestial maidens, they are all the principal consorts of Śakra.
As for his outer defenses against enemies and the inner chambers, there are forty-nine million four thousand nine hundred in total.

The principal consorts numbered three billion four hundred and sixty-four thousand three hundred; including the secondary consorts and handmaidens, there were a total of three billion nine hundred and fifty-nine thousand two hundred.
At the center of the uppermost story of the multi-storied palace of Vaijayanta is a circular chamber; it is thirty yojanas in width, ninety yojanas in circumference, and forty-five yojanas in height.
The abode where Śakra Devānām-indra dwells is composed entirely of vaidūrya; the ground is everywhere soft and smooth, inlaid with various jewels.

It is like a magnificent woolen carpet from the northern regions, wherein humans and non-humans, dragons, beasts, grasses, trees, and all manner of flowers are depicted without exception. It is also like an earring adorned with various jewels, filled and complete in every detail;
such is the dwelling place of Śakra, composed of vaidūrya and adorned with manifold jewels.
The ground there is soft and supple; as soon as the foot treads upon it, it sinks down, and when the foot is lifted, it returns to its original state, like a mass of fine cotton or *tūla* cotton.
The dwelling place of Śakra is likewise: when the foot treads upon it, it sinks, and as soon as the foot is raised, it springs back up.

Various flowers were scattered about and fragrant incense was burned; celestial garments and jeweled flower garlands were suspended. In such a place dwells Śakra Devānām Indra together with the Apsaras Śacī, daughter of the Asuras.
The Śakra manifested himself and lived together with his various consorts; all the consorts thought to themselves:
"The Śakra lives with me; it is the Śakra’s true body that lives with Śacī."
Within this city, the dwellings on all four sides, as well as the thoroughfares, lanes, and marketplaces, are all perfectly aligned and level.

In these celestial cities, there are some dwellings consisting of four-sided houses, some with multi-storied peaked roofs, some with high-rise buildings of many tiers, some with towers and pavilions soaring like clouds, and some with defensive walls surrounding them on all sides. According to their respective merits, these are composed of various jewels and are flat, upright, and straight.

This celestial city has five hundred streets, with four thoroughfares intersecting one another; their rows are clearly defined like the lines on a chessboard, and the four gates are interconnected, allowing for mutual visibility from east to west.

In every lane and marketplace, precious goods were abundant—first, the grain market; second, the clothing market; third, the incense market; fourth, the food and drink market; fifth, the flower-garland market; sixth, the craft market; and seventh, the courtesan market—in each place there was a market official.

In these various markets, devas and devīs come and go for trade, deliberate upon prices high and low, seek out increases or decreases, and weigh and measure quantities, fully observing the customs of the marketplace.
Although one performs these acts for the sake of amusement, being without grasping or giving, without the sense of "mine," and having freed oneself from what is required, one may then take them away.
If the object is suitable for his karmic affinity, he takes it according to his will;
if it is not suitable for his karmic affinity, he speaks thus:
"This object is exceptionally precious; it is not what I require."

At the crossroads, it was adorned with elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; there, various devaputras resided, either for the purpose of providing protection, or for amusement, or for adornment.
The central road in the city was made entirely of lapis lazuli; it was soft, smooth, and lovely, adorned with various jewels.

It was like the exquisite carpets of the northern regions, where dragons, beasts, flowers, and grasses were all as previously described; even the burning of incense, the scattering of flowers, and the hanging of celestial garments were likewise so.
Furthermore, banners and standards were erected everywhere.

Within the great celestial city, such sounds as these resounded constantly and without interruption: namely, the sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, conchs, *paṇava* drums, kettledrums, *mṛdaṅga* drums, flutes, and musical instruments.
Furthermore, a voice was heard saying:
"Welcome, welcome!
Please eat, please drink; I now offer this sustenance."
"This Great City of Sudarśana is the dwelling place of Śakra.
Furthermore, there are celestial districts, prefectures, counties, and villages that are distributed all around Mount Sumeru."

In the northwest corner of the Great City of Sudarśana, twenty yojanas outside the threshold of the gate, there is the Sudharmā Hall of the Trāyastriṃśa devas. It is thirty yojanas in length, ninety yojanas in circumference, and forty-five yojanas in height. It is composed entirely of vaidūrya; the ground is smooth and supple, inlaid with various jewels.

For example, it is like a magnificent carpet from the northern lands, which contains every representation of humans and non-humans, dragons and beasts, grasses, trees, and various flowers; it is also like an earring adorned with a multitude of jewels, filled and complete in every detail.

The Hall of Sublime Dharmas is likewise: soft, smooth, and lovely, such that when one steps upon it, the foot sinks in, and as the foot is lifted, it rises again; its various adornments are as previously described.
It is encircled by three layers of skin:
the first made of pure gold, the second of white silver, and the third of lapis lazuli.

Each layer is adorned with triple strings of precious bells; when stirred by a gentle breeze, they produce exquisite sounds like the fivefold music previously described, or like the sound of the *tāla* trees, which can cause sentient beings to give rise to the bonds of the five desires.
In the center of this hall, a great pillar made of various jewels rises up from within; at its summit is a golden dew-receptacle, fully adorned with every kind of ornament.
This central great pillar is one yojana in circumference and one-third of that in diameter.
Each rafter is surrounded by sixteen pillars, and each of those pillars is further surrounded by sixteen pillars; thus, each rafter is supported by two hundred and seventy-two pillars.

These rafters and beams are divided into three parts; one part consists of four thousand five hundred and two circuits, and three parts consist of twelve thousand one hundred and fifty-six. In total, there are thirty-two hundred and sixty-four million three hundred and thirty-two pillars.
These pillars reached from the ground up to the rafters, yet were separated by as much as a single hair’s breadth.
Or there was one pillar that reached from the rafters down to the ground, yet was separated by as much as a single hair’s breadth.
For this reason, this Hall of Good Dharma dwells in mid-air, such that it cannot be fully perceived.
There are four gate-halls:
first, due east; second, due west; third, due south; and fourth, due north.

Outside this Hall of Good Dharma, there are great jewel ponds everywhere, filled with celestial waters; their floors and banks are constructed from bricks made of the four jewels—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
The four sides of these ponds also have stairways made of precious bricks.
Within each pond are immeasurable flowers, composed of five kinds of jewels, namely: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and emerald.
Within these ponds, there are boats made of the four jewels floating and drifting amidst them.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds of water-play equipment: first, towers for plunging into the water;

second, caskets of the seven precious gems used to pour water over the body; third, instruments for striking the water to produce music; fourth, splashing water as a form of amusement; fifth, water-wheel chariots; sixth, floating houses; seventh, jewel-wheels and *pittika* (water-fowl) toys; and eighth, ropes and cords by which one descends to whirl and toss about.
Therein, men and women among the devas ride upon boats and sport, their speed swifter or slower according to their will.
Heavenly flowers naturally gather from the air to adorn the celestial bodies; even the many palaces of the devas are likewise completely filled in this same manner.
Outside this Hall of Good Dharma is a great park, surrounded by a golden wall one thousand yojanas in circumference; the wall is one yojana high, and its battlements are half a yojana high.
Each gate is two yojanas high, and there is one gate for every ten yojanas, totaling ninety-nine gates plus one small gate.
These gates are composed of various jewels and adorned with exquisite maṇi gems, like the exquisite carpets of the northern regions, decorated with all manner of carvings and ornaments.
This gate is also guarded by four armies, as described above;
the sevenfold outer enclosures of precious railings are also as described above.
It is likewise surrounded by sevenfold groves of *tāla* trees, as described above.
Between those trees are various jeweled ponds, each separated by a hundred bows (*dhanus*), adorned in every way as described above.
The five kinds of precious flowers are also as described above, as are the four types of jeweled boats.
The five kinds of jewel trees on the banks of the ponds are also as described above.
This continues up to the pavilions made of the four jewels, which are the dwellings of the male and female devas. Outside the city are three tiers of jewel moats; the rest is as described above.

Each moat is two yojanas wide and one and a half yojanas deep; its shape is like the mouth of a jar, being broad at the bottom and narrow at the top, filled with celestial water, all as described above.
Within these moats there were various court ladies.
Halls and palaces were arranged in rows, and outside the threefold moats, they were surrounded by groves of trees made of the seven precious substances, just as described above.

At that time, all the flowers in the outer grove were in full bloom and radiant; the goddesses played music and sang songs. Then, the sons of the gods emerged from the city of Dharmasabhā and entered this garden to observe and listen together.
Within this place, the sons of gods also perform music, and at that time, the daughters of gods emerge from the Hall of Good Dharma to go to the gardens for sightseeing.
Due to such circumstances, the male and female gods constantly enjoy playful pleasures.

From the northwestern corner gate of that great city, extending twenty yojanas toward the gate of the Sudharma Hall, there is a ground ten yojanas wide; it is smooth, composed of lapis lazuli, lovely and soft, and adorned with various jewels.

It is, for example, like a magnificent carpet from the northern lands, complete with all manner of humans and non-humans, elephants, horses, flowers, and trees; it is also like an earring fashioned from various jewels—the road is likewise so adorned.
As soon as they set foot upon it, they sink, and as soon as they lift their feet, they rise; the path is as soft as *tūla* cotton or *karpāsa* cotton.

It is adorned with three kinds of leather straps, each strap being composed of the four precious gems. Each leather strap is encircled by three tiers of jeweled bells, and each bell is likewise composed of the four precious gems. When stirred by a gentle breeze, they produce exquisite sounds that cause the devas to give rise to the bonds of the five desires.
On both sides of this road run two rivers called Dīrgha, each twenty yojanas long and ten yojanas wide, naturally filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities.
Both banks of that river were constructed and adorned with bricks made of the four precious substances; the rest is as previously described.
The four-sided stairways of the four precious substances along the river’s edges are also as previously described.
In these river waters there are flowers made of the five precious substances, as previously described.

Within them float boats made of four precious substances, and there are eight kinds of water-play equipment; one may ride these boats to play, with speed and direction according to one's own will, all as previously described.

When the devas therein require those flowers, they arrive as soon as they think of them; because of their virtuous karmic retribution, a rain of various precious flowers falls, scattering over the devas.

Furthermore, there is a special wind that blows the flower garlands, and according to whatever bodily adornments are required for their respective limbs—whether body, arms, head, or feet—they naturally fall into place.
On the outer banks of the two rivers, five kinds of jewel trees stand in dense rows, just as previously described.
Between these trees are various jewel ponds and jewel palaces, where male and female devas dwell together, filling them in immeasurable and infinite numbers.

At that time, when the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven wish to enter this grove, there is a wind in their Sudharmā Hall called Saṃghāta; it gathers up the withered flowers and blows them outside, so that the ground is pure and clean, free from any moreered blossoms.
Furthermore, there is another wind called "Razor" that blows through the outer groves and ponds, gathering various fresh flowers—flowers of blue, yellow, red, white, and mixed colors.

Once the flowers have been gathered, the wind of "Converging and Collecting" then assembles these flowers and brings them into the Sudharmā Hall, spreading them across the ground to form various images. Some appear in the shape of golden or silver staffs; some in the shape of lotus flowers; some in the shape of woolen carpets; some in the shape of rams; some in the likeness of lions at play; some in the likeness of elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, and so forth; some in the likeness of deer and wild beasts; and some in the likeness of garuḍas, nāgas, and horses. Following this sequence, they completely fill the ground of the Sudharmā Hall on all sides, with the flowers reaching up to the knees in thickness, perfectly adorned.
At that time, the various devas surrounded Śakra, honoring him as their sovereign, and entered this grove.
Within the Hall of Good Dharma, beside the central pillar, was a lion throne; Śakra Devānām Indra ascended the throne and sat there.
On both the left and right sides, sixteen celestial kings sat in rows; the remaining devas sat in order according to their respective ranks.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, had two crown princes—one named Candana and the other named Supriya—who were the two great generals of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, sitting on the left and right of the thirty-three gods.
At that time, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra sat at the eastern gate together with his ministers and military hosts; having paid homage to the devas, he was permitted to enter and sit within.
At that time, the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka sat at the southern gate together with his various ministers and military hosts; having paid homage to the devas, he was permitted to enter and sit within.

At that time, the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa sat at the western gate together with his various ministers and military hosts; having paid homage to the devas, he was permitted to enter and take his seat within.
At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa, dwelling by the northern gate together with his ministers and military hosts, paid homage to the devas and was permitted to enter and take his seat within.
"These Four Great Kings, in the Hall of Good Dharma, report the good and evil of the world to Śakra and the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke these words: "Bhikṣus!"

On the eighth day of this month, the ministers of the Four Heavenly Kings travel throughout the world to observe in succession whether, on this very day, many or few people receive and uphold the eight precepts.
Whether much or little, do they all practice giving?
Whether much or little, do they cultivate meritorious deeds?
Whether much or little, do they show reverence to their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the elders within the household?

"Monks! On the fourteenth day of the month, the princes of the Four Great Kings travel throughout the world, observing in succession: 'On this very day, how many people, whether many or few, observe the eight precepts?'"
Whether much or little, do they all practice giving?
Whether much or little, do they all cultivate merit?
Whether much or little, do they all show reverence to their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the elders within their households?

"Monks! On the fifteenth day of the month, the Four Great Kings personally traverse the world in succession to observe: 'On this day, how many people, whether many or few, are observing the eight precepts?'"
Whether much or little, do you all practice giving?
Whether much or little, do you all cultivate merit?
Whether much or little, do you all show reverence to your parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the elders within your households?
The dark fortnight is also like this, O Bhikṣus! At that time,

if there are not many people who observe the eight precepts, if there are not many people who practice generosity, if there are not many people who cultivate meritorious deeds, and if there are not many people who show reverence to their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the elders of their households, O Bhikṣus!

At that time, while the Trāyastriṃśa gods were seated and assembled within the Sudharmā Hall, the Four Kings went to the place of the Dharma Hall and consulted Śakra, reporting on the affairs of the world, saying:
"O Illustrious One!..."
Not many people observe the eight precepts; not many people practice generosity; and not many people show reverence toward their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the elders within their households.
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and Śakra Devendra, having heard this matter, gave rise to a mind of distress and spoke these words:
"This matter is not good; this matter is not in accordance with the Dharma."

If among these people there are not many who observe the eight precepts, not many who practice generosity, not many who cultivate meritorious deeds, and not many who show reverence toward their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and elders within their families, then the retinues of the devas will surely diminish, while the companions of the asuras will increase day by day.

"Monks! If many people uphold the eight precepts, extensively practice giving, extensively cultivate meritorious deeds, and extensively show reverence to their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the elders within their households, then at that time the Four Great Kings go to the Hall of Dharma, consult Śakra, and recount the affairs of the world, saying:
'O Noble Lord!'"

Many people observe the eight precepts; many practice generosity; many cultivate meritorious deeds; and many show reverence toward their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the elders within their families.
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, having heard the words of the Four Heavenly Kings, felt great joy in their hearts and spoke these words:
"This matter is most excellent; this matter is in accordance with the Dharma."

If many people extensively observe the eight precepts, extensively practice generosity, extensively perform meritorious deeds, and extensively show reverence to their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and elders within their families, the retinues of the devas will increase day by day, while the companions of the asuras will gradually diminish.
"O Bhikṣus!
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra sat upright in the very center of his celestial throne, and in accordance with the hearts of the devas, he spoke these verses to bring them joy:
'On the eighth day of this month, And on the fourteenth and fifteenth, ...'"
On the twenty-third day of the month, on the ninth and the thirtieth, during these three times one observes the fifteen-fold fast;
by receiving and upholding the eightfold precepts, one disciplines and pacifies the mind. If one receives and maintains the poṣadha, [one attains purity].
"This person practices seven dharmas; in the future, he shall be like me now. "Bhikṣus!
These verses of Śakra Devānām Indra are a false song, not a good song; they are a false speech, not a good speech."
Why is this so? Bhikṣus!

This Śakra Devānām Indra is not yet liberated from birth, not yet liberated from old age, not yet liberated from death, not yet liberated from sorrow, not yet liberated from lamentation, not yet liberated from suffering, not yet liberated from affliction, and not yet liberated from the five aggregates.

"Monks! If there is a monk who has become an Arhat, who has extinguished all taints, perfected the path, is liberated through right knowledge, and has exhausted all fetters of existence—such a monk, if he were to speak this verse, would be speaking words that are well-spoken."
"On the eighth day of this month, The fourteenth and fifteenth,
As well as the twenty-third, And the twenty-ninth and thirtieth—
At these three periods, one observes the fifteen fasts And upholds the eightfold precepts."
"Tranquility is the remedy encompassed by the mind;
if one upholds the poṣadha, that person cultivates the seven dharmas and shall become like me in the future. "O Bhikṣus!"
This verse of the bhikṣu is indeed a virtuous song and not a perverse song; it is indeed a virtuous speech and not a perverse speech. Why is this so?

This bhikṣu is already liberated from birth, already liberated from old age, already liberated from death, already liberated from sorrow, already liberated from lamentation, already liberated from suffering, already liberated from vexation, and already liberated from the five aggregates.
He then spoke in gāthā:
"These ministers of the Four Kings patrol the world on the eighth day;
the princes of the Four Heavenly Kings observe the world on the fourteenth."
At the fifteenth day, most excellent, the Four Kings, who delight in a good reputation,
travel through the world themselves to observe all that is wholesome and unwholesome.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings go up to the Hall of the Good Dharma.
The great assembly of devas reports all good and evil deeds.
Those people of this world whose intentions accord with the Dharma,
those virtuous and honored ones who practice giving and observe the uposatha— [they shall be reborn among them].
Subduing anger, one is able to cultivate the Path; the merit of both men and women increases.
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven attained faith and were exceedingly joyful;
they repeatedly gave rise to sympathetic joy as the Great Kings spoke well.
May the hosts of celestial beings and their retinues increase more and more;
may the companions of the asuras diminish day by day.
May they follow mindfulness of the Perfectly Awakened One, the Dharma, the True Teaching, and the Noble Sangha.
The devas dwell in peace and happiness, their hearts always filled with joy.
Whether it be worldly fruits or supramundane fruits that can be attained by human beings—
if one relies upon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, abiding within the sphere of the Triple Gem.
I now declare for you all the three noble and virtuous paths.
If a person seeks the truth, abandoning evil and practicing good,
there is no such commodity by which one gains much from little.
Just as the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven— having performed minor acts of merit and been reborn there—
such as Śakra and the other deities, possessing great merit and renown,
gather in the Sudharmā Hall and their various other abodes.
"The men and women offer fine incense; the Four Kings report this to the ears [of the gods].
Loved by the pure devas, its fragrance permeates all the heavens.
"The forms and colors of these sons of the gods differ, as do their garments; they are adorned with various jewels in manifold ways."
Within the Hall of Good Dharma are lotus flowers of four precious colors; these human-like blossoms shine brilliantly, reflecting one another.
Just as a jeweled house might be filled with various treasures, so too is the Hall of Good Dharma lovely in this way.
Why is this hall called the Hall of the Good Dharma?

It is because these devas gather therein and frequently praise the Buddha, frequently praise the Dharma, and frequently praise the Saṃgha; they distinguish between the false and the correct matters of the world and proclaim the various supramundane paths.
"In places such as gardens and the like, such things do not exist; therefore, that place is called the Hall of the True Dharma (Saddharmasabhā).
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Buddha.
Thus have I heard.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-śāstra on the Establishment of the World*, Fascicle Two.
*The Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-śāstra on the Establishment of the World Spoken by the Buddha*, Fascicle Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Western India during the Chen Dynasty.
Chapter Nine: The Garden of Joy (Nandanavana).
Outside the northern gate of the Great City of Sudarśana, at a distance of twenty yojanas, the Trāyastriṃśa devas have a great grove named Nandana.

Within this [grove] there is also a pond named Nandā, one hundred yojanas square and likewise deep; it is filled with celestial water, its bottom and banks are lined with bricks made of the four precious substances, and the rest is as previously described;
the jeweled stairways on its four sides are also as previously described, and the five kinds of precious flowers are also as previously described.
There are four kinds of precious ships and eight kinds of playthings that move according to the speed of one's mind.

When the gods therein require those flowers, they arrive as soon as they think of them; due to the ripening of their virtuous fruits, a rain of various precious flowers falls, scattering over the gods.

Furthermore, there is a special wind that blows upon the various flower garlands; according to whatever bodily adornments are required for each part of the body, these naturally attach themselves to the body, arms, head, and feet.
On the banks of these ponds, trees made of five kinds of jewels stand in rows, filling the area completely; the rest is as previously described.
In the spaces between those trees and within the various jeweled halls and palaces, male and female devas dwell in full abundance, as described above.

Within the garden there is a tree named *Nandana*; the flowers produced by this tree are called *Mandārava*. Their size is like that of a celestial chariot wheel, their color and appearance are like flames of fire, and their weight is like that of human flowers.
As for the Tree of Joy (*nandana-vṛkṣa*), it exists within this grove and nowhere else.
This grove is one thousand *yojanas* in circumference and three hundred and thirty-three and one-third *yojanas* in diameter, surrounded by a golden wall.
This city is one yojana high, with battlements half a yojana high; the city gates are two yojanas high, and the gate towers are one and a half yojanas high.
At intervals of ten yojanas there is one gate; with ninety-nine such gates and one additional small gate, they total one hundred gates.
These gates are composed of various jewels and adorned with exquisite maṇi gems, like the exquisite carpets of the northern regions, intricately carved and engraved in every variety.
This gate is also guarded by the fourfold army,
as described above;
the sevenfold outer jeweled fences are also as described above.
It is surrounded by seven tiers of *tāla* groves, as described above.
Between those trees are various jeweled ponds, each separated by a distance of one hundred *dhanus*, adorned in various ways, also as described above;
there are five kinds of precious flowers, also as described above, as well as boats made of the four jewels, also as described above.
The five kinds of jewel trees on the banks of the pond are also as described above, up to the pavilions and palaces made of the four jewels, which are the dwellings of the male and female devas.
Outside the city are three tiers of jewel moats; the rest is as described above.

Each of these moats is two yojanas wide and one and a half yojanas deep; their shape is like the mouth of a jar, being broad at the bottom and narrow at the top, filled with celestial water, all as described above.
Within these moats, there are rows of palaces for various court ladies.
Outside the threefold moats, the area is surrounded by groves of trees made of the seven precious substances, as described above.
At that time, all the flowers in the outer groves were in full bloom and radiant; the goddesses played music and sang songs, while the devaputras emerged from the Nandana Grove to observe and listen.
As the devaputras played music and sang songs in the outer groves, the goddesses within the grove likewise came out to observe and listen.
The female devas within the grove further performed music, and the male devas from outside entered the grove to observe and listen;
the male devas within the grove also performed music, and the female devas from outside likewise entered the grove to listen.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, they experience various playful delights.

From the northern gate of the Great City of Sudarśana to the southern gate of the Nandana Garden, the intervening road is twenty yojanas long and ten yojanas wide. Its ground is composed entirely of lapis lazuli, smooth, soft, and adorned with myriad jewels. It is like a magnificent carpet from the northern lands, fully endowed with all manner of human and non-human figures, birds, beasts, flowers, and grasses; it is also like an earring fashioned from a multitude of precious gems.
The appearance of that road is likewise such.
As soon as the foot is set down, it sinks, and as soon as the foot is lifted, it rises; the softness of the path is like that of *tūla* cotton or silk-cotton (*kārpāsa*).
It is further adorned with three kinds of leather straps, each strap being composed of the four jewels.

Each layer of hide is encircled by three tiers of precious bells; each precious bell is composed of the four jewels, and when stirred by a gentle breeze, they produce wondrous sounds that can cause the devas to give rise to the bonds of the five desires.
On both sides of this road are two rivers named Dīrgha, each twenty yojanas long and ten yojanas wide, naturally filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities.
On both sides of that river, the embankments are constructed of bricks made of the four precious substances, as described previously.
The four-sided stairways of the four precious substances along the banks of the river are also as described previously.
Within these river waters are five kinds of precious flowers, as previously described;

there are also four kinds of precious boats floating within them, along with eight kinds of water-play equipment. One may board these boats to travel and observe at a speed according to one's own will, all as previously described.

Therein, whenever the devas require those flowers, they arrive immediately upon thought; because of their virtuous karmic retribution, a rain of various precious flowers falls, scattering over the devas.

Furthermore, there is a special wind that blows the flower garlands so that, according to whatever bodily adornment is required for their respective limbs—whether body, arms, head, or feet—they naturally adhere to them.
On both outer banks of the two rivers, five kinds of jewel-trees stand in dense rows, filling the space entirely; the rest is as previously described.
Between these trees are various jewel-pools and jewel-palaces, where male and female devas dwell together, and immeasurable hosts of devas fill the land.
Why is this garden named "Joy" (Nandana)?
This garden has a great pond called "Joy," and it also has trees called "Joy"; its flowers are named Mandārava. These three things exist only in this garden and are not found in any other garden.
Furthermore, for what reason is it called "Joyous" (Nandana)?

At that time, when the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven wish to enter this garden, they give rise to great joy; they experience the highest play and pleasure, and delight in one another to the utmost. Therefore, it is called "Joyous."
This meaning was spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Thus have I heard. Chapter Ten:

The Grove of the Chariots (Sudatta). Twenty yojanas outside the eastern gate of the Great City of Sudarśana, there is a grove belonging to the Trāyastriṃśa devas called the Grove of the Chariots (Caitraratha).

In the center of the garden is a great pond named Citrā, one hundred yojanas square and as deep; it is filled with celestial water. Its bottom and banks are lined with bricks made of the four precious substances, as described above;
there are stairways of the four precious substances and five kinds of precious flowers, also as described above.
There are four kinds of precious boats and eight water-sports.

Whenever the gods therein desire those flowers, they arrive as soon as they think of them; by virtue of their wholesome karmic retribution, a rain of various precious flowers falls, scattering over the gods.

Furthermore, there is a distinct wind that blows upon the various flower garlands; according to whatever ornaments are required for each part of the body, they naturally adhere to the body, arms, head, and feet.
Along the banks of these ponds, trees made of five kinds of jewels stand in rows and fill the area, as described previously.
In the spaces between those trees and within the various jeweled halls and palaces, male and female devas dwell in complete abundance, as described above.
This garden is one thousand yojanas in circumference and one-third of that in diameter, and it is surrounded by a golden wall.
This city is one yojana in height, with battlements half a yojana high; the city gates are two yojanas high, and the gate towers are one and a half yojanas high.
At intervals of ten yojanas there is a gate; with ninety-nine such gates and one additional small gate, they total one hundred gates.
These gates are composed of various jewels and adorned with exquisite maṇi gems, like the exquisite carpets of the northern regions, featuring all manner of intricate carvings and engravings.
This gate is also guarded by four armies, as described above;
the sevenfold outer enclosures of precious railings are also as described above.
It is likewise surrounded by sevenfold groves of *tāla* trees, as described above.
In the intervals between those trees, there are various jeweled ponds, each a hundred *dhanus* apart, adorned in various ways as described above.
There are also five kinds of precious flowers, likewise as described above.
The four-jeweled boats are also as described above.
The five kinds of jewel trees on the banks of the ponds are also as described above.
Furthermore, there are pavilions and halls made of the four jewels, which are the dwellings of the male and female devas.
Beyond the city are three tiers of precious moats; the rest is as described above.

Each individual moat is two yojanas wide and one and a half yojanas deep, shaped like the mouth of a jar—broad at the bottom and narrow at the top—and filled with celestial water, all as described above.
Within these moats, there are various palaces for the ladies-in-waiting arranged in rows.
Beyond the three tiers of moats, the area is surrounded by groves of trees made of the seven precious substances, as described above.
In this outer grove, all the flowers are in full bloom and radiant; the goddesses play music and sing songs, while the sons of gods emerge from the Saṃtāna Garden to observe and listen.
When the sons of gods play music and sing songs in the outer grove, the goddesses within the garden also come out to observe and listen.
The female devas within the grove also performed music, and the male devas from outside entered the grove to watch and listen;
the male devas within the grove likewise performed music, and the female devas from outside also entered the grove to listen.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, they enjoy various forms of play and pleasure.

From the eastern gate of the great city of Sudarśana to the western gate of the Caitraratha Garden, the intervening road is twenty yojanas long and ten yojanas wide. Its ground is made entirely of lapis lazuli, smooth and soft, adorned with various jewels. It is like a magnificent carpet from the northern regions, complete with all manner of human and non-human figures, birds, beasts, flowers, and grasses; it is also like an earring composed of many precious gems.
The appearance of that road is likewise such.
As soon as the foot is set down, it sinks, and as soon as the foot is lifted, it rises; the path is as soft and supple as *tūla* cotton or *karpāsa* cotton.
It is adorned with three kinds of leather straps, each of which is composed of the four jewels.

Each layer of hide is encircled by three tiers of precious bells; each bell is composed of the four jewels, and when stirred by a gentle breeze, they produce exquisite sounds that cause the devas to give rise to the fetters of the five desires.
On both sides of this road run two rivers called Dīrgha, each twenty yojanas long and ten yojanas wide, naturally filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities.
On both sides of that river, it is constructed with bricks made of the four precious substances, as described previously.
The four-sided stairways of the four precious substances along the banks of that river are also as described previously.
Within these river waters there are five kinds of precious flowers, as previously described;

four kinds of precious boats float upon them, along with eight kinds of water-play equipment. One may board these boats to travel and observe at a speed according to one’s own will, all as previously described.

When the gods therein require those flowers, they arrive as soon as they think of them; by virtue of their excellent karmic retribution, a rain of various precious flowers falls, scattering over the gods.

Furthermore, there is a special wind that blows upon the flower garlands, so that whatever ornaments are required for their respective bodies—whether for the body, arms, head, or feet—they naturally adhere to them.
On both outer banks of the two rivers, five kinds of jewel-trees stand in dense rows, filling the space entirely; the rest is as previously described.
Between these trees are various jewel ponds and jewel palaces, wherein male and female devas dwell together, and immeasurable hosts of devas fill the land.
Why is this garden named Saṃkha?
Within it there is a great pond named Caitra, and within it there is a tree also named Caitra; from this tree grow various kinds of flowers.
This garden alone possesses it, while other gardens do not.
Furthermore, there is a reason why it is named Caitraratha.
At that time, when the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven wish to enter this garden, they adorn their bodies with various precious ornaments of the most exquisite and sublime nature.
Adorned with various weapons as if for the time of battle, they mounted various vehicles and entered this grove.

While within the grove and when about to depart, they took the various exquisite flowers of the *citrataṛu* trees to adorn their vehicles; the shafts, yokes, hubs, and rims were all fully decorated, and it was thus for every single vehicle.
The radiance emitted by these *citrataṛu* tree blossoms, as well as the celestial bodies' necklaces and the various precious chariots, mutually reflect and enhance one another.
By this cause and condition, manifold lights gather within this wondrous grove.
For this reason, it is called the Saṃkhyāvana Park;
furthermore, it has a natural name, Saṃkhyāvana Park.
This meaning was spoken by the Blessed Buddha.
Thus have I heard. Chapter Eleven:

The Garden of Harsh Speech. Twenty yojanas outside the threshold of the southern gate of the Great City of Sudarśana, there is a garden belonging to the Trāyastriṃśa devas called Akkosa (Harsh Speech).

In the garden is a great pond named Durbhāṣita, one hundred yojanas square and likewise deep; it is filled with celestial water, and its bottom and banks are lined with bricks made of the four precious substances, as described above;
there are stairways of the four precious substances and flowers of five kinds of jewels, also as described above.
There are four kinds of precious boats and eight water-sports.

Whenever the gods therein require those flowers, they arrive as soon as they think of them; by virtue of their excellent karmic retribution, a rain of various precious flowers falls, scattering over the gods.

Furthermore, there is a special wind that blows upon the various flower garlands; according to whatever bodily adornments are required, they naturally attach themselves to the body, arms, head, and feet.
On the banks of these ponds, trees made of the five kinds of jewels stand in rows, filling the area completely; the rest is as described above.
The spaces between those trees and within the various jeweled halls and palaces were completely filled with male and female devas dwelling there, as described above.
This garden was one thousand yojanas in circumference and one-third of that in diameter, surrounded by a golden wall.
This city was one yojana in height, with its battlements being half a yojana high; the city gates were two yojanas high, and the gate towers were one and a half yojanas high.
At intervals of ten yojanas there was a gate, making ninety-nine gates, plus one small gate, totaling one hundred gates.
These gates are composed of various jewels and adorned with exquisite mani gems, like the exquisite carpets of the northern regions, featuring all manner of intricate carvings and engravings.
This gate is also guarded by four armies, as described above.
The sevenfold outer enclosures of precious railings are also as described above.
It is surrounded by sevenfold groves of *tāla* trees, also as described above.
Between those trees are various jeweled ponds, each separated by a hundred bows, adorned in every way as described above;
they also contain the five kinds of precious flowers, likewise as described above.
As for the boats made of the four jewels, they are also as described above.

The five kinds of jewel trees on the banks of the ponds are also as described above, up to the pavilions and palaces made of the four jewels, which are the dwelling places of the male and female devas.
Beyond the city are three tiers of precious moats; the rest is as described above.

Each individual moat is two yojanas wide and one and a half yojanas deep, shaped like the mouth of a jar—broad at the bottom and narrow at the top—and filled with celestial waters, all as described above.
Within these moats, there are various palaces for the court ladies arranged in rows.
Beyond the threefold moats, the area is surrounded by groves of trees made of the seven precious substances, as described above.

At that time, in the outer grove, all the flowers were in full bloom and radiant; the goddesses played music and sang songs, while the devaputras emerged from the Kuṭaśodhana Garden to observe and listen.
When the devaputras played music and sang songs in the outer grove, the goddesses within the garden also came out to observe and listen.
The female devas within the garden again performed music, and the male devas outside entered the garden to watch and listen;
the male devas within the garden also performed music, and the female devas outside likewise entered the garden to listen.
For this reason, they enjoy various forms of play and pleasure.

From the southern gate of the Great City of Sudarśana to the northern gate of the Uddāla Garden, the intervening road is twenty yojanas long and ten yojanas wide. Its ground is made entirely of lapis lazuli, smooth and soft, adorned with various jewels. It is like a magnificent carpet from the northern lands, complete with all manner of human and non-human figures, birds, beasts, flowers, and grasses; it is also like an earring composed of many precious gems.
The form and appearance of that road are likewise so.
As soon as the foot is set down, it sinks; as soon as the foot is lifted, it rises. Its path is as soft and supple as *tūla* cotton or silk-cotton (*kārpāsa*).
It is adorned with three types of leather straps, each of which is composed of the four precious gems.

Each layer of hide is encircled by three tiers of precious bells; each precious bell is composed of the four jewels, and when stirred by a gentle breeze, they produce wondrous sounds that can cause the devas to give rise to the bonds of the five desires.
On both sides of this road run two rivers called Long Shape (Dīrghākāra), each twenty yojanas long and ten yojanas wide, naturally filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities.
Both banks of that river were constructed and adorned with bricks made of the four precious substances; the rest is as previously described.
The four-sided stairways of the four precious substances along the river’s perimeter are also as previously described.
Within these river waters there are five kinds of precious flowers, as previously described;

four kinds of precious boats float upon them, along with eight kinds of water-play equipment. One may board these boats to travel and observe at a speed according to one’s own will, all as previously described.
Within this realm, whenever the various devas require those flowers, they arrive as soon as they think of them due to their virtuous karmic retribution.
A rain of manifold precious flowers falls, scattering over the devas.

Furthermore, there are distinct winds that blow upon the flower garlands; according to whatever bodily ornaments each requires—whether for the body, arms, head, or feet—they naturally adhere to those very parts.
On the outer banks of the two rivers, five kinds of jewel trees are arranged in rows and fill the space entirely; the rest is as previously described.
Between these trees are various jewel ponds and jewel palaces where male and female devas dwell together, and immeasurable multitudes fill the land.
Why is this garden named "Harsh Speech"?
Within the garden there is a great pond called "Harsh Speech," and within it there is a tree also named "Harsh Speech," and that tree has flowers likewise named "Harsh Speech."
Only this garden possesses it; it does not exist elsewhere.
Furthermore, there is a causal condition known as "harsh speech.
At that time, when the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven wish to enter this garden, they engage in such quarreling, reflecting with vitarka and vicāra:
"We shall now go there to attack and wage war against the asuras.

Furthermore, they harbor mutual jealousy toward one another, are greedily attached to the five desires, and contend over who comes first or last; because of these matters, they utter various evil words. For this reason, this place is named the Garden of Evil Speech (Durbhāṣita).
Furthermore, there is that which arises spontaneously called "harsh speech.
This meaning was taught by the Blessed One, the Buddha.
Thus have I heard.

12. Chapter on the Miscellaneous Garden (Miśrakavana-varga), the Twelfth. "From the threshold outside the western gate of the Great City of Sudarśana to the eastern gate of the Miscellaneous Garden, the road between them is twenty *yojana*s long."

Within these gardens of the Trāyastriṃśa devas, there is a square pond named Citra-udaka (Variegated Pond), measuring one hundred yojanas on each side and likewise in depth. It is filled with celestial water, and its bottom and banks are lined with bricks made of the four precious substances; the rest is as described above.
There are stairways made of the four precious substances and five kinds of jewel flowers, also as described above.
There are four kinds of precious boats and eight water-sports.

Whenever the devas therein require those flowers, they arrive as soon as they think of them; by virtue of their wholesome karmic retribution, a rain of various precious flowers falls, showering upon the devas.

Furthermore, there is a special wind that blows upon the various flower garlands; according to what each part of the body requires for adornment, the ornaments naturally attach themselves to the body, arms, head, and feet.
Along the banks of these ponds, trees made of five kinds of jewels stand in rows and fill the area, as previously described.
In the spaces between those trees and within the various jeweled halls and palaces, male and female devas dwell in great numbers, as described above.
This garden is one thousand yojanas in circumference and one-third of that in diameter, surrounded by a golden wall.
This city is one yojana high, with battlements half a yojana high; the city gates are two yojanas high, and the gate towers are one and a half yojanas high.
At intervals of ten yojanas there is one gate; with ninety-nine such gates and one additional small gate, they total one hundred gates.
These gates are composed of various jewels and adorned with exquisite maṇi gems, like the exquisite carpets of the northern regions, featuring all manner of intricate carvings and engravings.
This gate is also guarded by four armies, as described above.
The ten layers of precious railings outside are also as described above.
It is surrounded by seven layers of *tāla* groves, also as described above.
Between those trees are various jeweled ponds, each separated by a distance of one hundred bows, adorned in various ways as described above.
There are flowers made of the five kinds of jewels, boats made of the four jewels, and the eight types of water sports, and so forth.
The five kinds of jewel trees on the banks of the pond are also as described above, up to the pavilions made of the four jewels, which are the dwellings of the male and female devas.
Outside these cities are three tiers of jewel moats, the rest being as described above.

Each of these moats is two yojanas wide and one and a half yojanas deep; their shape is like the mouth of a jar, being broad at the bottom and narrow at the top, filled with celestial waters, all as previously described.
Within these moats, there are palaces for various court ladies arranged in rows.
Outside the threefold moats, the area is surrounded by groves of trees made of the seven treasures, as described above.
At that time, all the flowers in the outer grove were in full bloom and radiant; the goddesses played music and sang songs, while the devaputras emerged from the Varied Garden to come out and listen.
When the devaputras played music and sang songs in the outer grove, the goddesses within the garden also came out to listen.
The female devas within the garden again performed music, and the male devas from outside entered the garden to observe and listen;
the male devas within the garden also performed music, and the female devas from outside likewise entered the garden to listen.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, they enjoy various forms of play and pleasure.

From the western gate of the Great City of Sudarśana to the eastern gate of the Caitraratha Garden, the road is twenty yojanas long and ten yojanas wide. Its ground is made entirely of lapis lazuli, smooth and soft, adorned with various jewels; it is like a magnificent carpet from the northern lands, complete with all manner of human and non-human figures, birds, beasts, flowers, and grasses, and is also like an earring composed of many precious gems—the form and appearance of that road are likewise so.
As soon as one’s foot touches it, it sinks; as soon as the foot is lifted, it rises again. Its path is as soft and supple as *tūla* cotton or silk-cotton (*kārpāsa*).
It is adorned with three types of leather straps, each of which is composed of the four precious substances.

Each layer of hide is encircled by three tiers of precious bells; each precious bell is composed of the four jewels, and when stirred by a gentle breeze, they produce exquisite sounds that cause the devas to give rise to the fetters of the five desires.
On both sides of this road run two rivers named Dīrgha, each twenty yojanas long and ten yojanas wide, naturally filled with water possessing the eight virtues.
On both sides of that river, the embankments were constructed of bricks made of the four precious substances; the rest is as previously described.
The four-sided stairways of the four precious substances along the banks of the river are also as previously described.
In these river waters there are five kinds of precious lotuses, as previously described;

four kinds of precious boats float within them, along with eight kinds of water-play equipment. One may travel by boat to view the scenery at a speed according to one's own will, all as described above.

Among them, whenever the devas require those flowers, they arrive immediately upon thought; because of their virtuous karmic retribution, a rain of various precious flowers falls, scattering over the devas.

Furthermore, there is a special wind that blows the flower garlands, so that whatever ornaments are required for their respective bodies—whether for the torso, arms, head, or feet—they naturally adhere to them.
On both outer banks of the two rivers, five kinds of precious trees stand in dense rows, filling the area; the rest is as described above.
Between these trees are various jeweled ponds and halls made of many treasures, where male and female devas dwell together, and immeasurable hosts of devas fill the land.
Why is this garden called the Variegated Garden?
It is because within this garden there is a great pond named the Variegated Pond, as well as variegated trees and various variegated flowers; these exist only in this garden and not elsewhere.
Furthermore, there is a cause and condition for which it is named the Grove of Mixture (Miśrakāvana).

At that time, the male and female devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven enter this grove and gather in great numbers; they engage in singing, dancing, music, and various amusements, all mingling together in a state of total intermixture.
When the other gardens assemble, all the gods from the outer regions are forbidden from entering and are completely excluded;

however, when this garden assembles, there is no obstruction, and the gods of the great city as well as the outer gods enter the garden to play and enjoy themselves together in mingled company. For this reason, it is called the Garden of Mixture (Miśraka).
Furthermore, there is a natural grove named Miśrakāvana.
This meaning was spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Thus have I heard.
Chapter 13: The Pāriyātra Grove Twenty yojanas outside the gate in the northeast corner of the great city of Sudarśana, there is a great grove belonging to the Trāyastriṃśa gods called Pāriyātra.

In this garden there is a square pond, also named Pāriyātra, measuring one hundred yojanas on each side and the same in depth. It is filled with celestial water, and its bottom and banks are lined with bricks made of the four precious substances; the rest is as previously described.
The jeweled staircases on its four sides are also as previously described, and the five kinds of precious flowers are likewise as previously described.
There are four kinds of precious boats and eight kinds of playthings that move according to the speed of one's mind.

Whenever the gods therein require those flowers, they arrive as soon as they are thought of; by virtue of their excellent karmic retribution, a rain of various precious flowers falls, scattering over the gods.
Furthermore, there is a special wind that blows upon the flower garlands; according to whatever bodily adornments are required, they naturally attach themselves to the body, arms, head, and feet.
Upon the banks of those ponds, five kinds of jewel-trees stand in rows, filling the area completely, as described previously.
In the spaces between those trees and within the various jeweled halls and palaces, male and female devas dwell in great numbers, as described above.
Within the garden is a tree named Pāriyātra, also called Kovidāra.

This tree grows to full maturity with a lovely appearance; its branches and leaves overlap one another, dense and thick with foliage, remaining for a long time without withering, such that no wind or rain can penetrate it.

It is like a master florist adorning flower garlands and ear-ornaments; the form and appearance of this tree are likewise lovely. Above, it is like a parasol, with layers covering one another; it is one hundred yojanas in height, and its base is broad and straight, entirely free of knots or swellings, with branches appearing only at fifty yojanas from the ground.

The trunk of the tree is five yojanas in diameter and fifteen yojanas in circumference; each of its branches extends fifty yojanas outward, spanning one hundred yojanas across the intervals between them, with a total circumference of three hundred yojanas.
