Below is a precious stone named Banzhoujian-bala, fifty yojanas in length and ten yojanas in width; it is composed entirely of lapis lazuli, soft, smooth, and lovely, adorned with various jewels.

It is like a magnificent woolen carpet from the northern lands, intricately carved and engraved with various figures of humans and non-humans, birds, beasts, flowers, and grasses, all fully represented;
it is also like an earring composed of many jewels—the *paṭṭa-cīvara* robe is likewise so.

When his feet step down, they sink; when he lifts them, they immediately spring back up, like *tūla* cotton or silk-cotton; the body of Bandhula Kambalabhadrika is likewise soft and supple in this way.
It is adorned with three kinds of leather straps, each strap being composed of the four jewels.

Each strap is encircled by three tiers of jeweled bells, and each bell is likewise composed of the four jewels. When stirred by a gentle breeze, they produce exquisite sounds that can cause the devas to become bound by the five desires; the rest is as described above.
The stairways on its four sides are composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
Throughout the garden there are ponds, as described above;
even the pavilions and halls made of the four jewels, which serve as the dwellings for the male and female devas, are as described above.
This garden is one thousand yojanas in circumference and one-third of that in diameter, surrounded by a golden wall.
This wall is one yojana high, with battlements half a yojana high; the city gates are two yojanas high, and the gate towers are one and a half yojanas high.
Every ten yojanas there is one gate; with ninety-nine such gates and one additional small gate, they total one hundred gates.
These gates are composed of various jewels and adorned with exquisite maṇi gems, like the exquisite carpets of the northern regions, featuring all manner of carvings and engravings.
This gate is also guarded by four armies, as described above.
Outside are sevenfold jeweled railings, also as described above.
It is surrounded by sevenfold groves of *tāla* trees, also as described above.

Between those trees are various jeweled ponds, each separated by a distance of one hundred bows, adorned in various ways as described above; there are five kinds of precious flowers, also as described above;
and there are four jeweled boats, likewise as described above.

On the banks of that pond are trees made of five kinds of jewels, as described above, up to the pavilions and palaces made of the four precious substances, which serve as the dwellings for the male and female devas.
Beyond the city are three tiers of precious moats; the rest is as described above.
Each moat is two yojanas wide and one and a half yojanas deep, shaped like the mouth of a jar—broad at the bottom and narrow at the top—and filled with celestial water, all as described above.
Within these moats, there are various palaces for the court ladies arranged in rows.
Outside the threefold moats, the area is surrounded by groves of trees made of the seven precious substances, as described above.

At that time, all the flowers in the outer grove were in full bloom and radiant; the goddesses played music and sang songs, while the sons of gods emerged from the Pāriyātra grove to observe and listen.
As the sons of gods played music and sang songs in the outer grove, the goddesses within the garden also came out to observe and listen.
The female devas within the garden also performed music, and the male devas from outside entered the garden to watch and listen;
the male devas within the garden likewise performed music, and the female devas from outside also entered the garden to listen.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, they enjoy various forms of play and pleasure.

From the gate at the northeast corner of the great city of Sudarśana to the gate at the southwest corner of the garden, the road between them is twenty yojanas long and ten yojanas wide; its ground is made entirely of lapis lazuli, smooth and soft, and adorned with all kinds of jewels.

It is like a magnificent woolen carpet from the northern lands, fully adorned with various human and non-human figures, birds, beasts, flowers, and grasses; it is also like an earring composed of many jewels—the forms and features of that road are likewise so.
As soon as one places the foot, it sinks; as soon as the foot is lifted, it rises again. The path is as soft as tūla-cotton or śālmalī-cotton, and it is likewise so.
It is adorned with three kinds of leather straps, each strap being composed of the four precious substances.

Each layer of hide is encircled by three tiers of precious bells; each precious bell is composed of the four jewels, and when stirred by a gentle breeze, they produce exquisite sounds that cause the devas to give rise to the bonds of the five desires.
On both sides of this road are two rivers named Dīrgha, each twenty yojanas long and ten yojanas wide, naturally filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities.
On both sides of that river, the embankments were constructed of bricks made of the four precious substances, as described previously.
The four-sided stairways of the four precious substances along the banks of the river were also as described previously.
Within these river waters there are five kinds of precious flowers, as previously described;

four kinds of precious boats float and drift therein, along with eight kinds of water-play equipment; one may travel by boat to view the scenery at whatever speed one desires, all as previously described.

When the gods therein require those flowers, they arrive immediately according to their thoughts; because of their virtuous karmic retribution, a rain of various precious flowers falls, scattering over the gods.

Furthermore, there is a special wind that blows upon the flower garlands, so that whatever ornaments are required for their respective bodies—whether for the body, arms, head, or feet—they naturally adhere to them.
On the outer banks of the two rivers, five kinds of jewel trees stand in dense rows, filling the space; the rest is as previously described.
Between these trees are various jewel ponds and jewel palaces where male and female devas dwell together, and immeasurable hosts of devas fill the land.
Thus the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, said: "Bhikṣus!
At that time, the leaves of the Pārijāta-kovidāra tree of the Trāyastriṃśa devas turn yellow and are about to fall; at that moment, the devas leap for joy and exult, saying these words:"
"At this time, the Pārijāta tree of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven has its leaves turning yellow; it will not be long before they wither and fall. "Monks!
When the leaves of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven's Pārijāta tree have fallen, at that time the devas leap for joy and exult, saying these words:"
"The leaves of the Pārijāta tree of the devas have already fallen; before long, its sprouts will emerge. Monks!
At that time, once the sprouts of the Pārijāta tree of the Trāyastriṃśa devas had emerged, all the devas leaped for joy and spoke thus:
"At this time, once the Pāriyātra tree has produced its sprouts, it will before long manifest a pale blue color. "Monks!
When the Pāriyātra tree manifests that pale blue color, the devas at that time rejoice and leap for joy, saying these words:"
"When the Pāriyātra tree manifests its pale blue color, it will not be long before it produces flower buds. Monks!
At that time, once the Pāriyātra tree has produced its flower buds, the devas then rejoice and leap for joy, saying these words:
"Once the *pārijāta* tree has produced buds, its flowers will soon begin to open slightly.
Once they have opened slightly, the gods at that time will leap for joy and exult, saying:
'Since the *pārijāta* tree has already begun to open slightly, it will soon be fully blossomed.'"
"Monks! When the Pāriyātra tree has thus blossomed, the color of its flowers illuminates fifty yojanas, and their exquisite fragrance also perfumes fifty yojanas."
When there is an easterly wind and rain, it blows the fragrance of this tree’s flowers, perfuming the western direction for one hundred yojanas.
When there is a westerly wind and rain, it blows the fragrance of these flowers, perfuming the eastern direction for one hundred yojanas.
When the south wind and rain prevail, they waft the fragrance of these flowers for one hundred yojanas to the north.
When the north wind and rain prevail, they waft the fragrance of these flowers for one hundred yojanas to the south.
"Monks! Such is the supernatural power and majestic virtue of the Pārijāta tree of the Trāyastriṃśa devas. Monks!"

If a disciple of the Buddha relies upon the True Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata, then by virtue of the faculty of faith, they leave their own home to cultivate the homeless life; for this purpose, they give rise to a resolute mind.
“Monks! Such a person is like the *pāriyātra* tree when its leaves turn yellow.
“Monks! [he said.]
At that time, the disciples of the Buddha— having shaved off their hair and beards, donned the dharma robes, and departed from their own homes to practice the homeless life—
O Bhikṣus!
such persons are like the leaves of the Pāriyātra tree when they have already fallen.

"Monks! If a disciple of the Buddha, having departed from all sensual desires and departed from all unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, cultivates and dwells in the first dhyāna."
"Monks! Such a person is like the pāriyātra tree when its sprouts first emerge. Monks!"

At that time, because applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) have already been stilled, and by relying on the internal clarity of the mind through the single means of mental activity, one enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and accompanied by joy and bliss, having cultivated it.
"Monks! Such a person is like the pāriyātra tree when it displays its pale blue color. Monks!"

At that time, the disciples of the Buddha, through detachment from joy, abide in equanimity (*upekṣā*), with right mindfulness (*sati*) and right clear comprehension (*sampajañña*); their bodies experience bliss.
Therefore, the Noble Teacher has given this instruction: "Abiding in bliss, with equanimity and mindfulness, one cultivates the third dhyāna and enters into its middle abiding."
"Monks! Such a person is like a pāriyātra tree when its flower buds are beginning to form. Monks!"

If a disciple of the Buddha, because suffering has been extinguished, because pleasure has already passed away, and because former sorrow and joy have been completely extinguished, dwells having entered and abided in the fourth dhyāna—neither painful nor pleasant, with purity of equanimity and mindfulness.
Such a person is like a *pāriyātra* tree when its flowers are just beginning to open. Bhikṣus!

If a disciple of the Buddha, because all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted, attains the outflow-free liberation of mind and the liberation through wisdom, having realized them in the present life and dwelling therein—his birth being ended, the holy life fulfilled, what was to be done accomplished, and there being no further state of existence—he thereby attains this knowledge.
"Monks! Such a person is like the pāriyātra tree when all its blossoms have opened. Monks!"

These bhikṣus have exhausted all outflows, perfected the cultivation of the path, and attained liberation through right wisdom; with their fetters exhausted, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and others spoke words of praise, saying:
"O virtuous friends!..."

That person there, of such-and-such a surname and such-and-such a name, from such-and-such a commandery and county in all lands, having left his own home to cultivate the homeless path, is a bhikṣu of such-and-such a name.

Because these ordained disciples and their followers have exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), they have realized in this very life the liberation of mind through the absence of outflows (*anāsravacittavimukti*) and the liberation through wisdom (*prajñāvimukti*). Abiding therein, they have reached the end of birth, perfected the path of cultivation, completed all that was to be done, and have no further existence; thus, they have attained this knowledge.

These bhikṣus, whose outflows are exhausted, who are liberated through right knowledge, and for whom existence has been extinguished, possess such supernormal powers and majestic virtue as that of the pāriyātra tree.
At that time, all the Pārijāta trees of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven blossomed; furthermore, the various devas who guard the grove went to Śakra’s abode and addressed Śakra, saying:
"Lord of Devas!..."
"Since the Pāriyātra tree has fully blossomed, the World-Honored One should know that the time has come.

Furthermore, among the devas there is an elephant king named Airāvaṇa, which serves as the mount for traveling through the gardens; its body is nine yojanas long and three yojanas high, with its proportions perfectly symmetrical.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra sent a messenger to inform the elephant, saying:
"Good friend!
The Pārijātaka tree has now blossomed in its entirety; the gods shall go there to enter the garden for recreation. Therefore, you must now adorn yourself."
Upon hearing the messenger’s words, the elephant leaped for joy.
Just as when people first seek a marriage alliance or welcome a bride, experiencing all manner of auspicious and rare events, the joy of the elephant king was likewise so.

At that time, the Elephant King transformed his head into thirty-three heads; each head had six tusks, and on each tusk was a pond made of the seven precious gems. In each pond grew seven lotuses, on each lotus grew seven flowers, on each flower grew seven leaves, and on each leaf were seven celestial maidens. Thus, these celestial musicians, arranged in seven times seven tiers, surrounded the lotus seeds, appearing most lovely.
By these causes and conditions, all the adornments of various flowers were fully perfected.

The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven paid homage to Śakra as their leader; they ascended the elephant first and sat according to the central head, with sixteen gods on each of the left and right sides.
All the devas each thought to themselves,
"I am sitting in the central seat.
If this were true, then only Śakra, Lord of the Devas, would sit alone in the central seat.
Once the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three had first mounted the elephant, the rest of the celestial hosts ascended in succession.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had two crown princes—one named Candana and the other named Supriya—who served as the greatest generals of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven; they also ascended the elephant.

Among the various exquisite goddesses, there were most excellent ones: first, Āraṇvasā; second, Miśrakeśī; third, Puṇḍarīkā; fourth, Nīlā; fifth, Aruṇā; sixth, Eṇiprabhā; seventh, Śubhāprabhā; eighth, Padmā; ninth, Supadmā; tenth, Mādhukaravatī. These and other such women likewise ascended upon the elephant.

Furthermore, there were male celestial beings: first, Āraṇemi; second, Daṭṭhāraha; third, Sunimmita; and fourth, Vessavaṇa. These deities likewise ascended the elephant and stood together upon it, singing and playing music.
When all the devas had mounted the elephant, the Elephant King leaped for joy and exulted.

It was as if various kings had received their consecration, or as when a youth stands at the threshold of his wedding; having completed the practice of the True Dharma, he adorns his body and head with exquisite flowers—the Elephant King’s joy was likewise so.
At that time, the elephant king let out a great thunderous roar, sent down sweet rain, and flashed forth lightning.
The elephant king then transformed himself into celestial maidens atop flowers, performing songs and dances with various graceful gestures.
The celestial maidens and male musicians performed songs and dances to provide musical entertainment.

At that time, the Elephant King let out a great thunderous roar as he galloped and then walked slowly, like one stringing a flower garland; thus he circled three times and arrived at the Pāriyātra garden.
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven descended together from above and ascended the Mañjūṣaka jewel-stone.
If they were not seated around it completely, the stone would grow larger; this is due to the merit of the gods.

This elephant king, Airāvaṇa, further transformed his body into that of a celestial youth, wearing jeweled armlets and jeweled earrings, adorned with various ornaments, and enjoying the play and pleasures associated with the five objects of sensory desire.

Other sons of gods ride separately upon elephants, horses, chariots, and palatial towers; furthermore, various devas board ships made of many jewels and enter this garden from the long-shaped river with speed as swift as they desire.
Within that garden, there is a separate area for singers, a separate area for dancers, a separate area for string and wind instruments, and a separate area for great assemblies.
Therein, the devas enjoy the five sensory desires for four celestial months, fully engaged in playful delights;
according to the days and months of the human realm, this amounts to twelve thousand years.
The lifespan of the gods is ten years plus one-third; within this period, their time in the gardens is fully exhausted.
Among the various gardens of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, these six are the largest, and there are also numerous large and small gardens spread throughout the heavens.
This meaning was spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Thus have I heard.

Chapter Fourteen: The City of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Chapter Fourteen: The City of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

“Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, has four peaks in the east, west, south, and north. Its eastern peak is composed of pure gold; its western peak is composed of white silver; its northern peak is composed of lapis lazuli; and its southern peak is composed of crystal.”
Furthermore, it is composed of all kinds of jewels and abounds in the seven precious substances.

As for these four peaks, they are broad at the top and narrow at the base, resembling lotus buds. Their narrowest point is one thousand five hundred yojanas in circumference; their widest point has a diameter of seven hundred yojanas and a circumference of two thousand one hundred yojanas.

In these four summit regions there are many beasts, as well as various birds, lions, tigers, and leopards; all are born through transformation and all partake of the divine *sudhā* nectar, never harming one another.
There is Vajrapāṇi, upon whom all the devas rely for their dwelling.
There are four Yugandhara mountains:
first, the eastern; second, the western; third, the northern; and fourth, the southern.
To the east lies Mount Gandhamādana, which has two peaks;
the same is true for the west, north, and south.

The two eastern peaks are composed of pure gold; the two western peaks are composed of white silver; the two northern peaks are composed of lapis lazuli; and the two southern peaks are composed of crystal.
Furthermore, it is composed of all kinds of jewels and possesses seven distinct natures.

It is broad at the top and narrow at the bottom, shaped like a lotus bud. Its narrowest point has a diameter of three hundred and fifty yojanas and a circumference of one thousand five hundred yojanas; its widest point has a diameter of five hundred yojanas and a circumference of one thousand five hundred yojanas.

In these eight summit regions there are many beasts, as well as various birds, lions, tigers, and leopards; all are born through transformation and all partake of the divine *sūdha* flavor, never harming one another.
There is Vajrapāṇi, and the various devas dwell therein.
Thus, each successive mountain peak is twice the size of the one before it; reaching the seventh mountain, Nimindhara, there are five hundred and twelve peaks in total.
These seven mountain peaks are high and broad, decreasing by half in each successive direction outward.

Between the two peaks of Mount Yugandhara in the east, there is a kingdom named Dhṛtarāṣṭra, one thousand yojanas in circumference, surrounded by a golden wall one yojana high. The battlements are half a yojana high, the city gates are two yojanas high, and the gate towers are one and a half yojanas high.
Every ten yojanas there is one gate; with ninety-nine such gates and one additional small gate, they total one hundred gates.
These gates are composed of various jewels and adorned with exquisite maṇi gems, like a magnificent carpet intricately carved and inlaid in diverse patterns.
This gate is also guarded by four armies, as described above;
the sevenfold outer enclosures of precious railings are also as described above.
It is likewise surrounded by sevenfold groves of *tāla* trees, as described above.
Between those trees are various jeweled ponds, each separated by a distance of one hundred bow-lengths; they are adorned in various ways as described above.
There are five kinds of precious flowers, also as described above.
The four-jeweled boats are also as described above.
The five kinds of jewel-trees on the banks of the ponds are also as described above, up to the pavilions and palaces made of the four jewels, which are the dwellings of the male and female devas.
Outside the city wall are three tiers of precious moats; the rest is as described above.
Each moat is two yojanas wide and one and a half yojanas deep, shaped like the mouth of a jar—broad at the bottom and narrow at the top—and filled with celestial waters, all as described above.
Within these moats, there are various palaces for the court ladies arranged in rows.
Outside the threefold moats, the area is surrounded by groves of trees made of the seven precious substances, as described above.

At that time, in the outer groves, all the flowers were in full bloom and radiant; the goddesses played various kinds of music. Then the sons of the gods emerged from the great city to view and listen to the music, and the goddesses likewise emerged from the great city to view and listen to the music; through these causes and conditions, they enjoyed various forms of play and pleasure.

In the southwest corner of the city of Dhṛtarāṣṭra is the dwelling place of the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra. It is surrounded by a golden wall two hundred and fifty yojanas in circumference, one yojana in height, with battlements half a yojana high; the city gates are two yojanas high, and the gate towers are one and a half yojanas high.

It is surrounded by a golden wall and adorned in various ways, as described above.
Even up to the devaputras who fill the entire land, it is likewise so.

The circumference of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, increases by another four hundred yojanas, totaling one thousand six hundred yojanas. This is the fourth terrace; its breadth is fifty yojanas on each of its four sides, as are the three upper terraces. Rising fifty yojanas from the surface of the ocean, this is the fourth terrace of Sumeru, the King of Mountains; its breadth is fifty yojanas, equal to that of the third terrace, and its thickness is likewise the same.
It is surrounded by golden walls one yojana high, with parapets one and a half yojanas high; the city gates are two yojanas high, and the gate towers are one and a half yojanas high.
Every ten yojanas there was a gate; there were countless thousands of gates, composed of various jewels and adorned with diverse mani-gems.

They were like exquisite carpets from the northern regions, where no detail—whether humans, non-humans, dragons, beasts, grasses, trees, or various flowers—is left unrepresented; they were also like earrings complete with every kind of jewel.
These city gates were likewise.
At the sides of all the city gates, the fourfold army of elephants and horses provides defense; this is for the protection of the realm, for recreation, and for adornment.
There are various jeweled ponds, the bottoms and banks of which are lined with bricks made of the four precious substances.
Even up to the various devaputras who fill the entire land, it is likewise so.
This fourth terrace is the dwelling place of the armies of the Four Great Kings.
Beyond this layer, extending another four hundred and fifty yojanas with a circumference of one thousand eight hundred yojanas, lies the abode of various nāgas and garuḍas.
"The various tiers of Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, are each fifty yojanas in thickness.
The various tiers within the ocean are all dwelling places for asuras."
These asuras go forth to wage war for the sake of five things belonging to the devas.
What are these five? First, the flavor of *sūda*;
second, the level ground of the devas; third, the gardens and groves of the devas; fourth, the cities and towns of the devas; and fifth, the celestial maidens of the devas.
For these five matters, they go forth to attack the devas;
the devas likewise, desiring those same five matters, go forth to attack the asuras.
What are these five?

First, the *asura* flavor of *sūta*; second, the level ground of the *asuras*; third, the groves and forests of the *asuras*; fourth, the cities and towns of the *asuras*; fifth, the young maidens of the *asuras*.
For these five reasons, they went forth to strike the asuras.
At that time, when the asuras came to strike the devas, they first fought with the nāgas and birds at the edge of the waters; if they were not victorious, they would retreat back to their own abodes.
If they won the battle, they ascended to the lowest tier, where they joined the armies of the Four Great Kings and the various nāgas and birds, all ascending this tier to fight together at once.
If the asuras are defeated, they retreat back to their original abodes.

When they are victorious in battle, they ascend to the second tier and fight simultaneously with the armies of the Four Great Kings, the gods who carry precious vessels, and the various nāgas and birds.
If they do not prevail in time, they retreat back to their original abodes;

if they are victorious in battle, they ascend to the third tier from below to fight simultaneously against the gods of the Heaven of Constant Victory (Suyāma), those who hold precious vessels, the armies of the Four Great Kings, and the various nāgas and birds.
If they do not prevail in time, they retreat back to their original positions;

if they are victorious in battle, they ascend and descend through the four tiers, engaging in combat simultaneously with the Mālādhāra devas, the lower devas, the armies of the Four Great Kings, and the various nāgas and birds.
If they are defeated, they return to their original abodes;
if they are victorious in battle, they ascend to the summit of Mount Sumeru.
Then these Garland-Holding Devas go to the abode of Śakra and report these matters to him as follows:
"Venerable Sir!
The asuras have arrived.

At that time, Śakra drove a chariot yoked with a thousand horses, using the robes of arhats as its banners and standards; the four divisions of elephants and cavalry remained unmixed as the host of troops surrounded him and proceeded to the site of battle.
At that time, the thirty-two celestial kings of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, each likewise surrounded by their fourfold armies, also arrived at the site of battle.
The two crown princes, Candana and Subī, also surrounded by their four armies, went together to the site of battle.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings were also surrounded by their four armies and went together to the site of battle.
The Sun and Moon Devas were likewise surrounded by their four armies and went together to the site of battle.
Thus, these various devas, together with General Purandara, engaged in a great battle against the asuras at that location.
The elephant army fought with the elephant army, and the same applied to the chariot, cavalry, and infantry armies.
"When engaged in battle, those who arrive first will surely retreat from the front; such is the nature of things.
Thus did the Buddha, the World-Honored One, speak.
"O Bhikṣus!"
In the past, when the devas and asuras were engaged in battle, as their armies clashed with blades drawn, the celestial army prevailed and the asuras retreated in dispersal. Monks!
When the asuras retreat, they run facing south, returning to their original abodes while being pursued by the devas.
Bhikṣus! At that time, the asuras think to themselves:
"The gods have achieved a great victory; we are retreating and dispersing.
The gods pursue us with great urgency; our army must still engage in a decisive battle.
During this second engagement, the gods achieved a great victory, and the asuras retreated once more.
At that time, the asura turned his face southward and fled back to his original abode, while the devas pursued and drove him back.
Bhikṣus! At that moment, the asura reflected once more:
"The gods have achieved great victory, and we are being driven back in retreat.
The gods pursue us with great urgency; our forces are not yet exhausted, and we must certainly resolve this matter once more."
"Monks! During the third battle, the devas were again victorious.
The asuras retreated in dispersal and returned to their own city, where they remained with the gates closed."
"O Bhikṣu!
At that time, the asura reflected again:
'I have already entered the city; even if the devas come, they will not be able to attack me.'"
"Monks! The devas also think thus:
'Since the asuras have already entered their city, it can no longer be attacked.'"
At that time, the various devas surrounded him on all sides, causing his domain to be confined within the city walls.

The devas subsequently obtained the *sūdhā* essence of the asuras; they seized the level plains and the various gardens, and captured all the young maidens of the cities and towns. They took their wealth and treasures, and bound every male and female inhabitant without exception.
If the devas form the intention to enter that city, thinking:
"I and the asuras share food and drink; since we are kinsmen, I should go to visit them, coming and going at will, eating, drinking, and conversing."
Once they have entered the city, if they give rise to an inappropriate state of mind, because of that mind they naturally exit again. Why is this so?
Because this city is a place of fearlessness for the asuras.
The various devas dwell at will in this land; once the asura maidens have been captured and bound, they intend to take them back to the heavens when they depart.
At that time, the asuras wrap the *sūdhā* flavor and go to ransom their family members, entering the cities of the devas and inquiring after them everywhere.
If one sees one's kinsmen being appraised by the various devas as to their value—whether high or low—and if they are ransomed, they return home together;
it is likewise when the devas are defeated and captured.
In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is the Great City of Sudarśana, the dwelling place of Śakra Devānām Indra.
The city of the asuras is the dwelling place of the asura kings.
Just as there is the elephant king Airāvaṇa in the Caitraratha Park of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, so too the Asuras have an elephant king named Bhadrapāla, who travels through their pleasure groves.
Just as the elephant king Supratiṣṭhita is mounted by the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven during battle, so too is the elephant king Airāvaṇa mounted by the Asuras during battle.
Just as there are provinces, districts, and counties among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the realms of the Asuras are likewise.
The clothing, food and drink, and various ornaments of the Asuras are likewise like those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
with the exception of the Sudharmā Hall and the multi-storied pavilion of Vaijayanta.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Buddha.
Thus have I heard. Chapter Nineteen:
The Movement of the Sun and Moon. At a height of forty thousand *yojanas* above the land of Jambudvīpa, it is there that the sun and moon travel, level with Mount Sumeru and Mount Yugandhara.
These palaces of the sun and moon are perfectly round like drums.
This lunar palace is fifty yojanas in thickness and fifty yojanas in width, with a circumference of one hundred and fifty yojanas.

This lunar palace is composed of lapis lazuli and covered with silver; it consists predominantly of the element water, and at its lower limit, the water is even more abundant, such that the radiance at its lower limit is also most excellent.

This is its upper limit: it is surrounded by a golden wall; the wall is one yojana high, the battlements are half a yojana high, the city gates are two yojanas wide, and the gate towers are one and a half yojanas high.
Every ten yojanas there is one gate, totaling fourteen gates plus one small gate.
These city gates are composed of various precious jewels and adorned with diverse mani gems.

It is, for example, like a magnificent carpet from the northern lands, which contains every representation of humans and non-humans, dragons, beasts, grasses, trees, and various flowers; it is also like an ear-ornament, fully adorned and filled with a multitude of jewels.
These city gates are likewise so.

At the gates of this city, the fourfold army of elephants and chariots provides a magnificent array; therein gather the sons of the gods, adorned with armor and weapons, for the purpose of protecting the land and for their sport and adornment.
In every place, the jeweled ponds are filled with celestial water; their bottoms and banks are lined with bricks made of the four precious substances, as described above.
Even so, male and female devas fill them completely, just as previously stated.
This palace is called Candana; it is where the Moon Deva-son dwells.
It is also called Candana, for the palace and the deva-son are both named Candana.
Thus, this palace remained for more than forty kalpas; due to the predominant influence of the karma of sentient beings, it constantly moved while emitting light.
When the devaputra was present, the palace moved constantly; even when the deva was not there, the palace continued to move.
When the Son of Heaven returns, he descends into whichever palace is his destination.
This solar palace is fifty-one yojanas in thickness and fifty-one yojanas in width, with a circumference of one hundred and fifty-three yojanas.

This solar palace is composed of crystal and covered with red gold; it consists predominantly of the fire element, and its lower limit is even more abundant in the fire element, such that the radiance at its lower limit is also most excellent.

This is its upper limit: it is surrounded by a golden wall; the wall is one yojana high, the parapets are half a yojana high, the city gates are two yojanas wide, and the gate towers are one and a half yojanas high.
Every ten yojanas there is one gate; thus there are fourteen gates along with one small gate.
These city gates are composed of various jewels and adorned with diverse mani-gems.

It is like a magnificent carpet from the northern regions, upon which all manner of humans and non-humans, dragons, beasts, grasses, trees, and various flowers are depicted without exception; it is also like an ear-ornament, fully adorned and filled with every kind of jewel.
These city gates are likewise so.
At the side of these city gates, the fourfold army of elephants and chariots provides defense; this is for the purpose of protecting the kingdom, as well as for adornment and recreation.
Everywhere there are jewel ponds filled with celestial water, their bottoms and banks lined with bricks made of the four precious substances, as described above.
Even so, it is likewise filled with gods, both male and female.
This palace is called Sūrya; the Sun Deity (Sūryadeva) dwells within it.
It is also called Sūrya, for both the palace and the deities therein are all named Sūrya.
This palace remains for more than forty kalpas; by the dominant condition of the karma of sentient beings, it constantly moves while emitting light.
When the deva-son is present, the palace moves constantly; even when the deva is not there, the palace continues to move.
When the Son of Heaven returns, he descends into whichever palace is occupied.
Among these stellar palaces, the smallest has a diameter of half a krośa and a circumference of one and a half krośas.
The larger of these stars have a diameter of sixteen yojanas and a circumference of forty-eight yojanas.
Before the sun and moon there are the Devaputras who Wander for Pleasure; when these devaputras travel about, they experience playful delights.
Due to the predominant condition of the karma of sentient beings, there is a wind-wheel that blows and revolves constantly.
Because of this blowing wind, the palaces of the sun, moon, and other celestial bodies revolve without ceasing.
The solar palace travels one hundred and eighty paths, while the lunar palace travels fifteen paths; twelve paths of the sun constitute one path of the moon.
When the sun rises or sets, it traverses the paths traveled by twelve days [of the moon].
When the moon rises and sets, it traverses one degree in a single day.
From the southernmost path to the northernmost path, the distance is two hundred and ninety yojanas; the sun and moon travel within this range without their dimensions decreasing or increasing.
Furthermore, there are two paths:
first, the outer path; second, the inner path.

As for the inner path, it extends from within the Jambudvīpa path to within the northern Uttarakuru path, measuring four hundred and eighty million, eight thousand, and eight hundred yojanas, with a circumference of one billion, four hundred and forty-two thousand, four hundred yojanas.

As for its outer path, it is separated from [the inner path] by four hundred and eight million one thousand three hundred and eighty *yojanas*, and its circumference is fourteen hundred and forty-four million one hundred and forty *yojanas*.
As for the movement of the moon, it travels swiftly when moving obliquely and slowly when moving in a circuit.
As for the movement of the sun, it travels swiftly when moving in a circuit and slowly when moving obliquely.
The sun and moon either conjoin or separate.
Within each day, the sun travels forty-eight thousand and eighty *yojanas*; the same applies to both their conjunctions and separations.

As they gradually come into alignment, each day they cover the moon by three yojanas plus one-third of a yojana; by this process, on the fifteenth day, it is entirely covered and the moonlight does not appear.
When they gradually move apart, each day the sun travels forty-eight thousand and eighty *yojanas*.
During this separation, the sun moves three *yojanas* plus one-third of a *yojana* away from the moon; by this means, on the fifteenth day, the moon becomes perfectly full and radiant.
"By such a measure, the daily circuit of the sun is forty-eight thousand and eighty *yojanas* faster than that of the moon.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Forty-eight thousand, And eighty *yojanas*."
"The sun moves in this manner every day, and the same is true for the distance it leaves from the moon.
"The sun constantly travels one and a half yojanas, plus one-ninth of a yojana."
The first [period] is thus at the time the sun rises, and likewise when it sets.
For six months, the sun moves from the inner path out to the outer path;
for six months, it moves from the outer path back into the inner path.
The moon constantly travels nineteen yojanas and one-third of a yojana [each day].
Its emergence on each successive day is likewise, and its setting is likewise.
For fifteen days it travels from the inner path to the outer path, and for fifteen days it travels from the outer path to the inner path.

When the sun travels on the inner path of Pūrvavideha in the east, it reaches the southern limit of the land of Pūrvavideha at a distance of six hundred and eighty-three yojanas plus one-third of a yojana; during this time, it travels on the inner path.

If the sun travels along the inner path within Jambudvīpa, it takes the southern limit of the Jambudvīpa land as its boundary; at a distance of three hundred and fifty yojanas from that, the sun travels upon the inner path.

If the sun travels along the inner path within Aparagoyānī, it takes the southern limit of the land of Aparagoyānī as its boundary; the distance between them is six hundred and eighty-three yojanas plus one-third of a yojana, and it is within this that the sun travels on its inner path.

When the sun travels along the inner path within Uttarakuru, it reaches the southern boundary of the land of Uttarakuru at a distance of three hundred and fifty yojanas; this is when the sun travels on the inner path.

If the sun travels on the outer path outside of Pūrvavideha, it proceeds through a distance of three hundred and ninety-three yojanas plus one-third of a yojana from the southern limit of the earth to that outer path. It moves therein.
If the sun travels on the outer path outside Jambudvīpa, from the southern limit of the earth to the outer path of the sun, it is sixty yojanas; therein the sun travels on the outer path.

If the sun travels on the outer path outside of Aparagoyānī, taking it from the southern limit of the earth to the outer path of the sun, the distance is three hundred and ninety-three yojanas plus one-third of a yojana; within this distance, the sun travels.
If the sun travels on the outer path to the north of Uttarakuru, it traverses sixty *yojana*s from the southern limit of Jambudvīpa; this is when the sun moves through the central region.

If the sun travels on the inner path to the east of Pūrvavideha, it then travels on the outer path to Aparagoyānī in the west, and on the middle path between Jambudvīpa in the south and Uttarakuru in the north. At that time, in Pūrvavideha in the east, the day is longest at eighteen *muhūrta*s, and the night is shortest at twelve *muhūrta*s;
in Aparagoyānī in the west, the night is longest at eighteen *muhūrta*s, and the day is shortest at twelve *muhūrta*s.
In Jambudvīpa and Uttarakuru, day and night are equal in duration, each consisting of fifteen muhūrtas; of these, six muhūrtas are always in motion, while twenty-four muhūrtas are unmoving.

If the sun travels on the outer path of Pūrvavideha in the east, it travels on the inner path of Aparagoyānī in the west, and it travels on the middle path of Jambudvīpa in the south and Uttarakuru in the north.
At that time, in Pūrvavideha in the east, the night is longest at eighteen muhūrtas and the day is shortest at twelve muhūrtas;
in Aparagoyānī in the west, the day is longest at eighteen muhūrtas and the night is shortest at twelve muhūrtas;
in Jambudvīpa in the south and Uttarakuru in the north, day and night are equal, each being fifteen muhūrtas.
If the sun travels on the inner path within Jambudvīpa, it travels on the outer path of Uttarakuru, and on the middle path of Pūrvavideha and Aparagoyānī.
In this Jambudvīpa, the day is longest at eighteen muhūrtas and the night is shortest at twelve muhūrtas;
in Uttarakuru to the north, the night is longest at eighteen muhūrtas and the day is shortest at twelve muhūrtas;
in Pūrvavideha to the east and Aparagoyānī to the west, day and night are equal, each being fifteen muhūrtas.

If the sun travels along the outer path south of Jambudvīpa, it travels along the inner path north of Uttarakuru, and along the middle path between Pūrvavideha in the east and Aparagoyānī in the west.
At that time, in Jambudvīpa, the night is longest at eighteen muhūrtas and the day is shortest at twelve muhūrtas;
in Uttarakuru to the north, the day is longest at eighteen muhūrtas and the night is shortest at twelve muhūrtas;
in Pūrvavideha to the east and Aparagoyānī to the west, day and night are equal, each being fifteen muhūrtas.
The same is said for Aparagoyānī and Uttarakuru.
In the world, thirty muhūrtas are invariably and constantly reckoned as one day and night.
One muhūrta consists of thirty parts; each of these parts is called a lava.
When the days increase, they increase by one lava per day; when the days decrease, they likewise decrease by one lava per day;
the same applies to the nights.
When the days decrease, the nights increase by one lava;
when the nights decrease, the days increase by one lava.
When the days are at their longest—eighteen muhūrtas—the nights are then at their shortest—twelve muhūrtas.
If the night is at its longest at eighteen muhūrtas, then the day is at its shortest at twelve muhūrtas.
When day and night are equal, the day is fifteen muhūrtas and the night is fifteen muhūrtas.

If the fifteenth day of the fifth month is the full moon, it marks the beginning of the summer retreat (*varṣā*) in the Western Regions, while in China the summer retreat has already been completed for one month. At that time, the days are at their longest, lasting eighteen *muhūrtas*, and the nights are at their shortest, lasting twelve *muhūrtas*.

From the sixteenth day, one *lava* is subtracted; in the [first] month, one *muhūrta* is subtracted; in the second month, another *muhūrta* is subtracted; and in the third month, yet another *muhūrta* is subtracted. By the fifteenth day of the eighth month—the time of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony in the Western Regions and the time of receiving the *kaṭhina* robe in the land of Han—the day and night are equal, each consisting of fifteen *muhūrtas*.

Furthermore, from the sixteenth day until the end of the month, one *muhūrta* is further reduced; in the second month, another *muhūrta* is reduced; and in the third month, yet another *muhūrta* is reduced. By the fifteenth day of the eleventh month, that night is at its longest at eighteen *muhūrtas*, and that day is at its shortest at twelve *muhūrtas*.

From this time on that night, the day decreases by one lava; thus, during the first month, the night decreases by one muhūrta, the second month decreases by another muhūrta, and the third month decreases by yet another muhūrta, until on the fifteenth day of the second month, day and night are equal, each being fifteen muhūrtas.

Furthermore, from the sixteenth day until the end of the month, one *muhūrta* is again subtracted; in the second month, another *muhūrta* is subtracted; and in the third month, yet another *muhūrta* is subtracted. By the fifteenth day of the fifth month, that day is at its longest at eighteen *muhūrtas*, and the night is at its shortest at twelve *muhūrtas*.

Furthermore, at another time—specifically during the summer season in the Western Regions, on the ninth day of the second half of the first month, which corresponds to the ninth day of the sixth lunar month—the days are at their longest at eighteen muhūrtas, and the nights are at their shortest at twelve muhūrtas.
On the ninth day of the ninth month, day and night are equal, each being fifteen muhūrtas.
On the ninth day of the eleventh month, this night is the longest at eighteen muhūrtas, and the day is the shortest at twelve muhūrtas.
On the ninth day of the third month, day and night are equal, each consisting of fifteen muhūrtas.
Revolving in this manner for a full five years, there occurs one *yuga*, which consists of two intercalary months.
The first follows the moon and the second follows the sun.
Within the five-year period, there are twelve days, nine days, six days, three days, and fifteen days; it is during these that the lengths of day and night vary.
The moon has three functions to distinguish:
first, to distinguish the month; second, to distinguish the fifteenth day; and third, to distinguish the full moon.
The sun distinguishes night and day, distinguishes the seasons of summer, winter, and autumn, and distinguishes the year.
These three functions are accomplished through the day.
As for the occurrence of an intercalary month, there are two factors: one from the month and one from the day.
This intercalary month is produced by the month.
In the fourth month, two small months should be observed:
one small month occurs within the third half-month, and the second small month occurs within the seventh half-month.
Within a single year, there should thus be six small months; over five years, this amounts to a deficiency of thirty days.
These thirty days should compensate for the five years.
If one does not establish a small month (*kṣayamāsa*), then the full moon will not coincide with its proper time.

This small month is established based on the solar day; according to worldly convention, thirty *muhūrtas* are determined to constitute one day and night. By dividing thirty *muhūrtas* into sixty parts, because the sun moves swiftly, it completes the cycle in fifty-nine parts, leaving a surplus of one part.
Because of this matter, one day is added in the second month, and another day is added in the next second month; thus, over the course of a year, six days are fully added.
In this manner, after five years, one full month is added.
Using this one month to compensate for the five-year period constitutes the intercalary month of the solar calendar (*sūrya-māsa*).
If one does not perform the intercalation, the seasons and the years will fall out of alignment and become corrupted.
Furthermore, over a period of five years, there should be two intercalary months: the first occurs in the third year, and the second in the fifth year.

If the month is in Jambudvīpa, it takes three additional months to reach Aparagoyānī; if it is in Uttarakuru, six months; if in Pūrvavideha, nine months; and after completing one full year, it returns to Jambudvīpa.
Within the world, there are always three seasons: summer, winter, and spring. Summer is followed by spring; winter is followed by summer; and spring is followed by winter.

When it is the time for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony on the fifteenth day of the eighth month in Pūrvavideha, it is the time for entering the summer retreat (*varṣā*) on the fifteenth day of the fifth month in Jambudvīpa; it is the fifteenth day of the second month in Aparagoyānī, and the fifteenth day of the eleventh month in Uttarakuru.
The three months of the summer season in Pūrvavideha have already passed, and [the sun] is situated between the two continents of Pūrvavideha and Jambudvīpa.
The three months of the spring equinox in Aparagoyānī have not yet arrived, and [the sun] is situated between the two continents of Jambudvīpa and Aparagoyānī.

In Godānīya, one month of spring has already passed; in Uttarakuru, two months of the winter season have not yet ended; thus, for three months, [the sun] remains between the two continents of Godānīya and Uttarakuru.

When two months of the winter season in Uttarakuru have already passed and one month of the summer season in Pūrvavideha has not yet begun, this constitutes the three-month period between the two continents of Uttarakuru and Pūrvavideha.
Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, stands at the center of the four continents; how then can it be said that Mount Sumeru is on the northern side of the four continents?
This is because its location is determined according to the movement of the sun.

To the east of Pūrvavideha is Jambudvīpa to the north; to the west of Pūrvavideha is Jambudvīpa to the south; to the north of Pūrvavideha is Jambudvīpa to the west; and to the south of Pūrvavideha is Jambudvīpa to the east.
It is the same for Uttarakuru and Aparagoyānī.
Jambudvīpa in the south and Uttarakuru in the north face each other directly; Pūrvavideha in the east and Aparagoyānī in the west face each other directly.
At that time, when the sun and moon first descended into the world, they were separated by a very great distance.

At that time, the sun was at the center of Pūrvavideha in the eastern quarter under the sun, and the moon was at the center of Aparagoyānī in the western quarter under the moon; the radiance then shone universally, filling the four continents, with the sun illuminating one half and the moon illuminating the other half.
If the sun has already passed the center of Pūrvavideha in the east, it has already set in Uttarakuru in the north, and it has already risen in Jambudvīpa in the south.
If the moon has already passed the center of Aparagoyānī in the west, it has already set in Jambudvīpa and has already risen in Uttarakuru.
When the night of the full moon has arrived and the moon is at its zenith in Uttarakuru, the sun is at its zenith in Jambudvīpa in the south.
When the sun passes over the center of Jambudvīpa, it has already set in Pūrvavideha in the east and has just risen in Aparagoyānī in the west.
If the moon passes through the center of Uttarakuru to the north, it has already risen over Pūrvavideha in the east and has already set over Aparagoyānī in the west.
When it is the night of the full moon and the moon is at its zenith in Pūrvavideha, the sun is at its zenith in Aparagoyānī.
When the sun passes through the center of Aparagoyānī, Jambudvīpa has already set and Uttarakuru has already risen.
When the moon passes through the center of Pūrvavideha, Uttarakuru has already set and Jambudvīpa has already risen.
When it is the full moon at midnight in Jambudvīpa, it is midday in Uttarakuru to the north.
How is it that the sun and moon are joined in one place?
It is because the sun constantly follows the path of the moon.
Each day they approach one another by forty-eight thousand and eighty *yojanas*, and each day they recede from one another by the same amount.
When they are at their closest, the solar disk is obscured by three *yojanas* and one-third of a *yojana*.
For this reason, when the moon is completely covered on the fifteenth day, it is called the completion of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).

Day by day, the moon recedes from the sun by forty-eight thousand and eighty *yojanas*, and each day the moon uncovers three *yojanas* plus one-third of a *yojana*. For this reason, on the fifteenth day the moon becomes fully uncovered and perfectly round; in the world, this is called the completion of the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*).
When the sun and moon move at their greatest distance from one another, the moon is full, and the world says that the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) is complete.
When the sun and moon are in the same place, moving together, the world says that the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) is complete.
The diameter of the Sun is seventy-two million one thousand two hundred yojanas, and its circumference is two hundred and one million six thousand three hundred and sixty yojanas.
When the sun rises in Jambudvīpa, it sets in Uttarakuru; at that same moment, it is midday in Pūrvavideha and midnight in Aparagoyānī.
These four seasons for a single continent are established by means of the sun.
Such is the meaning taught by the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Thus have I heard.
*Lishi Apitan Lun*, Fascicle Five.
The Treatise on the Abhidharma of the Establishment of the World Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Six.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of West India during the Chen Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty: "What Is It? (Yǒushé Pǐn) / "What Is It? (Yǒushé Pǐn) Chapter Twenty.
"What is night? What is day?
It is because of the sun that there is night; it is because of the sun that there is day."
The realm of desire (kāmadhātu) is dark by its very nature; when the sunlight is obscured, it is night, and when the sunlight is manifest, it is day.
What is the dark fortnight?
What is the bright fortnight?
It is by means of the sun’s dark fortnight and the sun’s bright fortnight.
The sun constantly pursues the moon in its course; every day it draws near by forty-eight thousand and eighty *yojanas*, and every day it moves away by the same distance.

When they are near each other, the disk of the sun covers three yojanas and one-third of a yojana of the moon; for this reason, when the moon is covered on the fifteenth day, it is daytime, while during the dark fortnight it is full.

Day by day, the moon also moves away from the sun by forty-eight thousand and eighty *yojanas*. Each day, the moon opens up by three *yojanas* plus one-third of a *yojana*. Because of this, on the fifteenth day, the moon becomes completely open, pure, and full; in the world, this is called the "fullness of the bright fortnight."
When the sun and moon move at their greatest distance from one another, the moon is full; at that time, the world says the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) is complete.
When the sun and moon are in the same place, this is called their conjunction (saṃyoga); at that time, the world says the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) is complete.

If the sun moves behind the moon, the sunlight illuminates the moon; because the moonlight is coarse, it is illuminated and produces a shadow. This shadow of the moon then obscures the moon itself, and for this reason, the latter part of the moon is seen as not full.

Due to this process, [the moon] is gradually obscured until, on the fifteenth day, the covering of the moon is complete; the period when it subsequently moves away is called the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).
If the sun moves ahead of the moon, the daily clearing and brightening occurs in the same manner.
When the fifteenth day is fully reached and complete, the period preceding it is called the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*).
Why is the winter season called *haimanta*?
Because at this time snow ought to fall and the cold has already arrived; therefore, the winter season is named *haimanta*. The world establishes this intrinsic nature as *haimanta*.
Why is the spring season called *grīṣma*?

Because it is the time when the sun’s heat blazes, the time of intense heat, and the time of parching thirst, the spring season is therefore said to be named *grīṣma*; the world establishes this intrinsic nature and names it *grīṣma*.
Why is the summer season called *varṣā*?

It is the time of rain, the time when rain is expected, and the beginning of the year; therefore, the summer is called *varṣā*. This name *varṣā* is established by worldly convention based on its inherent nature.
What is winter cold?
What is spring heat?
What is the cold and heat of the summer season?

This is during the winter season, when the water element is at its maximum and has not yet diminished; when grasses and trees are still moist and have not yet withered; when the earth element is damp and slippery; and when the fire element moves downward while the vapor of water ascends.
We know this to be so because deep water is warmest while shallow water is cold.

When the cold season has arrived, the sun travels along its outer path and shines for only a short time; the yang energy remains within, causing food to be digested quickly. For these reasons, it is cold during the winter.
What is the heat of spring?

At this time of the *kṣāra-nadī* (the saline river), the water element (*ab-dhātu*) that had previously increased has diminished and been exhausted; the grasses and trees have withered, the earth has become parched and cracked, the moisture of the water sinks downward, and the heat of the fire rises upward.
How is this known to be so?
Deep water is cold, while shallow water is warm.
Since winter has already passed, the sun travels its inner path and its scorching heat lasts for a long time; because the internal fire of the body is weak, it is hot during springtime.
What is meant by cold and heat during the summer season?

During the eight months of this great earth, the sun constantly shines and scorches it throughout the day; when great clouds send down rain that sprinkles and disperses [the heat], the terrestrial vapors become steaming and oppressive. When the wind blows, these vapors are dissipated and it becomes cold; if the wind does not arise, it remains hot. For this reason, Vatsa, there is both cold and heat at certain times.
"What is meant by the name 'niraya' for the hells?
It is because there is no play or sport, no joy or delight, no way of escape, and no merit."
Because one does not eliminate or abandon karma, one is born therein;
furthermore, it is said that this path is the most inferior within the desire realm and is called a "non-path. For these reasons, hell is termed *niraya*.
Why are the birds and beasts called *tiryañc*?
Because they take birth therein due to karma characterized by flattery and crookedness;
furthermore, it is said that the beings in this realm mostly move with their bodies covered, and for this reason they are called *tiryañc*.
Why is the realm of hungry ghosts (preta) called Śmāśāna-Yama?
Because the king is named Śmāśāna, those born there belong to the same category as the king, and are thus called Śmāśāna;
furthermore, it is said that this path communicates with other paths, where good and evil intermingle, and for this reason it is called Śmāśāna.
Why is the path of the asuras called "asura"?

Because they cannot endure what is wholesome, cannot listen with single-minded attention to well-spoken words, and their minds remain unmoved despite various forms of instruction; because of their arrogance, they are not virtuous heroes, and because they are not devas, they are called asuras.
Why is the heavenly realm called *deva*?
The term *deva* is a name for virtuous conduct; because of such virtuous conduct, one is born into this realm.
Furthermore, *deva* is said to mean "radiance," because they are constantly possessed of light.
Furthermore, "Deva" is called the Noble Path; "Deva" is called the Intentional Resolve; "Deva" is called the Supreme Path.
Moreover, "Deva" refers to one who should cultivate and increase all wholesome karmas; for these reasons, he is named Deva.
Why is the human realm called *mānuṣya*? First, because of their intelligence; second, because they are superior;

third, because their mental faculties are subtle; fourth, because of their correct awakening; fifth, because their wisdom is preeminent; sixth, because they can distinguish between the false and the real; seventh, because they are the proper vessels for the Noble Path; and eighth, because they are born from the karma of wisdom. For these reasons, the human realm is called *mānuṣya*.
"Why is this land named Jambudvīpa?
It receives this name because of the Jambu tree.
Why is it called Aparagoyānī?"

Because this land is to the west of Jambudvīpa, all its economic activities and trade are conducted using oxen; since these oxen are called Go-yani, this land is therefore named Aparagoyānī (Western Go-yani).
Why is it called Pūrvavideha?
Because this land lies to the east of Jambudvīpa, and because its physical appearance is lovely and its material provisions are superior, it is therefore called Pūrvavideha.
Why is it called Uttarakuru?

Because this land lies to the north of Jambudvīpa; because its inhabitants are upright in mind and virtuous; because it is further superior and excellent; and because all its resources surpass those of other places—it is therefore called Uttarakuru.
“What is meant by the first heaven being called the Heaven of the Great Kings?
It is because the four great kings, such as Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the others, exercise sovereign authority and serve as the leaders therein.
What is meant by the second heaven being called Trāyastriṃśa?”
Among these, the King of the Thirty-three Gods is the sovereign lord; because his royal authority is autonomous, he is called the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Why is the third heaven named Yāma?
As the divisions of time pass day and night, they speak these words: "Alas!
How inconceivable is this joy!"
Therefore, it is named Yāma.
Why is the fourth heaven named Tuṣita?

Because they are fully satisfied with joy; regarding their requisites, they know for themselves that they have attained sufficiency, yet they do not give rise to complacency regarding the Eightfold Noble Path; therefore, it is called the Tuṣita Heaven.
Why is the fifth heaven named Veṇu-vana?

Because the devas therein create palaces, groves, and all manner of articles of pleasure by means of their supernormal powers as they wish, and experience enjoyment therein; therefore, it is called Veṇu-vana.
Why is the sixth heaven named Paranirmita-vaśavartin?
Because they exercise sovereign control over the palaces, gardens, groves, and all articles of pleasure created by others, thinking: "This is mine."
Because one experiences bliss therein, it is called Parīttābha (Limited Light).
What is the first Brahma realm called Brahmakāyika (The Retinue of Brahmā)?
Because a person who is about to enter the Form Realm from the Desire Realm first arrives at this place, it is called Brahmakāyika.
Why is the second named Brahmakāyika?
Because the retinue of the Great Brahmā King is vast, they are called the Brahmakāyikas (the Retinue of Brahmā).
Why is the third named Mahābrahmā?

Because he is born from karma created during the intermediate state of the supreme first dhyāna, because he is sovereign and not dependent on others, and because he is able to observe distinct external matters, he acts as the master over those already born and those yet to be born; therefore, he is named Mahābrahmā.
Why is the first deva realm of the second dhyāna called Limited Light (Parīttābhā)?
Because when they speak, only a small amount of light issues from their mouths; therefore, it is called Limited Light.
Why is the second named Immeasurable Light (Apramāṇābhā)?
When these devas speak, immeasurable light radiates from their mouths; therefore, they are called "Immeasurable Light.
Why is the third Brahmā named "Pervasive Supreme Light"?
When these devas speak, light issues from their mouths, pervading all places completely and without exception; therefore, they are named "Universal Radiance" (Samantābhāsvara).
Why is the first heaven of the third dhyāna named "Limited Purity" (Parittaśubha)?

In this realm, the pleasure experienced by the various devas is slight; because they experience this slight pleasure through a joy associated with the third dhyāna that is characterized by tranquility, it is called "Slight Purity" (Parīttaśubha).
Why is the second heaven named "Immeasurable Purity" (Apramāṇaśubha)?
Among these, the gods delight in a tranquility superior to that of the former [heaven], and because this is associated with the third dhyāna, it is called "Immeasurable Purity" (Apramāṇaśubha).
Why is the third named "Universal Purity" (Śubhakṛtsna)?

Within this state, the experience of bliss pervades the body and mind completely and without exception; being characterized by a serene fondness associated with the third dhyāna, the devas therein experience this, and thus it is called "Universal Purity" (Śubhakṛtsna).
Why is the first deva realm of the fourth dhyāna called "Cloudless" (Anabhraka)?

Because suffering and pleasure have previously ceased, and because joy and sorrow have been exhausted through prior application; because within this state, equanimity, wisdom, and mindfulness are purified; and because the devas therein experience this equanimity, it is therefore called "Cloudless."
Why is the second heaven named "Born of Merit" (Puṇyaprasava)?

Because it is produced by various meditative absorptions associated with merit—namely, wisdom, mindfulness, and equanimity—and because once born there, one experiences these three factors, it is therefore called "Born of Merit."
Why is the third [heaven] named Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala)?

"Vast" refers to the fruit produced by the power of great capacity and its maturation; since these two can encompass meditative concentration, wisdom, and the basis for freedom from desire, it is therefore called Vast Fruit.
Why is the fourth [heaven] called the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva-deva)? It is because the gods therein possess no thought.
What is meant by "thought"?

The two types of perception—the general and the specific—each produce distinct karmic retributions; since these are absent here, and there exist only the aggregate of form and the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind, it is called the Heaven of Non-perception (asaṃjñisattva).
What is the Heaven of Non-returners (Anāgāmin)?

One name is "Excellent Manifestation" (Sudṛśa). Formerly, while on the causal ground, he was able to cause others to see the reality of the non-erroneous meaning, and was able to cause them to receive and understand it; therefore, he is named "Excellent Manifestation."
Why is the second named "Good Vision" (Sudarśana)?

Formerly, while on the causal ground, he increased his lifespan, possessed the wealth of the four types of shrines (*caitya*) as well as the assets of others, and properly protected beneficial matters; therein, he gave rise to right view, neither rejecting nor grasping.
Because of his previous excellence as *Sudṛśa* and for these reasons, he is named *Sudarśana*.
Why is the third named *Avṛha*?

Formerly, while on the causal ground (*hetubhūmi*), he did not harm or afflict others; he had no intention of causing obstruction and no intention of coercion. Because of his previous excellence as *Sudṛśa* and due to this karma, he is therefore named *Avṛha*.
Why is the fourth named "Unburned"?

Because when these devas were formerly on the causal ground, they did not burn themselves nor afflict their own bodies, nor did they burn others nor afflict others; because both self and others joyfully practiced and swiftly attained penetration, due to those previous wholesome manifestations and this karma, it is therefore called "Unburned."
Why is the fifth called Akaniṣṭha?
"Kaniṣṭha" means "inferior grade," because the preceding seventeen stages have all been transcended;
furthermore, it is so called because there are those who attain parinirvāṇa within the interval from the lower-grade heavens up to the ultimate heaven.
Furthermore, there are devas named Akaniṣṭha; because they have reached parinirvāṇa, they are therefore called Akaniṣṭha.
Why is the first heaven of the formless realm called the Sphere of Infinite Space?

Space is uncreated, unconditioned, and unobstructed; it transcends the characteristics of obstruction and the various characteristics of existence. Because it is the object of a single-pointed mind, it is non-dual and undifferentiated. Since it arises through the activity of this space, it is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (ākāśānantyāyatana).
Why is the second named the Heaven of Infinite Consciousness? "Consciousness" refers to the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Because this consciousness is internal, it is subtler than external space; it transcends obstructive characteristics and transcends external appearances. Since it is the object of a single-pointed mental state, it is non-dual and undifferentiated. Because it is produced by the karma of this consciousness, it is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
Why is the third named the Heaven of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)?

"Nothingness" means that, having removed the two previous coarse characteristics, there is no distinct objective realm apart from these two; it transcends internal and external marks because it is the single object of the mind of unified perception. Since it is produced by the karma of this mind which is non-dual and undifferentiated, it is called the Sphere of Nothingness.
Why is the fourth [heaven] called the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception?
It is called "neither perception" because its perception is so subtle that it is not like the seven preceding meditative absorptions;

it is called "nor non-perception" because, unlike the two concentrations of the attainment of non-perception and the attainment of mindlessness—which are both termed "attainment of non-perception" due to being without mind—this state possesses mind, and is therefore called the "attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
Because it arises from karma that is fixed by this meditative concentration, it is called the "Entry of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
Twenty thousand yojanas downward from Jambudvīpa is the location of the Avīci Great Hell.
Ten thousand yojanas downward from Jambudvīpa is the realm of the Yama hell;
between these two there are other hells.
Forty thousand yojanas upward from Jambudvīpa is the realm of the Four Great Kings (Cāturmahārājakāyika).
Eighty thousand yojanas upward from Jambudvīpa is the abode of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
One hundred and sixty thousand yojanas upward from Jambudvīpa is the abode of the Yāma devas.
Three hundred and twenty million yojanas above Jambudvīpa is the abode of the Tuṣita Heaven.
Six hundred and forty million yojanas above Jambudvīpa is the abode of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
"Twelve hundred and eighty million yojanas upward from Jambudvīpa is the dwelling place of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas.
A bhikṣu asked the Buddha, the World-Honored One:
"From Jambudvīpa to the Brahma realm, how near or far is it?"
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus! From Jambudvīpa to the Brahma realm, it is extremely distant and exceedingly high; they differ in character and are separated from one another."

"Monks! Suppose, for example, on the fifteenth day of the ninth month when the moon is full, a person were to stand in that Brahma realm and drop a square stone measuring a hundred fathoms toward the lower realms. Without any obstruction along the way, it would reach Jambudvīpa on the fifteenth day of the ninth month of the following year."
The distance from the Brahma realm to Jambudvīpa is as described above.
From the Brahma realm to the Parīttābha Heaven, it is again double the previous distance.
From the Parīttābha Heaven to the Apramāṇābha Heaven, it is again twice as far.
From the Heaven of Immeasurable Light to the Heaven of Universal Radiance, the distance is again doubled.
From the Heaven of Universal Radiance to the Heaven of Limited Purity, the distance is again doubled.
From the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven to the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, it is again twice as far;
from the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven to the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, it is again twice as far.
From the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven to the Anabhraka Heaven, the distance is again doubled.
From the Anabhraka Heaven to the Puṇyaprasava Heaven, the distance is again doubled.
From the Puṇyaprasava Heaven to the Bṛhatphala Heaven, the distance is again doubled.
From the Bṛhatphala Heaven to the Āsaṃjñika Heaven, it is again twice as far.
From the Āsaṃjñika Heaven to the Sudarśana Heaven, it is again twice as far.
From the Sudarśana Heaven to the Sudṛśa Heaven, it is again twice as far.
From the Sudarśana Heaven to the Abṛha Heaven, it is again twice as far;
from the Abṛha Heaven to the Atapa Heaven, it is again twice as far;
and from the Atapa Heaven to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, it is again twice as far.
And he spoke in verse:
"From the Akaniṣṭha heaven down to the land of Jambudvīpa,
he cast down great mountains of dense rock for sixty-five thousand years."
"Five hundred and thirty-five [yojanas], and if there is no obstruction in between,
one will then reach Jambudvīpa.
"If the people of Jambudvīpa were devoid of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) or the assistance of others' efforts, none would be able to pass through mountains, walls, or fences without obstruction."

If a person from Jambudvīpa goes on a journey, they can reach only as far as the Great Black Mountain (Mahā-kāla-parvata) and the Small Black Mountain (Kṣudra-kāla-parvata); unless they possess supernatural powers (ṛddhi) or the assistance of others' power, they cannot go beyond this.

If the people of Aparagoyānī were devoid of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) or the assistance of others' efforts, none would be able to pass through mountains, walls, or enclosures without obstruction; if they were to travel, they could only reach the edge of that land at the seashore, for without supernormal powers or the assistance of others' efforts, they could not go beyond this.

If the people of Pūrvavideha were devoid of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) or the assistance of others' efforts, none would be able to enter or exit mountains, walls, or enclosures without obstruction; if they were to travel, they could only reach the edge of their land at the seashore, for without supernormal powers or the assistance of others' efforts, they could not go beyond this.

If the people of Uttarakuru were devoid of supernormal powers or the assistance of others' power, none would be able to pass through walls, fences, or mountains without obstruction; if they were to travel, they could only reach the inner edge of the boundary mountains, for without supernormal powers or the assistance of others' power, none can go beyond this.

From their own palaces, the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings cannot pass through walls, fences, or mountains without obstruction unless they possess supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) or the assistance of others' power; if they travel as wanderers, they can only reach within the Cakravāḍa Mountains, for without supernatural powers or the assistance of others' power, they cannot go beyond this.

From their own palaces, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are unable to pass through walls, fences, or mountains without obstruction unless they possess supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) or the assistance of others' power; if they travel on foot, they can reach only as far as the edge of the Cakravāḍa Mountains, for without supernormal powers or the assistance of others' power, they cannot go beyond this.

The Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, as well as the Brahmakāyika and Brahmapurohita devas, within their respective palaces—if they were devoid of supernormal powers (ṛddhi) or the assistance of others—would have no ability to pass through walls, fences, or mountains without obstruction; if they were to travel, it would be only within a single world-system, for without supernormal powers or the assistance of others, they could not go beyond this.

From the palace of the Great Brahmā King himself, if one lacks supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) or the assistance of another's power, there is no one who can pass through walls, enclosures, or mountains without obstruction. If a wanderer remains within a thousand-world system (*sāhasra-lokadhātu*), and lacks supernormal powers or the assistance of another's power, they cannot go beyond it. From the second dhyāna up to the palace of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven itself, it is as previously stated: if a wanderer remains within a thousand-world system and lacks supernormal powers or the assistance of another's power, they cannot go beyond it.
"In the great hells, the great hell-wardens act as kings with sovereign power and wealth.
In the realm of Yama, King Yama acts as king with sovereign power and wealth."
All birds, beasts, and water-rākṣasas have King Bhāruṇḍa as their sovereign, possessing wealth and power.
All snakes, nāgas, and the like have the Nāga King Vāsuki as their sovereign, possessing wealth and power.
Among the great dragon kings, the Dragon King Mānasvin rules with sovereign wealth and power.
Among the elephant-dragon kings, the Elephant King Loujiaqili (Lūśakīli) rules with sovereign wealth and power.
Among all flying birds, the king of the garuḍas holds sovereign power and wealth;
among four-footed walking beings, the lion king holds sovereign power and wealth.
In all the realms of hungry ghosts, the King of the Ghost Lords rules with sovereign wealth and power.
In all the realms of asuras, the four asura kings rule with sovereign wealth and power:
first, Rāhu; second, Vemacitra; third, Vimalacitra; and fourth, Bali Virūḍhaka.
