Within Jambudvīpa, there are times when a universal monarch (cakravartin) rules as sovereign and master of wealth; times when a local king rules as sovereign and master of wealth; times when the elders of the nation rule as sovereigns and masters of wealth; and times when there is no king, such as at the beginning of an eon.

In Aparagoyānī, there are times when the sovereignty and wealth are exercised by a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), and times when they are exercised by the elders of the nation; at other times, there is no king, as was the case at the beginning of the eon.

In Pūrvavideha, sovereignty and wealth are exercised by a universal monarch (*cakravartin*); sovereignty and wealth are exercised by the elders of the nation; and at times there is no king, as was the case when established at the beginning of the eon (*kalpa*).
In Uttarakuru in the north, they rule with sovereignty and wealth as Universal Monarchs (cakravartin), though at times there is no king.
In the abodes of the Four Great Kings, they rule with sovereignty and wealth as the Four Great Kings.
As for the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, its sovereign is King Vaiśravaṇa, who possesses wealth and sovereignty.
As for the Yāma Heaven, its sovereign is King Suyāma, who possesses wealth and sovereignty.
In the Tuṣita Heaven, King Suyāma exercises sovereign power over wealth and mastery.
In the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, King Sunirmita exercises sovereign power over wealth and mastery.
In the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations, the King of Vaśavartin acts as the sovereign with sovereign wealth and power.
Within the entire realm of desire, the Māra King acts as the sovereign with sovereign wealth and power.
In a thousandfold world system, the Great Brahmā King rules as a sovereign with wealth and mastery.

Yet, within the realms of the world and its devas, including the abode of Māra and the Great Brahmās, and among the places of śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, humans, and devas, it is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha who, by the very nature of the Dharma, reigns as a sovereign with wealth and mastery.
"If an infant born in Jambudvīpa has completed four months, it is as large as a newborn infant in Aparagoyānī.
A newborn infant in Pūrvavideha is as large as a five-month-old infant in Jambudvīpa."
If an infant born in Jambudvīpa has reached the completion of six months, it is like an infant newly born in Uttarakuru.
An infant in Jambudvīpa who is six years old is likewise like an infant newly born in the realm of the Four Great Kings; from birth until the seventh day, they are as large as their parents.
Just as a child born in Jambudvīpa at the age of seven, so too is an infant newly born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; having been born for seven days, he is equal to a full-grown adult.
Just as a child born in Jambudvīpa at the age of eight, so it is for one newly born in the Yāma heaven; having been born, they become equal to adults within seven days.
Just as a child born in Jambudvīpa at the age of nine, so it is for one newly born in the Tuṣita heaven; having been born, they become equal to adults within seven days.
From the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, their physical forms are fully complete as soon as they arise.

One *vyāma* and a half in Jambudvīpa is equal to one *vyāma* in Aparagoyānī; one *vyāma* and a half in Aparagoyānī is equal to one *vyāma* in Pūrvavideha; and one *vyāma* and a half in Pūrvavideha is equal to one *vyāma* in Uttarakuru.
One *gavyūti* is one-quarter of a *yojana*. The bodies of the gods of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*) are two *gavyūtis* in height;

the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven are half a *yojana*; Śakra’s body is three *gavyūtis*; the gods of the Yāma heaven are one *yojana*; those of Tuṣita are two *yojanas*; the gods of Nirmāṇarati are four *yojanas*; and the gods of Paranirmita-vaśavartin are eight *yojanas*.
All the realms of the form realm up to Akaniṣṭha are twelve yojanas in length.
From Jambudvīpa up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, they are each four cubits in length relative to one's own body.
“The sentient beings of Jambudvīpa have various and different physical complexions: there are those who are white, such as those in the countries of Nepāla, Varika, and Ciṇa;
those who are black, such as those in the countries of Bāhlīka and Kamboja;
and those who are blue, such as those in the countries of Dramiḍa and Siṃhala.”
There are those that are reddish-white, such as the countries of Śūdrāpīra and others;
there are those that are yellow, such as the countries of Kīra and Kaśmīra and others.
In Pūrvavideha in the east and Aparagoyānī in the west, everything is exactly as in Jambudvīpa, except that the color black is absent.
In Uttarakuru in the north, all the inhabitants are entirely white and pure.

The gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings have four kinds of colors—there are those that are deep blue, red, yellow, and white—and the colors of all the gods in the realm of desire are likewise the same.
What are the four types of colors among the gods?
At the time of their initial birth, if they see a dark-blue flower, their bodies become dark-blue; the same applies to other colors.

Regarding the clothing of the people of Jambudvīpa, there are garments made of kārpāsa (cotton), kauśeya (silk), wool, hemp, flax, grass, tree bark, animal skins, wooden boards, and the seeds of the nyagrodha tree.

The garments worn by the people of Aparagoyānī are: kārpāsa (cotton) garments, kṣauma (linen) garments, kauśeya (silk) garments, woolen garments, ramie garments, hempen garments, grass garments, bark garments, animal-skin garments, wooden-board garments, and garments made from the fruit of the ṛmbhā tree.
The people of Pūrvavideha wear garments of kārpāsa (cotton), kṣauma (linen), kauśeya (silk), wool, ramie, and hemp.
The people of Uttarakuru wear garments made from the fruit of the nyagrodha tree; they are twenty cubits long and ten cubits wide, and one *pala* in weight is equivalent to one *nāna*.
The gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings also wear robes of fine cloth (*kṣauma*), forty cubits long and twenty cubits wide, weighing half a *pala*.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven also wear robes of fine cloth, eighty cubits long and forty cubits wide, weighing one-quarter of a *pala*.
The Yāma devas wear robes made of *karpāsa* cotton that are one hundred and sixty cubits long and eighty cubits wide, weighing one-eighth of a *pala*.
The Tuṣita devas wear *karpāsa* robes that are three hundred and twenty cubits long and one hundred and sixty cubits wide, weighing one-sixteenth of a *pala*.
From the Nirmāṇarati Heaven up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the garments worn by the inhabitants change in size according to their will, and their lightness or heaviness is likewise so.

The clothing and ornaments of the people of Jambudvīpa vary in many ways: some have long hair divided into two topknots; some shave off their hair and beards; some leave a single tuft of hair on the crown while removing all the rest, which is called the *cūḍā* topknot; some pluck out their hair and beards; some clip their hair and beards; some braid their hair; some let their hair hang loose;

some cut the front and let the back hang to form a circle; some go naked; some wear clothes that cover the upper body and leave the lower exposed; some expose the upper body and cover the lower; some cover both upper and lower; and some merely shield the front and back.
The people of Aparagoyānī adorn themselves by letting their hair hang loose, wearing garments both above and below, just as in the country of Śūdrāpila.

The people of Pūrvavideha adorn themselves by cutting the front of their hair and letting it fall behind; they wear two garments, upper and lower, putting on the lower garment while the upper garment merely encircles the body, just as in the two countries of Aṅga and Magadha.

The inhabitants of Uttarakuru in the north adorn themselves such that their beards and hair are a deep, lustrous black, always as if freshly shaved; every five days their hair grows naturally to a length of seven finger-widths, neither increasing nor decreasing.

The adornments of the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings vary in many ways: some have long hair parted into two topknots; some have shaved off their hair and beards; some leave a single tuft on the crown of the head while removing all other hair, which is called the *cūḍā* topknot; some have plucked out their hair and beards; some have trimmed their hair and beards; some have braided hair; some have loose, flowing hair; some have their front hair cut short while leaving the back long to form a circle;
and some are naked. Some wear garments; some cover the upper body while leaving the lower exposed; some cover the lower body while leaving the upper exposed; some cover both upper and lower;
and some merely shield themselves from the front and back. The adornments of the various gods of the Desire Realm are likewise such.

The gods of the form realm do not wear garments, yet they appear no different from those who do; though their heads lack topknots, they resemble celestial crowns. Having transcended the characteristics of male and female, their physical forms are of only one kind.
"The people of Jambudvīpa eat rice, wheat, and parched grain; they eat fish, meat, and various kinds of *khādya* (hard foods), such as roots and fruits."

The food and drink consumed by the people of Aparagoyānī consists of cooked rice, barley meal, and parched grain, as well as fish, meat, fine *khādaniya* (hard foods), root *khādaniya*, and fruit *khādaniya*; among these, milk and curd are most abundant.

The people of Pūrvavideha eat non-glutinous rice, wheat, and parched grain, as well as fish, meat, and various kinds of *khādya* (hard foods)—namely, root-vegetables, fruit-vegetables—and non-glutinous rice is most abundant there.

The people of Uttarakuru in the north eat only śāli non-glutinous rice; it grows spontaneously without being sown, is free of broken grains or chaff, and is naturally pure rice. Its color, fragrance, flavor, and texture are all exquisitely wonderful, and its sweetness is like that of fine honey.

Within it there is a tree named Tuṇḍicīra; this tree bears fruit shaped like a cauldron or a small cooking pot. If a person wishes to eat, they take the fruit of this tree and hold it to contain water.
Furthermore, there is another stone named Jyotiṣka; if one takes the seeds of this tree and places them upon the stone, fire spontaneously arises from it.
This person then takes śāli rice and pours it into a vessel; without the need for measurement or calculation, it naturally fills the vessel to its capacity.
When the rice was fully cooked, the stone naturally cooled, and they continued to use the previous bowls to store it in succession.
If other people came who wished to eat, they would take food as they pleased, without forming the thought:
"That person is giving to me."
The person preparing the food also does not form the intention:
"I am now giving this to him.
When the meal is finished, they cast it away and depart; the remaining vessels and leftover food are received by a fissure in the earth, which closes up again after receiving them.

The gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings all consume the essence of *sūda*; they eat one pinch in the morning and one pinch in the evening. Once this essence has entered their bodies, it is transformed into their physical substance.

This *sūda* essence arises spontaneously within the groves, gardens, and ponds; furthermore, this *sūda* essence can also manifest as the eight kinds of food and drink, such as *khādaniya* (solid foods) and so forth.
The food of all the devas in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is likewise.

As for the devas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), from those of the first dhyāna up to the Śubhakṛtsna heaven, they take joy (*prīti*) as their food; the devas above these take mental action (*manaskarma*) as their food.

"The goods used for trade by the people of Jambudvīpa consist of either wrought or unwrought gold and silver, or rice and grain, or various miscellaneous items such as pearls, *maṇi* gems, and all kinds of treasures; or they take living beings to serve as barter.
In Aparagoyānī, the transactions of trade and commerce are conducted using only milch cows;
in Pūrvavideha, the items used for the transactions of trade and commerce are rice and grain."
In Uttarakuru in the north, there is no commerce.

The goods for barter among the gods of the Four Great Kings consist of refined or unrefined gold and silver, or rice and grain, or various miscellaneous wares such as pearls, *maṇi* gems, and all kinds of precious jewels; or they take living beings to serve as trade.
All the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are likewise.
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there is none; it is the same as in Uttarakuru.
"The people of Jambudvīpa either kill [beings] themselves or cause others to kill them, and upon death, they eat their flesh;
it is likewise in Aparagoyānī."
The people of Pūrvavideha do not kill living beings themselves nor cause others to kill them; if there are those who have died naturally, they eat their flesh.
The people of Uttarakuru do not kill living beings themselves nor cause others to kill them, and when they die, they do not eat flesh.
The gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings do not eat the flesh of those who have killed themselves or been killed by others after death.
The various gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven likewise do not eat the flesh of those who have killed themselves or been killed by others after death.
From the Yāma Heaven up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, they do not kill living beings themselves, nor do they cause others to kill; when they die, they do not eat meat.

When the relatives of a person from Jambudvīpa die, they carry the corpse to the mountains to cremate it and discard the remains, or they place it in water, or bury it in the earth, or leave it in an open space;
it is the same in Aparagoyānī and Pūrvavideha.

When a member of a family dies in Uttarakuru in the north, they do not carry out funeral rites, nor do they cremate or discard the body; rather, birds carry away the corpse, and once they have transported it beyond the mountains, they devour it.
When the retinues of the gods of the Four Great Kings die, they neither carry off the corpses nor cremate them nor discard them; like a flame vanishing, no remains are left.
All the gods above them are likewise in this regard.
“In Jambudvīpa there are five kinds of trees—golden trees, silver trees, vaidūrya trees, sphaṭika trees, and haritāla trees—and it is the same for the trees in Aparagoyānī and Pūrvavideha.”
In Uttarakuru in the north, there are only *kalpavṛkṣa* trees, while the other four types do not exist there.
The Four Heavenly Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*) also possess five kinds of precious trees, all as described above.
In all the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are likewise five kinds of trees.
In the heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are no trees at all.
In Jambudvīpa, there are five kinds of flowers—gold, silver, *vaidūrya*, *sphāṭika*, and *ahrita*; it is the same in Aparagoyānī and Pūrvavideha.
In Uttarakuru to the north, there is a tree named Santāna, whose flowers are made entirely of sakhila jewels.
The gods of the Four Great Kings likewise possess five kinds of flowers; it is the same throughout the entire realm of desire, whereas in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are none at all.
"In Jambudvīpa there are palaces made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and coral; there are also palaces made of timber, as well as stone houses and earthen houses;
it is the same in Aparagoyānī."
In Pūrvavideha in the east, the halls are all made of gold and there are no other dwellings.
In Uttarakuru in the north, there is a tree named Mañjūṣaka that is like a lofty palace; its leaves overlap one another so as to exclude wind and frost, and all the people use it as their dwelling.
The Heaven of the Four Great Kings has five kinds of palaces—made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and emerald—and all the various heavens of the desire realm are likewise so.
The celestial palaces of the various devas in the realm of form are all made of white jewels.

Because these devas, while formerly on the causal ground, practiced giving with a narrow and stingy mind while hoping for karmic retribution, the palaces they have now obtained on the resultant ground are of a dull and dark luster, unable to be bright or pure.
If these devas, while still on the stage of causal ground, practice giving without a narrow or stingy mind and do not look for future rewards, thinking:
"I have it, but they do not; I am the master, but they are not."
"This is the correct principle; this is the correspondence with the Dharma.

If one who is a master gives to one who is not a master, and if one practices giving with a pure and tranquil mind, it is for the purpose of adorning the mind and purifying the mind; therefore, one practices giving.
Because of this mind, the palaces obtained in the stage of fruition possess subtle and wondrous radiance, free from darkness or turbidity.

"If the people of Jambudvīpa were to be devoid of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) or the power derived from others, they would not be able to see forms beyond mountains, walls, fences, cities, or obstructions.

Likewise, if the inhabitants of Aparagoyānī, Pūrvavideha, and Uttarakuru were to be devoid of the power derived from others, they would not be able to see forms beyond mountains, walls, fences, cities, or obstructions."

If the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings were devoid of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and the assistance of others, they would be unable to see forms beyond obstructions such as mountains, walls, fences, or cities from their own abodes; when looking at a distance, they would see only those forms within the Cakravāḍa Mountains.
If they were devoid of supernormal powers and the assistance of others, they could not see through to the exterior of these mountains.

The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, within their own palaces, cannot perceive forms beyond mountains, walls, fences, cities, or obstructions unless they possess supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) or the assistance of others; when looking from afar, they see only what is within the Cakravāḍa Mountains.
Without supernatural powers or the assistance of others, they cannot see through to the exterior of the Cakravāḍa Mountains.
This is likewise true for all the gods from the Yāma Heaven up to the Brahmakāyika Heaven.
From his own palace, the Great Brahmā King cannot perceive forms beyond mountains, walls, fences, cities, or obstructions unless he relies on supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) or the efforts of others;
even when looking from afar, he can see only within a single thousand-world system (*sāhasra-lokadhātu*), for without supernormal powers or the assistance of others, he cannot see through them.

"If the people of Jambudvīpa seek another's daughter, they may only receive her after the girl's family has granted permission; there are some who purchase concubines or others who trade for female slaves.
It is the same in Aparagoyānī and Pūrvavideha."
The people of Uttarakuru do not seek out other women; they neither take wives nor buy or redeem them.
When a man wishes to marry a woman, he gazes intently at her, and when a woman desires a man, she likewise must look upon him with focused attention.
If a woman does not see a man looking at another woman, she says:
"If this person looks at you,
you shall immediately become husband and wife.
If the man does not look at her, but she looks at another man, he says:
"This person is looking at you," he said,
"and they are also your husband or wife.
If you see one another, you shall immediately follow each other and go together to another place."
If the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings seek a goddess, they may only welcome her home after the bride's family has granted permission, whether by barter or purchase;
all the gods of the Desire Realm are likewise so.
In Jambudvīpa, there are male and female organs through which they unite;
it is the same in Pūrvavideha, Aparagoyānī, and Uttarakuru.
Among the gods of the Four Great Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the union of males and females is likewise the same.

The gods of the Yāma Heaven satisfy their desire by embracing; those of the Tuṣita Heaven by holding hands; those of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven by laughing together; and those of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven by gazing at one another.

The inhabitants of Aparagoyānī experience various sensual pleasures that are twice as superior as those of the people of Jambudvīpa; even the desires of the gods of Paranirmita-vaśavartin are twice as superior as those of the Nirmāṇarati gods.

Among the women of Jambudvīpa, there are those who eat unwholesome food, those whose pregnancies last for a long time, those who are giving birth for the first time, and those who nurse their infants;
it is the same in Aparagoyānī and Pūrvavideha.
Among the women of Uttarakuru in the north, there are those who have poor food, those whose pregnancies last for a long time, and those who give birth; however, they never suckle their infants.

Whether it be a son or a daughter, once born, the child is placed at a crossroads. The mother inserts her finger into the child’s mouth, and if a passerby happens to go by that way, they likewise insert their finger into the child’s mouth. Through this contact with the fingers, the child grows large.

The men and women of Uttarakuru dwell separately and do not intermingle; when a boy is born, he becomes an adult in seven days and enters the ranks of the men, and when a girl is born, she becomes an adult in seven days and enters the ranks of the women.
If a man and a woman first conceive a lustful intent and walk hand-in-hand beneath a tree, that *mañjuṣaka* tree will immediately provide them with cover, and their sexual act will be accomplished;
if it does not provide cover, they will separate from one another, knowing this to be improper sexual conduct and thus not daring to commit it.
Among the goddesses of the Four Heavenly Kings, there is no unwholesome food, nor is there gestation or growth in a womb; they neither give birth to children nor nurse them.
As for the male and female deities, they may give birth to children upon their laps or while in bed.
If one is born upon the mother’s lap or in the place where she sleeps,
the female deity thinks, "This is my child," and the male deity says the same.
"If it is said, 'This is my son,' then there is one father and one mother;
if he is born upon the father's lap or in the place where the father sleeps, he has only one father, yet all the wives and concubines may be considered his mothers."

The sensual desires of the people of Jambudvīpa throughout a single lifetime are innumerable and immeasurable; yet there are also some who practice pure conduct and remain free from desire until death.

As for those with many desires in Aparagoyānī, they reach a number of twelve instances within a single lifetime, while those with moderate desire reach ten; there are also some who practice pure conduct and remain free from desire until death.

In Pūrvavideha, those with excessive desire reach a number of seven times within a single lifetime; those of middling capacity reach five or six; and there are also some people who practice pure conduct until death and remain free from desire.

Among the people of Uttarakuru, those with many desires have at most five instances of desire in a single lifetime; those of middling quality may have three or four; and there are also some who practice pure conduct and remain free from desire until death.

Among the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, there are immeasurable and innumerable who engage in sexual desire throughout their lives; yet there are also gods who cultivate pure conduct until death remains free from desire.
It is the same for all the gods of the Desire Realm.
All women find pleasure in touch, and all men find pleasure when the impurity is emitted.
If all men take impurity as their desire, those among the gods who have desire find pleasure in the emission of vital energy.
“The people of Jambudvīpa have three causes and conditions by which they surpass those of Uttarakuru and the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
What are these three?
First, valor; second, mindfulness and retention; third, the presence therein of those who dwell in the holy life (brahmacarya).”
The inhabitants of Uttarakuru possess three causes and conditions by which they surpass those of Jambudvīpa and the Trāyastriṃśa devas:

first, they have no sense of "mine" and no hoarding of possessions; second, their lifespan is fixed at one thousand years; and third, they will inevitably ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven in the end.
The gods possess three causes and conditions by which they surpass those of Jambudvīpa and Uttarakuru:
first, their lifespan is exceedingly long; second, their physical forms are extraordinary; and third, their happiness is most abundant.
This meaning was spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Thus have I heard.
*Lishi Apitan Lun*, Fascicle Six.
The Abhidharma Treatise on the Establishment of the World Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Western India during the Chen Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-one: On Rebirth. Chapter Twenty-one: On Rebirth.
"Those who commit the most extreme forms of the ten paths of unwholesome action will be born in the Great Avīci Hell;
those who commit the next level of lighter evil will be born in the other minor hells;
and those who commit even lighter offenses will be born in the eight minor hells of Yama."
If it is even lighter, one will next be born into the realm of birds and beasts;
if it is yet lighter, one will next be born into the realm of hungry ghosts.

If one performs the ten paths of wholesome action in their lightest form, one will be born into the lowest class of families in Jambudvīpa—either into a family of scavengers, or a family of butchers, or a family of musicians, or a family of artisans, or a family of soldiers and slaves.

If one is superior by a degree, one is born into the family of a householder; if superior by another degree, one is born into the family of a brahmin; if superior yet again, one is born into the family of a kṣatriya.

If one is superior still, one is born in Aparagoyānī; if superior by another degree, one is born in Pūrvavideha; if superior by another degree, one is born in Uttarakuru; if superior by another degree, one is born among the Four Heavenly Kings; if superior by another degree, one is born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; if superior by another degree, one is born in the Yāma Heaven; if superior by another degree, one is born in the Tuṣita Heaven; if superior by another degree, one is born in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
If one performs the most excellent ten paths of wholesome action, one is reborn in the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations.
If an ordinary person cultivates the four dhyānas, each has three grades: namely, inferior, middling, and superior.

This person is born among the Brahmakāyika devas due to karma associated with the lower grade of the first dhyāna; by means of this karma, they attain this celestial realm, a celestial lifespan, a celestial abode, and companionship with those of their own kind.
Once one has been born there and experiences the retribution of that karma, there are two kinds of pleasure:
first, the pleasure of non-affliction; second, the pleasure of sensation.
When this karma has matured, it is exhausted through experience without remainder.

Due to karma associated with the initial stage of the middle-level first dhyāna, one is born among the Brahmakāyika devas; due to superior karma, one is likewise born in this heaven. Because of this karma, one attains the celestial realm, the celestial lifespan, the celestial abode, and birth among the celestial peers.
Once one has been born there and experiences the karmic retribution of that action, there are two kinds of pleasure:
first, the pleasure of non-affliction; second, the pleasure of sensation.
When this karma has matured, it is exhausted through experience without remainder.

Due to karma associated with the inferior grade of the second dhyāna, one is born in the Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*) because of that karma; due to karma associated with the middling grade of the second dhyāna, one is born in the Heaven of Infinite Light (*Apramāṇābha*); and due to karma associated with the superior grade of the second dhyāna, one is born in the Heaven of Utmost Pervasive Light (*Ābhāsvara*). By means of this karma, one attains the celestial realm, the celestial lifespan, the celestial abode, and birth among the celestial peers.
Once one has been born there and experiences the karmic retribution of that action, there are two kinds of pleasure: first, the pleasure of non-affliction; second, the pleasure of sensation.
Once this karma has matured and been fully experienced, nothing remains.

Due to karma associated with the lower grade of the third dhyāna, one is born in the Heaven of Limited Purity; due to karma associated with the middle grade of the third dhyāna, one is born in the Heaven of Infinite Purity; and due to karma associated with the superior grade of the third dhyāna, one is born in the Heaven of Universal Purity. By means of this karma, one attains this celestial path, the lifespan of the gods, the abode of the gods, and the commonality of the gods.
Once one has been born there and experiences the karmic retribution of that action, there are two kinds of pleasure:
first, the pleasure of non-affliction; second, the pleasure of sensation.
Once this karma has matured and been fully experienced, it leaves nothing remaining.

Due to karma associated with the lower grade of the fourth dhyāna, one is born in the Anabhraka Heaven; due to karma associated with the middle grade of the fourth dhyāna, one is born in the Puṇyaprasava Heaven; and due to karma associated with the superior grade of the fourth dhyāna, one is born in the Bṛhatphala Heaven. By virtue of this karma, one attains this celestial path, the lifespan of the gods, the abode of the gods, and the status of being a fellow-being among the gods.
Having already been born there, they experience the karmic retribution of that action; while there may be a lack of oppressive suffering, there is no further experience of pleasure.
Once that karma has matured and its effects have been fully exhausted, ordinary worldlings take birth in other realms in accordance with their remaining karma.
"If ordinary persons cultivate the four immeasurable minds, each has three grades, namely: inferior, middling, and superior.
As for the immeasurable loving-kindness (*maitrī*), it is cultivated in this manner and practiced repeatedly in this manner, just like the four dhyānas."
The immeasurable joy is cultivated in this manner and practiced repeatedly, as in the first dhyāna and the second dhyāna.
The immeasurable compassion is cultivated in this manner and practiced repeatedly, as in the fourth dhyāna.
The abandonment of the immeasurables is cultivated and practiced in this manner, just as in the third and fourth dhyānas.
"When ordinary persons cultivate the contemplation of impurity, there are three grades for each: namely, inferior, middling, and superior."
The contemplation of impurity practiced with aversion is cultivated and repeatedly performed in the same manner as the four dhyānas.
The contemplation of impurity practiced with aversion is cultivated and repeatedly performed in the same manner as the fourth dhyāna.
"When an ordinary person practices mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti), there are three grades for each: namely, inferior, middling, and superior.
Practicing and cultivating it in this manner involves counting in the same way as the three types of meditative concentration (dhyāna) mentioned previously."
“Ordinary persons cultivate five perceptions of existence, each of which has three grades—namely, inferior, middling, and superior.
What are these five? First, the perception of impurity;
second, the perception of faults; third, the perception of death and falling; fourth, the perception of satiety with food; and fifth, the perception that all worlds are without peace.”
Regarding the perception of the repulsive that is free from aversion: when one cultivates it in this way and practices it repeatedly, it is like the four dhyānas.
Regarding the perception of the repulsive with aversion and the subsequent four perceptions: when one cultivates them in this way and practices them repeatedly, it is like the fourth dhyāna.
“Ordinary persons cultivate the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭau kṛtsnāyatanāni*), each having three grades: namely, inferior, middling, and superior.
What are the eight?

First, possessing the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are limited; these limited forms may be beautiful or coarse, and with the thought ‘I pervade this,’ one knows and sees them as such; this is the first basis of mastery.”

2. Having internal perception of forms, one perceives external forms that are immeasurable, whether beautiful or coarse, thinking: "I pervade this perception, knowing and seeing it," and forms such a mental image; 3.
Having no internal perception of forms, one perceives external forms that are limited, as before;
4. Having no internal perception of forms, one perceives external forms that are immeasurable, also as before.

Fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth: in each case, while internally possessing the perception of formlessness, one contemplates the four colors—namely blue, yellow, red, and white—and forms the thought: "I pervade this perception, being able to know it and see it. Thus one conceives.
Among these eight perceptions, the first and second are cultivated and practiced repeatedly in the same manner as the four dhyānas.
As for the latter six perceptions, they are cultivated and practiced repeatedly in the same manner as the fourth dhyāna.
“Ordinary persons cultivate the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), each of which has three grades: namely, inferior, middling, and superior.
These eight totalities, when cultivated and practiced repeatedly in this manner, are like the fourth dhyāna.”

Regarding the latter two "all-encompassing" bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*), when they are thus cultivated and thus repeatedly practiced, they are, according to their respective stages, like the base of infinite space for the all-encompassing base of space, and like the base of infinite consciousness for the all-encompassing base of consciousness.
“Ordinary persons cultivate the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), each of which has three grades: namely, inferior, middling, and superior.

By means of an inferior karma associated with the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), such a person is born in the Heaven of Infinite Space; by means of a middling karma associated with the sphere of infinite space, they are likewise born in this heaven; and by means of a superior karma associated with the sphere of infinite space, they are likewise born in this heaven. Due to these karmas, they obtain the celestial realm, obtain a celestial lifespan, obtain a celestial abode, and obtain companionship with those of their own kind.”

Having been born there, they experience the karmic fruition of their actions; they possess unafflicted happiness, yet they do not experience [sensory] pleasure. Once this karma has matured, it is exhausted through its utilization.

Due to karma associated with the inferior degree of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), one is born in the Heaven of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness; due to karma associated with the middling degree of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, one is likewise born in this heaven; and due to karma associated with the superior degree of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, one is likewise born in this heaven. Because of this karma, one attains the celestial realm, the celestial lifespan, the celestial abode, and the celestial community.
Having been born there, one experiences the karmic retribution of that [meditative attainment]; there is only the absence of oppressive suffering, but no experience of pleasure.
Once this karma has matured, it is exhausted through its utilization.

By means of karma associated with the inferior degree of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one is born in the heaven of the sphere of nothingness; by means of karma associated with the middling degree of the sphere of nothingness, one is likewise born in this heaven; and by means of karma associated with the superior degree of the sphere of nothingness, one is likewise born in this heaven.
Due to this karma, one attains the celestial realm, the celestial lifespan, the celestial abode, and birth among celestial peers.
Having been born there, one experiences the retribution of that karma; however, there is only the absence of oppressive suffering, and no experience of pleasure.
Once this karma has matured, it is exhausted through its experience without remainder.

Due to karma associated with the lower grade of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one is born in the heaven of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; due to karma associated with the middle grade of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one is likewise born in this heaven; and due to karma associated with the superior grade of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one is likewise born in this heaven. By means of this karma, one attains the celestial realm, the celestial lifespan, the celestial abode, and the celestial community.
Having been born there, they experience the karmic retribution of their deeds; there is only the absence of oppressive suffering, but no experience of pleasure.
Once this karma has matured and been fully exhausted, these ordinary persons take birth in another realm according to their subsequent retributive karma.
This ordinary person, having practiced the first dhyāna concentration until it was produced and attained, subsequently falls away from it all.

This person abides in the inferior grade of the first dhyāna; by means of karma associated with the inferior grade of the first dhyāna, this person is born among the Brahmakāyika devas. Having been born there, they experience the retribution of the karma of the inferior grade of the first dhyāna, attaining the bliss of non-affliction and the bliss of sensation.

One experiences the karmic retribution of middling and superior grades of the first and second dhyānas within this very life, receiving both the pleasure of non-affliction and the pleasure of sensation.
One likewise experiences the karmic retribution of the third and fourth dhyānas within this very life; however, while there is no pleasure of non-affliction, there is no pleasure of sensation either.
When this karma has ripened and been fully experienced without remainder, one subsequently takes birth in another place due to the remaining karmic retribution.
The same applies to the middling and superior grades of the first dhyāna.
When ordinary persons have cultivated the four dhyanas, having already produced and attained them, they subsequently fall away from them all once again.

This person dwells within the lower grade of the second dhyāna; by means of karma associated with the lower grade of the second dhyāna, they are born in the Parīttaśubha Heaven. Having been born there, they experience the karmic retribution of the lower grade of the second dhyāna, attaining the bliss of non-oppression as well as the bliss of sensation.

One experiences the karmic retribution of the second and first dhyānas of medium and superior grades within this very life, attaining therein both the pleasure of non-affliction and the pleasure of sensation.
Within this same life, one also experiences the retribution of the third and fourth dhyānas; however, these consist only of the pleasure of non-affliction, lacking the pleasure of sensation.
When this karma has ripened and been fully experienced without remainder, one is subsequently reborn in another place due to the remaining karmic retribution.
The same applies to the middling and superior grades of the second dhyāna.
When an ordinary person has cultivated, produced, and attained the four dhyānas, they may subsequently fall away from them all once again.

This person dwells within the lower grade of the third dhyāna; by virtue of karma associated with the lower grade of the third dhyāna, they are born in the Heaven of Limited Purity (*Parīttaśubha*). Having been born there, they experience the karmic retribution of the lower grade of the third dhyāna, attaining the bliss of non-affliction as well as the bliss of sensation.
Experiencing the karmic retribution of the middle and superior grades of the third dhyāna, one attains both the pleasure of non-affliction and the feeling of pleasure within this life.
Regarding the karmic retribution of the first, second, and fourth dhyanas, one experiences the pleasure of non-affliction, but there is no feeling of pleasure.
Once this karma has ripened and been fully experienced without remainder, one is subsequently reborn in another place due to the remaining karmic retribution.
The same applies to the middle and superior grades of the three dhyānas.
When an ordinary person has practiced, produced, and attained the four dhyānas, they may subsequently fall away from them all once again.

This person dwells within the lower grade of the four dhyānas; by means of karma associated with the lower grade of the four dhyānas, they are born in the Anabhraka Heaven. Having been born there, they experience the karmic retribution of the lower grade of the four dhyānas, attaining a bliss free from oppression, yet it is not a bliss that is felt as sensation.

Having experienced the karmic retribution of the medium and superior grades of the fourth dhyāna and the other three dhyānas, one attains a bliss free from oppression during this life, yet there is no further experience of [sensory] pleasure.
Once this karma has matured and been fully exhausted, the ordinary person is born in another realm due to the remaining subsequent retributive karma.
The same applies to the middling and superior grades of the remaining four dhyānas.
When an ordinary person has cultivated the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments, having already produced and acquired them, they subsequently fall away from all of them once again.

This person dwells in the inferior level of the Sphere of Infinite Space; by means of karma associated with the inferior level of the Sphere of Infinite Space, they are born in the Heaven of the Sphere of Infinite Space. Having been born there, they experience the retribution of the inferior level of the Sphere of Infinite Space, attaining a pleasure free from oppression, yet not a pleasure that is felt.

Receiving the intermediate and superior grades of the sphere of infinite space, as well as the fruits of the three higher formless attainments, one experiences the bliss of non-affliction within this life, yet there is no experience of [sensory] pleasure.
When this karma has matured and been fully experienced without remainder, that ordinary person is reborn in another place due to the remaining karma of subsequent retribution.
The same applies to the remaining middling and superior levels of the Sphere of Infinite Space.
This ordinary person, having cultivated the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments and having already produced and acquired them, subsequently falls away from them all.

This person dwells in the inferior level of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*); by means of karma associated with the inferior level of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, they are born in the Heaven of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness. Having been born there, they experience the karmic retribution of the inferior level of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, attaining a pleasure free from oppression, yet without the experience of [sensory] pleasure.

Experiencing the intermediate and superior grades of the consciousness-infinity attainment (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), as well as the karmic retribution of the first and last three formless attainments (*ārūpya*), one attains the bliss of non-affliction within this life, yet there is no experience of [sensory] pleasure.
When this karma has matured and been exhausted through experience without remainder, that ordinary person is reborn in another place due to the remaining karma of subsequent retribution.
The same applies to the intermediate and superior grades of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
This ordinary person, having practiced the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) and having already produced and attained them, subsequently falls away from them all.

This person dwells in the inferior degree of the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana); by means of karma associated with the inferior degree of the sphere of nothingness, they are born in the deva realm of the sphere of nothingness. Having been born there, they experience the karmic retribution of the inferior degree of the sphere of nothingness, attaining a bliss free from oppression, yet not a bliss that is felt.

Experiencing the intermediate and superior grades of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and the karmic retributions of the three preceding formless spheres, one attains the bliss of non-oppression within this life, yet there is no experience of [sensory] pleasure.
When this karma has matured and been fully experienced without remainder, that ordinary person undergoes rebirth in another place due to the remaining subsequent retributive karma.
The same applies to other middling and superior grades of karma.
These ordinary persons, having practiced the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments until they had arisen and attained them, subsequently fall away from all of them.

Such a person dwells in the inferior attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; by means of karma associated with that inferior attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, they are reborn in the deva realm of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Having been born there, they experience the fruit of karma consisting of the inferior attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, obtaining a bliss free from oppression, yet it is not a bliss that is felt.

Experiencing the intermediate and superior grades of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and the karmic retributions of the three lower formless attainments, one attains a bliss free from oppression within this life, yet there is no feeling of pleasure.
When this karma has matured and been exhausted through experience without remainder, that ordinary person undergoes rebirth in another place due to the remaining subsequent retribution karma.
The same applies to the intermediate and superior grades of karma.
The noble disciples of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, cultivate the four dhyānas, each of which has three grades: namely, inferior, middling, and superior.

By means of an inferior karma associated with the first dhyāna, such a person is reborn in the Heaven of Brahma’s Retinue (Brahmapurohita). Due to this karma, they attain that celestial realm, attain a celestial lifespan, attain a celestial abode, and attain a celestial status among their peers.
Once one has been born there and experiences the karmic retribution of that action, there are two kinds of pleasure:
first, the pleasure of non-affliction, and second, the pleasure of sensation.
When this karma has matured, it is exhausted through experience without remainder.

Due to karma associated with the initial stage of the middle grade first dhyāna, one is born in the Brahmakāyika heaven; due to karma of the superior grade, one is likewise born in this same heaven. By means of this karma, one attains the celestial realm, the celestial lifespan, the celestial abode, and birth among the celestial peers.
Once one has been born there and experiences the retribution of that karma, there are two kinds of pleasure:
first, the pleasure of non-affliction; second, the pleasure of sensation.
When this karma has matured, it is exhausted through experience without remainder.

Due to karma associated with the lower grade of the second dhyāna, one is born in the Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*) because of that karma; due to karma associated with the middle grade of the second dhyāna, one is born in the Heaven of Infinite Light (*Apramāṇābha*); and due to karma associated with the superior grade of the second dhyāna, one is born in the Heaven of Utmost Pervasive Light (*Ābhāsvara*). Because of this karma, one attains the celestial realm, the celestial lifespan, the celestial abode, and the celestial community.
Once one has been born there and experiences the retribution of that karma, there are two kinds of pleasure:
first, the pleasure of non-affliction; second, the pleasure of sensation.
When this karma has matured, it is exhausted through experience without remainder.

Due to karma associated with the lower grade of the third dhyāna, one is born in the Heaven of Limited Purity; due to karma associated with the middle grade of the third dhyāna, one is born in the Heaven of Infinite Purity; and due to karma associated with the superior grade of the third dhyāna, one is born in the Heaven of Universal Purity. By means of such karma, one attains this celestial path, the celestial lifespan, the celestial abode, and birth among the celestial peers.
Once one has been born there and experiences the retribution of that karma, there are two kinds of pleasure:
first, the pleasure of non-affliction; second, the pleasure of sensation.
When this karma has matured, it is exhausted through experience without remainder.

Due to karma associated with the lower grade of the fourth dhyāna, one is born in the Anabhraka heaven; due to karma associated with the middle grade of the fourth dhyāna, one is born in the Puṇyaprasava heaven; and due to karma associated with the superior grade of the fourth dhyāna, one is born in the Bṛhatphala heaven. By virtue of this karma, one attains this celestial path, the lifespan of the gods, the abode of the gods, and the status of being a fellow-being among the gods.
Having been born there, they experience the karmic fruition of their deeds; they possess unsurpassed happiness and no longer undergo further suffering.

Once born there, by virtue of karma associated with the highest grade of the fourth dhyāna—cultivated through respectful and diligent practice, never turning away from constant cultivation, and refined by the practice of the various factors of enlightenment—they are reborn in the Sudṛśa Heaven because of that karma.

Ten times this karma produces rebirth in the Sudarśana Heaven; ten times more than that produces rebirth in the Abṛha Heaven; ten times more than that produces rebirth in the Atapa Heaven; and ten times more than that produces rebirth in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven. By means of this karma, one attains the celestial realm, celestial lifespan, celestial abode, and birth among the celestial peers.
Having been born there, they experience the karmic retribution of their deeds; they possess unconditioned bliss and no longer undergo further suffering.
Once this karma has matured and its effects have been fully exhausted, the karma that led them to the higher realms is spent therein, and they attain parinirvāṇa within that very state.

The disciples of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, cultivate the four immeasurable concentrations (*catur-apramāṇa-samādhi*), each of which has three grades: namely, inferior, middling, and superior.
Regarding the immeasurable loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*), it is cultivated and practiced repeatedly in this manner, just as in the case of the four types of dhyāna.
Regarding the immeasurable state of joy (*muditā*), one cultivates it and practices it repeatedly in this manner, as in the first dhyāna or the second dhyāna.
Regarding the immeasurable state of compassion (*karuṇā*), one cultivates it and practices it repeatedly in this manner, as in the fourth dhyāna.
Regarding the abandonment of the immeasurables: by practicing and cultivating them in this manner, they are like the third and fourth dhyānas.
When the noble disciples of the Buddha cultivate the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā), there are three grades for each: namely, inferior, middling, and superior.
The contemplation of impurity that involves aversion is cultivated and practiced repeatedly in the same manner as the four dhyānas.
The contemplation of impurity that does not involve aversion is cultivated and practiced repeatedly in the same manner as the fourth dhyāna.
The noble disciples of the Buddha cultivate mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti), each having three grades: namely, inferior, middling, and superior.
They cultivate it and practice it with such frequency, just as in the three kinds of meditative concentration (dhyāna) mentioned previously.

The noble disciples of the Buddha cultivate ten perceptions (*saṃjñā*), each of which has three grades: namely, inferior, middling, and superior. What are these ten? First, the perception of impermanence;

second, the perception of non-self; third, the perception of eradication; fourth, the perception of detachment from desire; fifth, the perception of cessation; sixth, the perception of impurity; seventh, the perception of faults; eighth, the perception of death and falling [into lower realms]; ninth, the perception of revulsion toward food; and tenth, the perception that all worlds are without security.
The first five types of perception, along with the perception of impurity that is free from aversion, are cultivated and repeatedly practiced in the same manner as the four dhyānas.
The latter four types of perception, along with the perception of impurity that involves aversion, are cultivated and repeatedly practiced in the same manner as the fourth dhyāna.
The noble disciples of the Buddha cultivate the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni*), each of which has three grades: namely, inferior, middling, and superior. What are the eight?

First, possessing the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are limited; these limited forms may be beautiful or coarse. "I pervade this perception," thus one knows and sees it; such is the first base of mastery.

2. Having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as immeasurable, whether beautiful or coarse, thinking: "I pervade this perception and am able to know and see it," forming such a mental image; 3.
Without the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as limited, whether coarse or beautiful, as described before;
4. Without the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as immeasurable, the categories of which are likewise as described before.

Fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth: in each case, one internally possesses the perception of formlessness while observing external forms of four colors—namely blue, yellow, red, and white—and forms the mental conception: "I pervade this perception, being able to know it and see it. Thus one conceives.
Among these eight, the first and second are cultivated and practiced repeatedly in the same manner as the four dhyānas.
The latter six perceptions are cultivated and practiced repeatedly in the same manner as the fourth dhyāna.

The noble disciples of the Buddha cultivate the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*), each of which has three grades: namely, inferior, middling, and superior. First, the liberation of one who possesses the perception of internal forms while observing external forms;

Second, the liberation of one who lacks the perception of internal forms while observing external forms; Third, the liberation of the beautiful (*śubha-vimokṣa*); Fourth, the liberation of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-vimokṣa*); Fifth, the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-vimokṣa*); Sixth, the liberation of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-vimokṣa*); Seventh, the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-vimokṣa*); Eighth, the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayita-nirodha-vimokṣa*).
The first liberation is cultivated and practiced repeatedly in this manner, just as in the four dhyānas.
The second liberation is cultivated and practiced repeatedly in this manner, just as in the fourth dhyāna.
The third liberation: if one possesses the perception of internal forms and contemplates external forms, practicing and cultivating it in this manner, it is like the four dhyānas;
if one lacks the perception of internal forms and contemplates external forms, practicing and cultivating it in this manner, it is like the fourth dhyāna.
The latter four formless liberations each correspond to their own respective levels.

As for the eighth liberation, the cessation of sensation and perception (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it transcends the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception solely by way of abiding therein, not by way of detachment from desire; therefore, its level is not that of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The noble disciples of the Buddha cultivate the ten universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*), each of which has three grades: namely, inferior, middling, and superior.
As for the first eight universal bases, when they are cultivated and practiced in this manner, they are like the fourth dhyāna.
The latter two universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana) are each like their own respective stages.
When the noble disciples of the Buddha cultivate the four formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti), each has three grades: namely, inferior, middling, and superior.

By means of karma associated with the lower grade of the sphere of infinite space, this person is born in the heaven of the sphere of infinite space; by means of karma associated with the middle grade of the sphere of infinite space, they are likewise born in this heaven; and by means of the upper grade of the sphere of infinite space, they are also born in this heaven. Due to this karma, they obtain the celestial realm, the celestial lifespan, the celestial abode, and birth among the celestial peers.

Having been born there, one experiences the karmic fruition of that action; there is only the absence of painful suffering, but no experience of pleasure. Once this karma has matured, it is exhausted through its utilization.

By means of karma associated with the lower grade of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), one is born in the Heaven of Infinite Consciousness; by means of karma associated with the middle grade of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, one is also born in this heaven; and by means of karma associated with the superior grade of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, one is also born in this heaven. Through such karma, one attains the celestial realm, the celestial lifespan, the celestial abode, and the celestial companionship.
Having been born there, one experiences the karmic retribution of that action; there is only the absence of oppressive suffering, but no experience of pleasure.

Once this karma has matured and been fully exhausted, through an inferior-grade karma associated with the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one is born in the heaven of the sphere of nothingness; through a medium-grade karma associated with the sphere of nothingness, one is likewise born in this heaven; and through a superior-grade karma associated with the sphere of nothingness, one is also born in this heaven. By means of this karma, one attains the celestial realm, the celestial lifespan, the celestial abode, and birth among the celestial peers.
Having been born there, one experiences the karmic retribution of that action; there is only the absence of oppressive suffering, but no experience of pleasure.
Once this karma has matured, it is exhausted through its utilization without remainder.

By means of an inferior-grade karma associated with the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one is born in the heaven of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; by means of a medium-grade karma associated with the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one is likewise born in this heaven; and by means of a superior-grade karma associated with the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one is likewise born in this heaven. Through this karma, one obtains the divine path, the divine lifespan, the divine abode, and birth among the divine kind.
Having been born there, they experience the karmic retribution of their deeds; they possess only the absence of oppressive suffering, but no experience of pleasure.
Once this karma has matured and been exhausted through experience without remainder, they attain parinirvāṇa therein.
When the noble disciples of the Buddha have cultivated the four dhyānas and have already given rise to and attained them, they may subsequently fall away from them all.

Such a person dwells within the lower grade of the first dhyāna; by means of karma associated with the lower grade of the first dhyāna, this person is born among the Brahmakāyika devas. Having been born there, they experience the retribution of the lower grade of the first dhyāna, attaining the bliss of non-affliction as well as the bliss of sensation.

One experiences the karmic retribution of middling and superior grades of the first and second dhyānas within this very life, attaining both the experience of non-afflictive bliss (*avyābādha-sukha*) and the experience of pleasure (*sukha*).
Regarding the third and fourth dhyānas, one likewise attains their karmic retribution within this very life, experiencing non-afflictive bliss, but not the experience of pleasure.
When this karma has ripened and been fully experienced without remainder, the noble disciple of the Buddha attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyī*).
The same applies to the intermediate and superior grades of the first dhyāna.
When a noble disciple of the Buddha has cultivated the four dhyānas, having already produced and attained them, he may subsequently fall away from them all.

Such a person dwells within the lower grade of the second dhyāna; by means of karma associated with the lower grade of the second dhyāna, this person is born in the Parittābha Heaven. Having been born there, he experiences the retribution of the lower grade of the second dhyāna, attaining the bliss of non-affliction as well as the bliss of sensation.

Regarding the karmic retribution of the second dhyāna and the first dhyāna of medium and superior grades, one experiences therein the pleasure of non-affliction (*avyābādha-sukha*) and the pleasure of sensation (*vedita-sukha*) within this very life.
Furthermore, the third and fourth dhyānas also yield their fruit-retribution within this same life; one experiences the pleasure of non-affliction, but there is no pleasure of sensation.
When this karma has ripened and been exhausted without remainder, the noble disciple of the Buddha attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyī*).
The same applies to the two remaining types of second dhyāna—those of medium and superior grade.

When a noble disciple of the Buddha has cultivated the four dhyānas such that they have been produced and attained, yet subsequently regresses from them all, this person dwells within the lower grade of the third dhyāna.

By virtue of karma associated with the lower grade of the third dhyāna, they are reborn in the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven (the Heaven of Limited Purity). Having been born there, they experience the retribution of the lower grade of the third dhyāna, receiving the pleasure of non-affliction and the pleasure of sensation.

One experiences the karmic retribution of the middling and superior grades of the third dhyāna, whereby in this life one attains the experience of non-afflictive bliss (*avyābādha-sukha*) as well as experienced bliss (*anubhava-sukha*).
One experiences the karmic retribution of the first, second, and fourth dhyānas, whereby one experiences non-afflictive bliss, but there is no experienced bliss.
When this karma has ripened and been fully experienced without remainder, the noble disciple of the Buddha attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*).
The same applies to the remaining middle and superior grades of the three dhyānas.

When a noble disciple of the Buddha has practiced the four dhyānas, having already produced and attained them, yet subsequently falls away from them all, such a person abides in the inferior grade of the four dhyānas.

Due to karma associated with the inferior grade of the four dhyānas, they are reborn in the Anabhraka Heaven. Having been born there, they experience the karmic retribution of the inferior grade of the four dhyānas, attaining a bliss free from oppression, though it is not the bliss of sensation.

Regarding the karmic retribution of the middle and superior grades of the fourth dhyāna and the other three dhyānas, one experiences non-afflictive bliss within this life, yet there is no experience of [ordinary] pleasure.
When this karma has matured and been exhausted without remainder, the noble disciple of the Buddha attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*).
The same applies to the medium and superior grades within the remaining four dhyānas.
When the noble disciples of the Buddha have cultivated the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments, having already produced and acquired them, they may subsequently fall away from them all.

Such a person dwells in the inferior degree of the Sphere of Infinite Space; by means of karma associated with that inferior degree of the Sphere of Infinite Space, they are reborn in the Heaven of the Sphere of Infinite Space. Having been born there, they experience the retribution of the inferior degree of the Sphere of Infinite Space, attaining a pleasure free from oppression, yet not a pleasure derived from sensation.

Experiencing the intermediate and superior grades of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), as well as the fruits of the three higher formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), one experiences the bliss of non-affliction during this lifetime, yet there is no experience of [sensory] pleasure.
When this karma has matured and been exhausted without remainder, the noble disciple of the Buddha attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāṇa*).
The same applies to the remaining intermediate and superior grades of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

When a noble disciple of the Buddha has cultivated and attained the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments, yet subsequently falls away from them all, that person dwells in the inferior level of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

Due to karma associated with this inferior level of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, they are reborn in the Heaven of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness. Having been born there, they experience the karmic retribution of the inferior level of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness: they obtain a pleasure free from oppression, yet it is not a pleasure consisting of sensation.

Experiencing the intermediate and superior grades of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), as well as the karmic retributions of the first and last three formless spheres, one attains in this life the bliss of non-affliction, yet there is no experience of [sensory] pleasure.
When this karma has ripened and been experienced until it is exhausted without remainder, the noble disciple of the Buddha attains parinirvāṇa therein.
The same applies to the intermediate and superior grades within the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
When a noble disciple of the Buddha has cultivated the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments, having already produced and attained them, he may subsequently fall away from all of them.

Such a person dwells in the inferior level of the base of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*); by means of karma associated with the inferior level of the base of nothingness, he is reborn in the deva realm of the base of nothingness. Having been born there, he experiences the retribution of the inferior level of the base of nothingness, attaining a bliss free from oppression, yet not the bliss of sensation.

Experiencing the intermediate and superior grades of the sphere of nothingness and the three formless attainments of the preceding and following stages, as well as the karmic retribution thereof, one attains in this life the bliss of non-affliction, yet there is no experience of [sensory] pleasure.
When this karma has ripened and been fully exhausted without remainder, the noble disciple of the Buddha attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*).
It is likewise for those in the intermediate, superior, and limitless attainments (*ākiṃcanyāyatana* and *naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
When the noble disciples of the Buddha have cultivated and attained the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments, they may subsequently fall away from them all.

Such a person dwells in the inferior attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Due to karma associated with this inferior attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, they are reborn in the heaven of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Having been born there, they experience the karmic retribution of the inferior attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; they obtain a pleasure free from oppression, yet it is not a pleasure that is felt.

Experiencing the intermediate and superior grades of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), as well as the karma of the three lower formless attainments, one attains the bliss of non-affliction within this life, yet there is no feeling of pleasure (*vedanā-sukha*).
When this karma has ripened and been fully experienced without remainder, the noble disciple of the Buddha attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*).
It is likewise for those who have attained the intermediate, superior, and supreme levels of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
“There are three types of *ūrdhvasrotas* *anāgāmins*:
first, those who are initially born in the *Brahmapurohita* heaven and, proceeding through the stages in succession up to the *Bṛhatphala* heaven, attain *parinirvāṇa* after being born therein;
second, those who are initially born in the *Bṛhatphala* heaven and, proceeding through the stages in succession up to the *Akaniṣṭha* heaven, attain *parinirvāṇa* after being born there.”

Third, they are first born into the Heaven of Infinite Space; proceeding in this sequence through successive births up to the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, they attain parinirvāṇa once born therein.
"Furthermore, there are two types of *ūrdhvasrotas* *anāgāmins*:
first, those in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and second, those in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

If one attains *parinirvāṇa* in the realm of form, they proceed through the heavens in successive order from the Brahmakāyika heaven up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven; having been born there, they attain *parinirvāṇa*."

Regarding those in the formless realm: first they are born in the Heaven of Infinite Space; proceeding in this sequence through successive births up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, having been born therein, they attain parinirvāṇa.

"Furthermore, there is another type of *ūrdhvasrotas* Anāgāmin who is born from the Brahmakāyika heaven; proceeding in this manner through successive births up to the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana, and having been born there, they attain parinirvāṇa."
This meaning was spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Thus have I heard.
Chapter Twenty-Two: On Lifespan. The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"Twenty thousand years among humans constitute one day and night in the Avīci hell; thirty such days and nights make one month, and twelve such months make one year."
For this number of years—many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, and many hundreds of thousands of years—one undergoes the ripened fruit of karma within this hell.
Among these beings, the maximum lifespan is one *kalpa*.
Six thousand years among humans constitute one day and night in the Yama hell; by this reckoning, thirty such days and nights make a month, and twelve months make a year.
For this number of years—many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, and many hundreds of thousands of years—they undergo the ripening of their karmic retribution within this hell.

Among the sentient beings of the animal realm, there are those who die and are reborn six or seven times within a single day and night; furthermore, there are animals whose lifespan lasts for an entire kalpa.

One month among human beings constitutes one day and night in the realm of ghosts and spirits (preta); likewise, one month among human beings constitutes one day and night within that realm of gods and ghosts.
Based on this reckoning, thirty such days and nights constitute one month, and twelve months constitute one year.
By this calculation of years, five hundred years is their lifespan; these five hundred years correspond to fifteen thousand years among human beings.

The people of Jambudvīpa may have a lifespan of ten years or an incalculable number of years (*asaṃkhyeya*); during this interval, their life span gradually increases and decreases, reaching a maximum of eighty thousand years and a minimum of ten years.

The lifespan of the people of Aparagoyānī is two hundred and fifty years; the lifespan of the people of Pūrvavideha is five hundred years; and the lifespan of those in Uttarakuru is fixed at one thousand years.
Fifty human years constitute one day and night for the Four Heavenly Kings; thirty such days and nights make one month, and twelve months make one year.
Based on these years, five hundred celestial years constitute their lifespan, which corresponds to nine million human years.
One hundred human years constitute one day and night for the Trāyastriṃśa gods; thirty such days and nights make one month, and twelve such months make one year.
According to these years, their lifespan is one thousand years, which corresponds to thirty-six million years among humans.
Two hundred human years constitute one day and night in the Yāma Heaven; thirty such days and nights make one month, and twelve months make one year.
According to these years, their lifespan is two thousand years, which corresponds to fourteen million four hundred thousand years among humans.
Four hundred human years constitute one day and night in the Tuṣita Heaven; thirty such days and nights make a month, and twelve such months make a year.
According to these years, their lifespan is four thousand celestial years, which corresponds to five trillion seven hundred and sixty billion human years.
Eight hundred human years constitute one day and night in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati); thirty such days and nights make one month, and twelve such months make one year.
According to these years, their lifespan is eight thousand years, which corresponds to twenty-three billion four hundred million years by human reckoning.

One thousand six hundred human years constitute one day and night in the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*). Based on this reckoning of days and nights, thirty such days make a month, and twelve such months make a year.
By this reckoning of years, their lifespan is sixteen thousand years, which corresponds to nine hundred twenty-one billion six hundred million years by human calculation.
On the summit beneath Mount Gandhamādana, the asuras have a lifespan equal to that of the Four Great Heavenly Kings.
The asuras dwelling at the base and summit of Mount Sumeru have lifespans equal to those of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.

One small kalpa is called one kalpa; twenty small kalpas are also called one kalpa; forty small kalpas are also called one kalpa; sixty small kalpas are also called one kalpa; and eighty small kalpas constitute one great kalpa.
What is meant by one kalpa being called a small kalpa?

At that time, the bhikṣu Devadatta was dwelling in hell undergoing the retribution of his matured karma; the Buddha, the World-Honored One, said he would dwell there for one kalpa. Thus, such a small kalpa is termed a kalpa.
How is it that twenty minor kalpas are also called one kalpa?

For example, the life span of the Brahmapurohita devas is twenty minor kalpas; regarding these Brahmā devas, the Buddha taught that their life span is one kalpa. Thus, those twenty [minor] kalpas are also called one kalpa.
How is it that forty minor kalpas are called one kalpa?
For example, the lifespan of the Brahmakāyika devas is forty minor kalpas; the Buddha says they dwell for one kalpa, and thus these forty kalpas are also called one kalpa.
How is it that sixty minor kalpas are called one kalpa?
Just as the lifespan of Mahābrahmā is sixty kalpas, yet the Buddha says he dwells for one kalpa, so too these sixty minor kalpas are called one kalpa.
How is it that eighty small kalpas constitute one great kalpa?

For example, the lifespan of the Parīttābha devas is one hundred and twenty small kalpas; the Buddha taught that their lifespan is one and a half great kalpas. Thus, eighty small kalpas are designated as one great kalpa.

The lifespan of the gods of Immeasurable Light is one hundred and forty small kalpas; the gods of Supreme Pervasive Light dwell for one hundred and sixty small kalpas; these constitute two great kalpas.

The life span of the Parīttaśubha devas is two and a half great kalpas; the life span of the Apramāṇaśubha devas is three and a half great kalpas; the life span of the Śubhakṛtsna devas is four great kalpas; the life span of the Anabhraka devas is three hundred great kalpas; the life span of the Puṇyaprasava devas is four hundred great kalpas; the life span of the Bṛhatphala devas is five hundred great kalpas; the life span of the Asaṃjñisattva devas is one thousand great kalpas; the life span of the Sudarśana devas is fifteen hundred great kalpas; the life span of the Sudṛśa devas is two thousand great kalpas; the life span of the Suddhāvāsa devas is four thousand great kalpas; the life span of the Atapa devas is eight thousand great kalpas; and the life span of the Akaniṣṭha devas is sixteen thousand great kalpas.
