For countless thousands of years they constantly cry out in lamentation, undergoing such suffering that even when their evil karma is not yet exhausted, they cannot seek death.

Having emerged from this hell, they see the intermediate alley-hell which resembles a great marketplace; therein is a forest named Śāmbūli, where hell-wardens seize the arms of the offenders and pull them up and down, all as previously described.

Furthermore, there are iron cauldrons filled to the brim with boiling molten iron; the hell-wardens seize the people and hurl them into the cauldrons. Only after five hundred human years have passed do they briefly emerge, at which time they can barely call out.
Why do you not call out?
You are repeatedly submerged within this.

Furthermore, there are sinners who are either face up or face down, with their bodies entirely nailed with red-hot iron nails and placed upon the ground of glowing iron; or else the tongues of these sinners are pulled out as large as ox-hides and spread upon the ground, where they are nailed with countless red-hot iron spikes.
Furthermore, there are sinners whose entire bodies are hacked like the joints of sugarcane.

There are also sinners whom the hell-wardens hack and chop; when they lower their swords, the heads are severed, and when they raise their swords, the heads grow back again. Because of this killing, the heads accumulate until they form a mountain;
the same occurs with their hands and feet.
Furthermore, there are sinners whose skin is flayed and spread upon the ground, and their flesh is sliced with swords and piled atop the skin.
Again, there are sinners who are cast into iron cauldrons, where the hell-wardens seize pestles and pound them until they are crushed to pieces.
Furthermore, there are sinners with the heads of beasts and human bodies, some pulling carts and so forth, as described in detail previously.
Moreover, there are countless sinners who are surrounded by various hell-wardens brandishing weapons, like those being hunted.

This is called the sinner undergoing such mutilation and slaughter; the suffering is of the highest grade, difficult to endure, most firm and intense, and most agonizing, such that as long as the evil karma is not exhausted, they cannot seek death even if they wish for it.
What karma did they perform in the past to receive this retribution of suffering?
In their former lives among humans, they committed the ten non-virtuous actions; because these were of a minor degree, they did not experience the great hells, but were instead born here.
Alternatively, having already experienced the fruits of the great hells, they are born here due to residual karma. Once born here, they fully undergo the various fruits of their residual karma.
At that time, the Buddha said: "Bhikṣus!
King Yama constantly makes this vow:”

"When shall I escape from here and be born into the human realm among my fellow men; born into a wealthy and noble family with abundant treasures, possessing a supple human body endowed with the marks of excellence and living in peace and happiness, traveling in carriages so that my feet do not tread upon the ground?"

Having reached maturity and with the six sense faculties fully developed, he has practiced generosity and performed various meritorious deeds; having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the dharma robes, out of right faith and wisdom, he has renounced the household life to embrace the homeless life.
Having gone forth, may I realize the ultimate holy life, just as those sons of good family in the past went forth, attained the Way, and perfected the holy life.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"What kind of karma is it that one performs, Which gives rise to sorrow and regret in the present life,
And leads to wailing and crying out in the future, As one undergoes various bitter fruits of suffering?"
When evil karma has not yet ripened, the deluded person calls it sweet;
once that karma has fully ripened, one only then knows it to be suffering and hardship.
When first committing an evil deed, it does not burn like fire immediately.
Like fire covered by ashes, it follows and burns the sinner.
Though the sinner be very clever, he brings about his own ruin;
he gradually destroys his own roots of goodness, just as a plantain tree perishes when it bears fruit.
Evil conduct born of ignorance brings self-destruction, just like harboring an enemy;
by committing various evil deeds, one will experience suffering in the future.
Practicing wholesome deeds through asceticism is excellent, for one will have no cause for regret in the present.
In the future, when one receives the retribution of the fruits [of one's actions], one will always be joyful and at peace.
Having seen this as it truly is, the Tathāgata, the Teacher of gods and humans,
spoke of the realm of Yama as the dwelling place for those who have committed evil.
The Chapter on Hells is concluded.
*Lishi Apitan Lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of the World), Fascicle Eight.
*Buddhabhāṣita Lishi Apitan Lun* (The Treatise on the Establishment of the World Spoken by the Buddha), Fascicle Nine.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Western India during the Chen Dynasty.
Chapter 24: The Minor Calamities. Section 1: The Calamity of Pestilence. Chapter Twenty-Four: The Calamity of Pestilence within the Minor Calamities.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:

"One small kalpa is called one kalpa; twenty small kalpas are also called one kalpa; forty small kalpas are also called one kalpa; sixty small kalpas are also called one kalpa; and eighty small kalpas are called one great kalpa."
How is it that one *antarakalpa* is called one *kalpa*?

At that time, the bhikṣu Devadatta was dwelling in hell undergoing the retribution for his matured karma; the Buddha, the World-Honored One, said he would dwell there for one *kalpa*. Thus, one such *antarakalpa* is called one *kalpa*.
How is it that twenty intermediate kalpas are also called one kalpa?

For example, the life span of the Brahmakāyika devas is twenty intermediate kalpas; yet the Buddha has taught that those Brahmā devas dwell for one kalpa. Thus, these twenty kalpas are also designated as one kalpa.
How is it that forty minor kalpas are called one kalpa?
For example, the lifespan of the Brahmakāyika devas is forty minor kalpas; the Buddha taught that their lifespan lasts for one kalpa, and thus these forty minor kalpas are also termed one kalpa.
How is it that sixty minor kalpas are called one kalpa?
Just as the lifespan of Mahābrahmā is sixty minor kalpas, yet the Buddha says he dwells for one kalpa; in this way, sixty minor kalpas are also called one kalpa.
How is it that eighty intermediate kalpas constitute one great kalpa?

The Buddha taught that within a kalpa the world is destroyed; within a kalpa the world remains in a state of destruction; within a kalpa the world is formed; and within a kalpa the world remains in a state of formation.
“Monk, how many are the kalpas of the world’s dissolution and so forth?
The Buddha said: “Monk!”

After twenty intermediate kalpas, the world undergoes dissolution; next, after twenty intermediate kalpas, it remains in a state of dissolution; next, after twenty intermediate kalpas, the world arises and is formed; and finally, after twenty intermediate kalpas, it remains in a state of formation.
Regarding these twenty small kalpas during which the world has arisen, formed, and remains:
how many have already passed, and how many have not yet passed?
Eight small kalpas have already passed; eleven small kalpas remain in the future; and one ninth kalpa—the current one—is not yet exhausted.
Of this ninth kalpa, how much has already passed, and how much remains in the future?
It is determined that six hundred and ninety years remain in the future; thus, the translation of this sutra was completed at the end of the Liang dynasty in the Jīmō year (579 CE).
Within these twenty intermediate kalpas, three minor calamities circulate in succession:
first, the calamity of great pestilence; second, the calamity of great warfare; and third, the calamity of great famine.
"Now this is the ninth kalpa, which is the third calamity.
This kalpa will come to an end because of famine.
Thus spoke the Buddha.

“Monks! During these twenty intermediate kalpas while the world is being formed and remains established, in the first intermediate kalpa when minor calamities arise, there will be great epidemics and various diseases, all of which will break out throughout Jambudvīpa.”
In all lands, the people will encounter epidemics, and all spirits and deities will give rise to wrathful and malevolent minds to harm the world’s inhabitants.

At that time, the lifespan of all people will be short, lasting only ten years; their physical stature will be stunted and small, measuring either two or three *vitasti* (the span of the hand), which by their own standard is eight *vitasti*.
As for their sustenance, they consider weeds and barnyard grass to be the best; they take human hair for clothing as their primary attire; and they possess only knives and weapons for self-adornment.

At that time, people do not practice the True Dharma; they are constantly defiled by attachment to what is not the Dharma and driven by irrational craving. Deceived by false teachings, they give rise to all manner of faults and evils; being perverse and difficult to instruct, they are unable to perform good deeds. They do not know how to cultivate merit nor rescue those in suffering and distress. Day and night they associate with evil and unwholesome dharmas, and through body, speech, and mind, they engage in the three types of wrong conduct. They cannot distance themselves from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, harsh speech, divisive speech, frivolous speech, greed, anger, and wrong views. They do not know to revere their parents, teachers, the Sangha, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or their friends and elders, but instead indulge their own minds in performing various kinds of evil karma.

These karmas can bring about a short lifespan, can bring about much illness, can bring about an ugly physical form, can bring about a lack of personal majesty, can bring about birth into a lowly family, can bring about poverty and hardship, and can bring about folly and false views; such karmas as these grow and increase day and night.

Such a person is associated with various afflictions and evil karma; because of these extremely heavy and perverse karmic actions, violent winds arise and blow, causing the spatial directions and the seasons to deviate from their regular order.
Because this wind blows unevenly, the rain falls without being distributed evenly.
When it is precisely the time for rain, the ministers of the Four Great Kings become angry with those who act wickedly and do not play in the water; therefore, no rain falls.
The Asura King Rāhu, wishing to afflict the people of Jambudvīpa, would either with his fingers or with his back, catch the falling rain and place it within the ocean.

Furthermore, there are spirits who wish to afflict the people of Jambudvīpa; using their supernatural powers, they ignite fires to consume the heavenly rain so that it dries up, or when it rains heavily, they raise great winds to blow and cast it back into the ocean.
For these reasons, the rains from heaven are not equal; all seeds, trees, vines, and medicinal herbs wither and burn away, no longer bearing fruit.
Even if they should bear fruit, it lacks color, fragrance, and flavor; it fails to grow large and possesses no strength.
If a person consumes [such food], they will lack five kinds of faculties: namely, physical form, strength, well-being, longevity, and eloquence.

Due to its evil nature, various grave illnesses arise within their own body—whether leprosy or consumption, insanity or carbuncles, parasitic worms or toxic blood, hemoptysis or diarrhea, dropsy or hiccups and asthma, wind-paralysis or emaciation from chronic fever, malignant sores or scrofula, or indigestion; such severe ailments and other minor illnesses will all arise simultaneously at that time.

At that time, people were afflicted by the suffering of grave illnesses and tormented by malevolent spirits; desiring auspicious protection for their lives, they performed sacrifices to celestial deities and recited incantations. Alternatively, relying on various evil practices born of false views, they killed living beings and falsely invoked spirits and ghosts in search of freedom from disease, making this calculation:
"No benefit or gain is equal to being free from illness."
In a single day and night, immeasurable sentient beings die from epidemics and disease.
It is thus with sentient beings in the final age; their transgressions arise spontaneously. Why is this so?

If people practice unwholesome dharmas and unbalanced dharmas, as a result of this retribution, because right conduct and balanced wholesome conduct cannot be found during that time, all sentient beings are born therein, and the turbidity of the kalpa (kalpa-kaṣāya) arises spontaneously.

At that time, people rely on coarse views and coarse actions, committing various evils; after they pass away, they are reborn in evil realms, falling into the path of suffering where there is no peaceful conduct.
At that time, sentient beings will mostly fall into the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and asuras;

at that time, the lineages of great kings will all perish, and all their territories will gradually become desolate and abandoned, with only small districts and counties remaining, situated far apart from one another in various locations.

At that time, people did not practice the True Dharma; they were constantly defiled by attachment to what is unrighteous and driven by irrational craving. Deceived by false teachings, they gave rise to all manner of faults and evils. Stubborn and perverse, they were difficult to instruct and unable to perform good deeds. Ignorant of how to cultivate merit, they offered no rescue to those in suffering and hardship. Day and night they associated with evil and wicked dharmas, and through body, speech, and mind, they engaged in the three types of wrong conduct. They could not distance themselves from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, harsh speech, divisive speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, malice, and wrong views. They did not know to show reverence to their parents, teachers, the Sangha, śramaṇas, brahmins, or their own elders and superiors, instead indulging their minds to give rise to all kinds of evil karma.

This karma can induce a short lifespan, can induce much illness, can induce an ugly physical form, can induce a lack of personal majesty, can induce birth into a lowly family, can induce poverty and hardship, and can induce folly and false views; such karmas grow and increase day and night.
Such people suffer from illness and hardship, yet no one provides them with medicine, broth, or food.
Due to these causes and conditions, their lifespans end prematurely in countless instances; in a single day and night, immeasurable sentient beings die of epidemics and disease.
Sentient beings in the final eon are thus; their faults arise spontaneously. Why is this so?
Because they practice unwholesome dharmas and unequal dharmas, they obtain such karmic retribution.
At that time, because the practice of Dharma and the practice of equanimity cannot be found, all sentient beings are born therein, and the defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) arises spontaneously.
At that time, these people, relying on coarse views and coarse karma, committed various evils; after their lives ended, they were reborn among asuras, hungry ghosts, animals, or in the hells.
At that time, the smaller districts and counties were in turn becoming desolate, with only a few families remaining, scattered far apart from one another.

During that period, people did not practice the True Dharma; the various kinds of evil karma they produced—which could bring about a short lifespan, as well as ignorance and false views—increased day and night.
At that time, among those people who died from pestilence, there was no one to bury them, cremate them, or cast them away; the land was covered with white bones.
In a single day and night, countless sentient beings died from disease and pestilence, until even the households were emptied one after another.

"At that time, when only seven days remain until the end of the kalpa, within those seven days, immeasurable sentient beings will perish from pestilence; those who happen to survive will each disperse to different places."
At that time, there was one person who gathered together all the men and women within Jambudvīpa until only ten thousand remained, whom he set aside as the seed for future generations.

During that period, everyone practiced unrighteousness, yet these ten thousand people were able to maintain virtuous conduct. Because various benevolent devas and spirits wished to prevent the human lineage from being severed, they protected these people and caused excellent flavors to enter their pores. By the power of this karma, the seeds of humanity remained naturally uninterrupted throughout the intermediate kalpa.
After seven days had passed, this great epidemic was suddenly extinguished, and all malevolent spirits departed entirely.

Whatever various needs and desires sentient beings had—be they food, drink, clothing, or other necessities—they were provided exactly as required upon their mere thought. Heaven sent down rain, the Yin and Yang were harmonized, and exquisite flavors emerged. Their physical forms became lovely, and their marks and signs were restored. All wholesome dharmas arose spontaneously; it became cool, serene, peaceful, and free from illness. Great compassion entered their hearts; because of great compassion, great kindness entered their hearts; because of great kindness, they were free from thoughts of harm. Being free from harmful intent, they were able to see one another, giving rise to hearts of joy, hearts of forbearance, and hearts of insatiability [for one another], supporting each other and never parting.

For example, when dear friends who have long been separated suddenly meet, they give rise to a heart of joy, a heart of forbearance, and a heart of no weariness; they support one another and do not part.
The meeting of people at such times is also like this: because of mutual affection and remembrance, men and women dwell together.

In the preceding kalpa, the human lifespan was ten years; from that time, the people of the subsequent kalpa were born, possessing the longest lifespans, extraordinary physical forms, supreme majesty and virtue, sovereign spiritual powers, and complete provisions for life, with a lifespan of twenty thousand years.
At that time, for sentient beings who are thus, merit is spontaneously accomplished.
Why is this so? Practice according to the Dharma, impartial practice, and virtuous practice are their karmic retribution.

At that time, these people were endowed with various wholesome dharmas: they practiced good conduct of body, speech, and mind; after their lives ended, they were reborn in the good realms and the heavens. After their lives there ended, they returned to be born among humans. Once born as humans, they were naturally virtuous and excellent, pure by nature and possessing moral integrity. Their mental disposition was gentle and refined, and they were fully endowed with the categories of precepts. They constantly performed superior goodness, remaining far removed from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter. They were free from covetousness and ill will, abandoned false views to practice right view, and showed reverence toward their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, friends, and elders, remaining in accord with various wholesome dharmas.

This karma can induce long life, can induce freedom from illness, can induce a handsome and upright physical form, can induce personal majesty and virtue, can induce birth into a wealthy and noble family, and can induce great wisdom; thus, such wholesome karma grows and increases day and night.

At that time, these people, by practicing according to merit and virtue, give rise to immeasurable qualities; after they relinquish their life-span, they are reborn in the heavenly realms and other auspicious paths, remaining in those auspicious paths for a very long period of time.

Thus, at the end of the first kalpa, it was brought to its ultimate conclusion by a great epidemic; thereafter, the second kalpa followed in succession, and twenty thousand years constituted the first lifespan during the intermediate period of that kalpa.

This person was born from one who lived twenty thousand years ago; this person’s lifespan is the longest, their physical form is extraordinary, their majestic virtue is supreme, their spiritual powers are sovereign, and their means of subsistence are complete; their lifespan is forty thousand years.
At that time, for all sentient beings, such merit will be spontaneously accomplished.
Why is this so? The practice of the Dharma, the practice of equanimity, and virtuous conduct are its retributive fruits.

At that time, these people were endowed with various wholesome dharmas: they practiced good conduct of body, speech, and mind; after relinquishing their life-span, they were reborn in the happy realms and the heavens; after relinquishing their life-span there, they returned to birth among humans. Having been born among humans, they were naturally virtuous and good, pure by nature and possessed of moral virtue. Their mental disposition was gentle and refined, they were complete in the categories of precepts, and they constantly performed supreme goodness. They stayed far away from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech; they were free from covetousness and free from ill will. They abandoned views of wrong and practiced right view; they honored their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, friends, and elders, remaining in accord with various wholesome dharmas.

This karma can induce long life, can induce freedom from illness, can induce a handsome and upright physical form, can induce personal majesty and virtue, can induce birth into a wealthy and noble family, and can induce great wisdom; thus, such wholesome karma grows and increases day and night.

At that time, these people, by relying on meritorious conduct, give rise to immeasurable virtue; after they relinquish their life-span, they are reborn in the heavenly realms and other auspicious paths, remaining in those auspicious paths for a very long period of time.
Thus is described the second intermediate kalpa; during this second intermediate period, the lifespan is forty thousand years.

These people are born from those with a lifespan of forty thousand years; their lifespan is the longest, their physical form is extraordinary, their majestic virtue is most supreme, their spiritual powers are sovereign, and their means of subsistence are fully provided, reaching a lifespan of sixty thousand years.

At that time, these people were endowed with various wholesome dharmas: they practiced good conduct of body, speech, and mind; after relinquishing their life-span, they were reborn in the good realms and the heavenly realms; after relinquishing their celestial lifespan, they returned to birth among humans. Having been born among humans, they were naturally virtuous and good, pure by nature and possessing morality by nature. Their mental disposition was gentle and refined, and they were fully endowed with the categories of precepts. They constantly performed supreme goodness, staying far removed from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech. They were free from covetousness and free from ill will. They abandoned the dharma of wrong views and practiced right view. They honored their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, friends, and elders, remaining in accord with various wholesome dharmas.

This karma can induce long life, can induce freedom from illness, can induce a handsome and upright physical form, can induce personal majesty and virtue, can induce birth into a wealthy and noble family, and can induce great wisdom; thus, such wholesome karma grows and increases day and night.

At that time, those people, by relying on meritorious conduct, generate immeasurable merit; after they relinquish their life-span, they are reborn in the heavenly realms and other auspicious paths, remaining in those auspicious paths for a very long duration.
This is called the third intermediate kalpa; during this third intermediate period, the lifespan is sixty thousand years.

Next, from among those people with a lifespan of sixty thousand years, there are born others whose lifespan is the longest, whose physical form is extraordinary, whose majesty and virtue are most excellent, whose spiritual powers are sovereign, and whose means of subsistence are fully provided; their lifespan is eighty thousand years.

Thus, during the intermediate kalpa of Jambudvīpa, the lifespan of the beings born therein is long and far-reaching, reaching a maximum of eighty thousand years; at that time, women do not marry until they are five hundred years old.
At that time, people had only seven ailments: namely, the need for excrement and urine, cold, heat, lustful desire, hunger, and old age.

During such a period, all lands were wealthy, noble, abundant, and joyful; there were no enemies, bandits, or thieves. Villages and hamlets of towns, districts, and counties were situated so close together that the crowing of roosters could be heard from one to another; though cultivation was sparse, the harvests were vast.

At that time, those people exert little effort in their current karma, yet they enjoy the abundant fruits of the virtuous deeds of their past lives; their dwellings, vehicles, clothing, wealth, and treasures, as well as all the necessities for life, are fully provided according to their wishes, and though they enjoy them throughout their lives, these things never perish.

At that time, all people sat peacefully and enjoyed happiness, having no need for restless seeking; their lifespan was eighty thousand years, and they remained for incalculable eons until sentient beings had not yet committed the ten unwholesome deeds.

From the moment the ten paths of unwholesome karma arise, the lifespan decreases by ten years because of them; every hundred years it diminishes by ten years, gradually decreasing in this sequence until only ten years remain, after which it stays at ten years and no longer declines.
The maximum lifespan is eighty thousand years, and the minimum reaches ten years;
if no Buddha appears in the world, the sequence is as such.

If a Buddha does appear in the world, the lifespan of sentient beings remains stable and does not diminish for as long as the True Dharma (Saddharma) abides; however, as the True Dharma gradually declines, the lifespan gradually decreases accordingly.
Thus spoke the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Thus have I heard. Chapter Two:
Weapons, on the Minor Calamities. Chapter Two: Weapons. Thus spoke the Buddha, the World-Honored One:
"One small kalpa is called one kalpa; the rest is as previously explained, up to eighty small kalpas being termed a great kalpa.
Why are eighty small kalpas called one great kalpa?"

The Buddha taught that within an eon, the world undergoes dissolution; having dissolved, it remains in a state of dissolution; within an eon, the world undergoes formation; and having been formed, it remains in a state of formation.
“World-Honored One!
What is the number of kalpas for the eons of dissolution and destruction?
The Buddha said:

“Monks! After twenty intermediate kalpas, the world undergoes dissolution; next, after twenty intermediate kalpas, the world remains dissolved; next, after twenty intermediate kalpas, the world undergoes formation; and next, after twenty intermediate kalpas, the world remains formed.”

During these twenty intermediate kalpas, the world arises, is formed, and remains stable; when the second intermediate kalpa of calamities occurs, that kalpa reaches its conclusion through the great weapons of war.

At that time, among all the lands and peoples within Jambudvīpa, they shall encounter great weapons and soldiers who mutually hate and harm one another; furthermore, pestilence shall arise, and all spirits and deities shall give rise to wrathful and evil hearts to injure the people of the world. At that time, the lifespan of all people shall be short, remaining for only ten years; their physical forms shall be stunted and small, measuring only two or three spans (vitasti); coarse weeds and panic seeds shall be considered the finest food, human hair shall be regarded as the most excellent clothing, and they shall have nothing but swords and staves for self-adornment.

At that time, people did not practice the True Dharma; they were constantly defiled by attachment to what is unrighteous and driven by irrational craving. Deceived by false teachings, they gave rise to all manner of faults and evils; being perverse and teaching one another such ways, they were unable to perform good deeds. They did not know how to cultivate merit nor did they seek to rescue others from suffering and hardship. Day and night they associated with evil and wicked dharmas, and through body, speech, and mind, they engaged in the three types of wrong conduct. They could not distance themselves from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, greed, malice, and wrong views. They did not know to revere their parents, teachers, monks, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or their friends and elders, instead giving rein to their own minds to give rise to all kinds of evil karma.

This karma can bring about a short lifespan, can bring about illness, can bring about an ugly physical form, can bring about a lack of personal majesty, can bring about birth into a lowly family, can bring about poverty and suffering, and can bring about folly and wrong views; such karmas grow and increase day and night.

Such persons are associated with various afflictions and evil karmas; because they engage in such extremely grave and perverse actions, parents and children contend with one another, and brothers, sisters, friends, and relatives contend among themselves—how much more so with others?

At that time, after the people had engaged in quarrels and disputes, they proceeded to dance against one another; some used tiles and stones, while others used clubs to inflict injury. Subsequently, they used swords and staves to terrify one another, even to the point of killing.
At that time, people gave rise to intense hatred and practiced various acts of killing as a source of amusement.
The kings of the eastern lands came to invade the western lands, and the kings of the western lands went to invade the eastern lands; the same was true for the kings of the south and north.
These kings took mutual abuse as their law, speaking of others' faults and transgressions as their standard practice, and seeking out vulnerabilities as their primary business.

Having engaged in strife, they conceived thoughts of enmity toward one another; wielding swords and staves, they slaughtered and exterminated each other, such that the number of those killed and harmed in a single day and night was immeasurable.
At the end of the kalpa, such faults naturally arise among sentient beings.
Why is this so? If a person practices unwholesome dharmas and unequal dharmas, they will obtain such karmic retribution.

At that time, because the practice of Dharma, the practice of equanimity, and virtuous conduct cannot be found, all sentient beings are born therein, and the turbidity of the eon arises spontaneously.

At that time, people rely upon coarse views and coarse actions, committing various evils; after their lives end, they are reborn in evil realms, falling away from the path of suffering and lacking any practice of peace and happiness.
At that time, many sentient beings will be reborn in the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and asuras;

at that time, the lineages of great kings will all perish, and all their territories will gradually fall into desolation and ruin, until only small districts and counties remain—scarcely worth mentioning—and these will be situated far apart from one another in different locations.

At that time, people did not practice the True Dharma; they were constantly defiled by attachment to what is unrighteous and driven by irrational craving. Deceived by false teachings, they gave rise to various evil karmas; being perverse and difficult to instruct, they were unable to perform good deeds. Ignorant of how to cultivate merit, they offered no rescue to those in suffering and hardship. Day and night they associated with evil and wicked dharmas, and through body, speech, and mind, they engaged in the three types of wrong conduct. They could not refrain from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, harsh speech, double-tongued speech, frivolous talk, covetousness, malice, and wrong views. They failed to show reverence to their parents, teachers, monks, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, as well as friends, elders, and superiors, giving rein to their own hearts to produce all manner of evil karma.

This karma can bring about a short lifespan, can bring about much illness, can bring about an ugly physical form, can bring about a lack of personal majesty and virtue, can bring about birth into a lowly family, can bring about poverty and suffering, and can bring about folly and wrong views; such karmas grow and increase day and night.
The people of the eastern regions came to attack those of the west, and likewise did those of the south and north.

At that time, it was the custom for people to revile one another; they took speaking of others' faults as their standard practice, and they regarded seeking out vulnerabilities as their primary concern.

Having engaged in strife, they conceived thoughts of enmity toward one another; grasping swords and staves, they slaughtered each other, such that the number of those killed and perished in a single day and night was immeasurable.
Sentient beings in the final age are thus; their faults arise spontaneously. Why is this so?
If a person does not practice wholesome conduct, the conduct of the Dharma, or impartial conduct, they will obtain such karmic retribution.

At that time, because the practice of Dharma, the practice of equanimity, and virtuous conduct cannot be found, all sentient beings are born therein, and the turbidity of the eon arises spontaneously.

At that time, people, relying on the aforementioned coarse karma, committed various evils; after their lives ended, they were reborn in evil realms, falling away from the path of suffering and lacking any practice of peace and happiness.

At that time, many sentient beings were reborn in the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and asuras; the various commanderies and counties subsequently became empty and desolate, with only a few families remaining, living far apart from one another in separate locations.

At that time, the eastern household would come to kill the western household, and the western household would in turn kill the eastern household; the same occurred among the households of the south and north.
At that time, people took mutual abuse as their practice, speaking of others' faults and transgressions as their standard, and seeking out vulnerabilities as their primary concern.

Having engaged in strife, they conceived thoughts of enmity toward one another; wielding swords and staves, they slaughtered each other, so that in a single day and night, the number of those killed was immeasurable.
Sentient beings in the final age are like this; faults arise spontaneously. Why is this so?
If a person does not practice wholesome conduct, nor practice the conduct of the True Dharma or impartial conduct, they will obtain the fruit of such evil karma.

At that time, because the practice of the True Dharma, the practice of equanimity, and virtuous conduct cannot be found, all sentient beings are born therein, and the turbidity of the kalpa arises spontaneously.

At that time, people rely upon coarse views and coarse actions, committing various evils; after their lives end, they are reborn in evil realms, falling away from the path of suffering without any practice of peace and happiness. At that time, many sentient beings are born in the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and asuras.
At that time, human households will perish all at once, and even those who remain will scatter in every direction.
These scattered people will not practice the True Dharma and will give rise to various evil karmas, which can cause their lifespans to be short and lead them to ignorance and false views.

"At that time, seven days remain until the end of the kalpa; during those seven days, when people grasp grasses and trees, these immediately turn into swords and staves. By means of these weapons, they harm one another, living in terror and perishing from exhaustion."

At that time, people, terrified of swords and staves, fled into forests and thickets; some crossed rivers to hide on solitary islands, while others entered pits and caves to avoid the calamities. Sometimes they encountered one another and yet each fled in alarm, their minds overwhelmed by terror; sometimes they fell prostrate to the ground like deer or hares meeting a hunter. Thus did these people treat one another with such dread.
During these seven days, those who died by the sword or through violent calamities were immeasurable in number; those who remained were each scattered to different places.
At that time, one person gathered together the men and women of Jambudvīpa until only ten thousand remained, whom he set aside as the seed for future generations.

At that time, all people practiced what was not the Dharma; yet these ten thousand people alone were able to cultivate wholesome conduct. Because various benevolent spirits wished to prevent the human race from becoming extinct, they protected these people by causing excellent flavors to enter their pores. By the power of this karma, the seeds of humanity were preserved throughout the intermediate kalpa so that they would naturally remain unbroken.

After seven days have passed, this great calamity of weapons will suddenly subside, and all malevolent spirits will depart entirely. According to the various needs and desires of sentient beings—such as clothing, food, and drink—whatever is required will appear instantly upon thought, and the heavens will send down rain. Yin and yang will be harmonized, exquisite flavors will emerge, physical forms will become lovely and their auspicious marks will be restored, and all wholesome dharmas will arise spontaneously.

With a mind that is cool, serene, peaceful, blissful, and free from illness, great compassion enters their hearts; because of great compassion, great loving-kindness enters their hearts; because of great loving-kindness, they are free from thoughts of malice or harm. Being free from harmful intent, they are able to see one another, giving rise to a heart of joy, a heart of endurance, and a heart of tireless devotion, supporting one another and never parting.

It is like dear friends who love one another but have not seen each other for a long time; when they suddenly meet, they give rise to a heart of joy, a heart of forbearance, and a heart of no weariness, supporting one another and never parting.
When people see one another, it is also like this: because of mutual affection and remembrance, men and women dwell together.

In the preceding kalpa, the human lifespan was ten years; from that point, the people of the subsequent kalpa were born, possessing the longest lifespan, most extraordinary physical forms, supreme majesty and virtue, sovereign spiritual powers, and complete material resources, with a lifespan of twenty thousand years.
At that time, for sentient beings who are thus, merit is spontaneously accomplished.
Why is this so? The practice of the Dharma, impartial practice, and wholesome practice are their karmic fruition.

At that time, these people were endowed with various wholesome dharmas: they practiced good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind. After passing away from their lives, they were reborn in the happy realms and the heavens; having passed away from there, they returned to be born among human beings. Once born among humans, they were naturally virtuous and excellent, pure by nature and possessing the qualities of the Way and its virtue. Their mental disposition was gentle and refined, they were fully endowed with the categories of precepts, and they constantly practiced superior goodness. They remained far removed from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech. They were free from covetousness and free from ill will. Abandoning the dharma of wrong views, they cultivated right view; they honored their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, friends, and elders, remaining in accord with various wholesome dharmas.

This karma can induce long life, can induce freedom from illness, can induce a handsome and upright physical form, can induce personal majesty and virtue, can induce birth into a wealthy and noble family, and can induce great wisdom; thus, such wholesome karma grows and increases day and night.

At that time, those people, by relying on meritorious conduct, generated immeasurable merit; after relinquishing their life-span, they were reborn in the heavenly realms and other auspicious paths, remaining in those auspicious paths for a very long period of time.

Thus, at the end of the first kalpa, the world is utterly destroyed by great weapons; subsequently, the third kalpa begins, and during this intermediate period, the lifespan of beings reaches twenty thousand years. This is the first measure of lifespan within that intermediate kalpa.

This person was born from one who lived twenty thousand years ago; this person’s lifespan is the longest, their physical form is extraordinary, their majestic virtue is supreme, their spiritual powers are sovereign, and their means of subsistence are complete; their lifespan is forty thousand years.
At that time, for all sentient beings, such merit is naturally accomplished.
Why is this so? The practice of the Dharma, the practice of equanimity, and virtuous conduct are its retributive fruits.

At that time, those people were endowed with various wholesome dharmas: they practiced good conduct of body, speech, and mind. After their lifespans ended, they were reborn in the happy realms and the heavens; having exhausted their celestial lifespans, they returned to birth among humans. Once born among humans, they were naturally virtuous and good, pure by nature and possessing natural morality. Their mental dispositions were gentle and refined, they were fully endowed with the categories of precepts, and they constantly practiced supreme goodness. They remained far removed from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter. They were free from covetousness and ill will, abandoned wrong views to cultivate right view, and showed reverence toward their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, friends, and elders, remaining in accord with various wholesome dharmas.

This karma can induce long life, can induce freedom from illness, can induce a handsome and upright physical form, can induce personal majesty and virtue, can induce birth into a wealthy and noble family, and can induce great wisdom; thus, such wholesome karma grows and increases day and night.

At that time, those people, by relying on the practice of merit, increase immeasurable virtue; after they relinquish their life-span, they are reborn in the heavenly realms and other auspicious paths, remaining within those auspicious paths for a very long period of time.
This is called the third intermediate kalpa; during this second intermediate period, the lifespan is forty thousand years.

Subsequently, beings are born from those with a lifespan of forty thousand years; these people possess the longest lifespan, extraordinary physical forms, supreme majesty, sovereign spiritual power, and full abundance of life's necessities, living for sixty thousand years.

At that time, these people were endowed with various wholesome dharmas: they practiced good conduct of body, speech, and mind; after relinquishing their life-span, they were reborn in the happy realms and the celestial worlds. Having passed away from the celestial worlds, they returned to birth among humans. Once born among humans, they were naturally virtuous and excellent, pure by nature and possessing the qualities of the Path. Their mental disposition was gentle and refined, and they were fully endowed with the categories of precepts. They constantly practiced supreme goodness, remaining far removed from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter. They were free from covetousness and free from ill-will, having abandoned views of wrong dharma to practice the True Dharma. They honored their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, friends, and elders, remaining in accord with various wholesome dharmas.

This karma can induce long life, can induce freedom from illness, can induce a handsome and upright physical form, can induce personal majesty and virtue, can induce birth into a wealthy and noble family, and can induce great wisdom; thus, such wholesome karma grows and increases day and night.

At that time, those people, by relying on meritorious conduct, generated immeasurable merit; after relinquishing their life-span, they were reborn in the heavenly realms and other auspicious paths, remaining in those auspicious paths for a very long period of time.
Thus, this is called the third intermediate kalpa; during the second intermediate period, the lifespan is sixty thousand years.

Next, those people are born from those with a lifespan of sixty thousand years; these people have the longest lifespan, their physical form is extraordinary, their majesty and virtue are supreme, their spiritual powers are sovereign, and their means of subsistence are complete, living for eighty thousand years.

Thus, during the intermediate kalpas of Jambudvīpa, the lifespan of the beings born therein is long and far-reaching, reaching a maximum of eighty thousand years; at that time, women do not marry until they are five hundred years old.
At that time, people suffered from only seven ailments: namely, the need for excretion and urination, cold, heat, lustful desire, hunger, and old age.

During such a period, all lands were wealthy, noble, and prosperous; there were no enemies, bandits, or thieves. Villages and settlements in the prefectures, commanderies, and counties were so close together that the crowing of roosters could be heard from one to another; though cultivation was sparse, the harvests were immense.

At that time, these people receive little fruit from their present efforts, yet they enjoy much fruit from the wholesome karma of their past lives; their dwellings, vehicles, clothing, wealth, and treasures—the necessities for life—are fully provided according to their wishes, and though they enjoy them throughout their entire lives, they never perish.

At that time, all people sat peacefully and enjoyed happiness, having no need for restless pursuit; their lifespan was eighty thousand years, and they remained for incalculable aeons until sentient beings had not yet committed the ten unwholesome actions.

From the time the ten paths of unwholesome action arise, the lifespan decreases because of these ten evils. Every hundred years it is reduced by ten years; subsequently, every further hundred years it is again reduced by ten years. It gradually diminishes in this sequence until only ten years remain, after which it stays at ten years and no longer decreases.
The maximum lifespan is eighty thousand years, and the minimum is ten years;
if no Buddha appears in the world, the sequence of lifespans follows this pattern.

If a Buddha does appear in the world, as long as the True Dharma remains, the lifespan of sentient beings will temporarily stabilize and not diminish; however, as the True Dharma gradually declines, the lifespan will also gradually decrease accordingly.
Thus spoke the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Thus have I heard. Chapter 3:
The Minor Calamities of Famine; Section on the Calamity of Famine. The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"One small kalpa is called one kalpa; the rest is as previously explained, up to eighty small kalpas being called one great kalpa.
Why are eighty small kalpas called one great kalpa? [Because]..."

The Buddha taught that within a kalpa the world-system disintegrates; having disintegrated, it remains so for a kalpa; within a kalpa the world-system arises and is formed; and having arisen and been formed, it remains so for a kalpa.
“World-Honored One!
What is the number of eons for the kalpas of dissolution and destruction?
The Buddha said:

“Bhikṣus! After twenty intermediate kalpas, the world undergoes dissolution; next, after twenty intermediate kalpas, the world remains dissolved; next, after twenty intermediate kalpas, the world arises and is formed; next, after twenty intermediate kalpas, the world remains formed.”
During these twenty intermediate kalpas, the world arises and remains. When the third intermediate kalpa of calamities begins, this kalpa reaches its conclusion through a great famine.

At that time, as the calamities are first about to arise, due to hunger, suffering, and celestial drought, all the people in every land within Jambudvīpa will encounter a great pestilence, and all the spirits and deities will give rise to malicious and hateful hearts to harm the people of the world.
At that time, the lifespan of all people will be short, lasting only ten years; their physical stature will be stunted and small, measuring only two or three spans (vitasti).

As for their sustenance, they take weeds and barnyard grass as their primary food; as for clothing, they take human hair as their finest garment; and they possess nothing but knives and staves to adorn themselves.

At that time, people did not practice the True Dharma; they were constantly defiled by attachment to what is unrighteous and driven by irrational craving. Deceived by false teachings, they gave rise to all manner of faults and evils; being perverse and difficult to instruct, they were unable to perform good deeds. Ignorant of how to cultivate merit, they offered no succor to those in suffering and hardship. Day and night they associated with evil and wicked dharmas, and through body, speech, and mind, they engaged in the three types of wrong conduct. They were unable to distance themselves from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, greed, malice, and wrong views. They did not know to show reverence toward their parents, teachers, the Sangha, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or their friends and elders, instead giving rein to their own minds to commit various kinds of evil karma.

These karmas can induce a short lifespan, induce illness, induce an ugly physical form, induce a lack of personal majesty, induce birth into a lowly family, induce poverty and hardship, and induce folly and wrong views; such karmas grow and increase day and night.

Such persons, being possessed of heavy afflictions and evil karma due to their extremely grave misconduct, cause the heavens not to send rain for two or three years; because of this great drought, grain becomes expensive, famine prevails, and people wander about like śaraka grass.
At that time, the people possessed little strength; seeing others with even a small amount of provisions, they would go and seize their food, all because they were driven by hunger.
Among all diseases, hunger is the most severe; for this reason, those who died of starvation in a single day and night were immeasurable in number.
Sentient beings in the final age are thus; their faults arise spontaneously.
Why is this so? If a person performs unwholesome deeds, unrighteous deeds, and unequal deeds, they will obtain such a retribution.
At that time, because the practice of Dharma, impartial practice, and wholesome practice cannot be found, all sentient beings are born therein, and the turbidity of the eon arises spontaneously.

At that time, people rely on coarse views and coarse actions, committing various evils; after their lives end, they are reborn in evil realms, falling away from the path of suffering into states lacking peaceful conduct. At that time, many sentient beings are born in the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and asuras.

At that time, the great kingdoms were successively abandoned and desolate; only small districts and counties remained, all of them too insignificant to mention, situated far apart from one another in different locations.

At that time, people did not practice the True Dharma; they were constantly defiled by attachment to what is unrighteous and driven by irrational craving. Deceived by false teachings, they gave rise to all manner of faults and evils; being perverse and difficult to instruct, they were unable to perform good deeds. Ignorant of how to cultivate merit, they did not rescue others from suffering and hardship. Day and night they associated with evil and wicked dharmas, or through body, speech, and mind, they engaged in the three types of wrong conduct. They were unable to distance themselves from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, greed, anger, and wrong views. They failed to show reverence toward their parents, teachers, the Sangha, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or their friends and elders, instead giving rein to their own minds to commit various kinds of evil karma.

This karma can induce a short lifespan, can induce much illness, can induce an ugly physical form, can induce a lack of personal majesty, can induce birth into a lowly family, can induce poverty and hardship, and can induce folly and wrong views; such karmas are associated with one day and night.

The heavens did not send down rain, and due to a great drought lasting four or five years, even living grass and vegetables could not be found upon the land of Jambudvīpa; how much less could there be rice and grain to sustain sentient beings?
Those creatures that have traditionally been loathed by humans as unfit for food—namely crows, owls, vultures, eagles, dogs, and jackals—all devour them, driven by the urgency of hunger.
Among all diseases, hunger is the most severe; for this reason, those who die of hunger in a single day and night are immeasurable in number.
At that time, small districts and counties were successively emptied until only a few families remained, scattered far apart from one another in different locations.

At that time, people did not practice the True Dharma; they were constantly defiled by attachment to what is contrary to the Dharma and driven by irrational craving. Deceived by false teachings, they gave rise to all manner of faults and evils; being perverse and difficult to instruct, they were unable to perform good deeds. Unaware of how to cultivate merit, they offered no succor in times of suffering and hardship. Day and night they associated with evil and unwholesome dharmas, or they engaged in the three types of wrong conduct through body, speech, and mind. They could not distance themselves from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, harsh words, frivolous talk, lying, covetousness, malice, and wrong views. They failed to show reverence toward their parents, teachers, the Sangha, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or their friends and elders, instead giving rein to their own hearts to commit various kinds of evil karma.

This karma can induce a short lifespan, can induce much illness, can induce an ugly physical form, can induce a lack of personal majesty, can induce birth into a lowly family, can induce poverty and hardship, and can induce folly and wrong views; such karmas are associated with [the mind] day and night.
At that time, for six or seven years, no rain fell from the heavens; due to this great drought, the people of Jambudvīpa could not even find water to look upon, let alone drink.

Only the waters of the four great rivers are so deep and vast that they connect with the ocean; even these must be crossed by boat, yet it is only within these rivers that water is available for use, and outside of these rivers there is no other water at all.

Even if there are surviving people who depend on this water to dwell, they will catch aquatic creatures such as soft-shelled turtles, crocodiles, fish, and tortoises for their own sustenance, driven by the pressure of hunger.
Among all diseases, hunger is the foremost; for this reason, those who die of hunger in a single day and night are beyond measure.
Such is the state of sentient beings in the final age, as their transgressions arise spontaneously.
Why is this so? If people engage in unwholesome conduct, unrighteous conduct, and uneven conduct, they will obtain this retribution.

At that time, because righteous conduct, impartial conduct, and wholesome conduct cannot be found, all sentient beings are born therein, and the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) arises spontaneously.

At that time, people rely on coarse views and coarse actions, committing various evils; after their lives end, they are reborn in evil realms, falling away from the path of suffering into a state devoid of peaceful conduct. At that time, many sentient beings are born in the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and asuras.
The remaining households were successively emptied, and even those who remained dispersed in all directions like stars.

At that time, people did not practice the True Dharma; they were defiled by attachment to what is unlawful and driven by irrational craving. They spread false teachings and gave rise to all manner of faults and evils. Stubborn and perverse, they were difficult to instruct and unable to perform good deeds. Ignorant of how to cultivate merit, they offered no rescue for those in suffering and hardship. Day and night they associated with evil and wicked dharmas, or they engaged in the three types of wrong conduct through body, speech, and mind. They could not distance themselves from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, greed, anger, and wrong views. They failed to show reverence to their parents, teachers, the Sangha, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, friends, or elders, instead indulging their own minds in the commission of various evil karmas.

This karma can bring about a short lifespan, it can bring about much illness, it can bring about an ugly physical appearance, it can bring about a lack of personal majesty, it can bring about birth into a lowly family, it can bring about poverty and hardship, and it can bring about folly and wrong views; such karmas are associated with one day and night.
"In the midst of this kalpa, only seven days remain; during these seven days, within a single day and night, those who die of hunger are immeasurable in number.
Even those who survive are each scattered to separate places."
At that time, there was one person who gathered ten thousand men and women from within Jambudvīpa and set them aside to serve as the seed for future generations.

During this period, unrighteous conduct prevailed widely; yet these ten thousand people alone were able to practice wholesome deeds. Because various benevolent spirits and deities wished to prevent the human lineage from being cut off, they protected these people and caused excellent flavors to enter their pores.
By the power of karma, during the intermediate kalpa, the seeds of humanity are preserved so that they naturally do not perish.
After seven days have passed, this great famine suddenly ceases, and all malevolent spirits completely depart.

At that time, whatever various needs and desires the sentient beings had—such as clothing, food, and drink—whatever they required would appear according to their thoughts. Heaven would then rain down [provisions], the yin and yang were harmonized, delicious flavors emerged, and their physical forms became lovely, with their marks and signs restored.

All wholesome dharmas arise spontaneously; they are cool, serene, peaceful, blissful, and free from affliction. Great compassion enters the mind, and because of great compassion, great kindness enters the mind. Because of great kindness, there is no intention to harm. From this lack of harmful intent, they attain the sight of one another, giving rise to a heart of joy, a heart of forbearance, and a heart of tirelessness, supporting one another and never parting.

It is like two dear friends who have long been separated and suddenly meet again; they give rise to a heart of joy, a heart of forbearance, and a heart of never-tiring affection, supporting one another and not wishing to be parted.
The meeting of people at such times is also like this: through mutual love and remembrance, men and women dwell together.

In the preceding kalpa, the lifespan of humans was ten years; from that point, the people of the subsequent kalpa were born, possessing the longest lifespans, extraordinary physical forms, supreme majesty, sovereign spiritual powers, and complete provisions for life, with a lifespan of twenty thousand years.
At that time, for sentient beings who are thus, merit is spontaneously accomplished.
Why is this so? Practice in accordance with the Dharma, impartial practice, and wholesome conduct are their karmic fruition.

At that time, these people were endowed with various wholesome dharmas: they practiced wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind; after relinquishing their life-span, they were reborn in the good realms and the heavens; having relinquished their life-span there, they returned to be born among humans. Once born among humans, they were naturally virtuous and good, pure by nature and possessing the qualities of the Path and its Virtue (*mārga-guṇa*). Their mental disposition was gentle and refined, they were fully perfected in the categories of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*), and they constantly practiced supreme goodness. They remained far removed from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter. They were free from covetousness and free from ill will. They abandoned views of wrong doctrine and cultivated right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*). They honored their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, friends, and elders, remaining in accord with various wholesome dharmas.

This karma can induce long life, can induce freedom from illness, can induce a handsome and upright physical form, can induce personal majesty and virtue, can induce birth into a wealthy and noble family, and can induce great wisdom; thus, such wholesome karma grows and increases day and night.

At that time, those people, by relying on meritorious conduct, generate immeasurable merit; after they relinquish their life-span, they are reborn in the heavenly realms and other auspicious paths, remaining therein for a very long period of time.

Thus, at the beginning of the kalpa, the intermediate period is brought to its ultimate end by a great famine; thereafter, the subsequent kalpa continues, and twenty thousand years is the first lifespan during that intermediate kalpa.

This person was born from one who lived for twenty thousand years; this person’s lifespan is the longest, their physical form is extraordinary, their majesty and virtue are supreme, their spiritual powers are sovereign, and their necessities of life are fully provided, with a lifespan of forty thousand years.
At that time, for all sentient beings, merit will be spontaneously accomplished.
Why is this so? The practice of the Dharma, the practice of equanimity, and virtuous conduct are their karmic fruition.

At that time, these people were endowed with various wholesome dharmas: they practiced good conduct of body, speech, and mind; after relinquishing their life-span, they were reborn in the happy realms and the heavens; having relinquished their celestial life-span, they returned to birth among humans. Once born among humans, they were naturally virtuous and good, pure by nature and possessing morality by nature; their mental disposition was gentle and refined, they were fully endowed with the categories of precepts, and they constantly performed supreme goodness. They remained far removed from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech; they were free from covetousness and ill-will, and having abandoned wrong views, they cultivated right view. They honored their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, friends, and elders, remaining in accord with various wholesome dharmas.

This karma can induce freedom from illness, can induce a handsome and upright physical form, can induce personal majesty and virtue, can induce birth into a wealthy and noble family, and can induce great wisdom; thus, such wholesome karma grows and increases day and night.

At that time, those people, by relying on meritorious conduct, increase immeasurable merit; after they relinquish their life-span, they are reborn in the heavenly realms and other auspicious paths, remaining in those auspicious paths for a very long period of time.
This is called the third intermediate kalpa; in this second intermediate period, the lifespan is forty thousand years.

Subsequently, from those born with a lifespan of forty thousand years, there arise beings whose lifespan is at its maximum, whose physical forms are extraordinary, whose majesty and virtue are supreme, whose spiritual powers are sovereign, and whose necessities of life are fully provided; their lifespan is sixty thousand years.

At that time, these people were endowed with various wholesome dharmas: they practiced good conduct of body, speech, and mind; after relinquishing their life-span, they were reborn in the happy realms and the heavens; having relinquished the heavenly realm, they returned to birth among humans; once born among humans, they were naturally virtuous and good, pure by nature and possessing morality by nature; their mental disposition was gentle and refined, they were fully endowed with the categories of precepts, and they constantly performed supreme goodness. They remained far removed from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech; they were free from covetousness and free from ill will; they abandoned views of wrong dharma and practiced the true Dharma; they honored their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, friends, and elders; and they were endowed with various wholesome dharmas.

This karma can induce longevity, can induce freedom from illness, can induce a handsome and upright physical form, can induce personal majesty and virtue, can induce birth into a wealthy and noble family, and can induce great wisdom; thus, such wholesome karma grows and increases day and night.

At that time, these people, by relying on meritorious conduct, generate immeasurable merit; after they relinquish their life-span, they are reborn in the heavenly realms and other auspicious paths, remaining therein for a very long period of time.
This is called the third intermediate kalpa; during this third intermediate period, the lifespan is sixty thousand years.

Furthermore, from those people with a lifespan of sixty thousand years, there are born others whose lifespan is even longer, whose physical form is extraordinary, whose majesty and virtue are most excellent, whose spiritual powers are sovereign, and whose means of subsistence are fully provided; their lifespan is eighty thousand years.

Thus, during the intermediate kalpas of Jambudvīpa, the lifespan of the beings born therein is long and far-reaching, reaching a maximum of eighty thousand years; at that time, women do not marry until they are five hundred years old.
At that time, people suffered from only seven ailments: namely, the need for excretion and urination, cold, heat, desire, hunger, and old age.

During such a period, all lands were wealthy, noble, and prosperous; there were no enemies, bandits, or thieves. Villages and hamlets of towns, districts, and counties were situated so close together that the crowing of roosters could be heard from one to the next; though cultivation was sparse, the harvests were immense.

At that time, those people receive little fruit from their current efforts, but much fruit from the wholesome karma of their past lives; their dwellings, vehicles, clothing, wealth, treasures, and means of subsistence are fully provided according to their wishes, and though they enjoy them throughout their lives, these things never perish.

At that time, all people lived in peace and enjoyed happiness, having no need for restless pursuit; their lifespan was eighty thousand years, and they remained for incalculable eons until sentient beings had not yet committed the ten unwholesome deeds.

From the moment the ten paths of unwholesome karma arise, the lifespan decreases because of these ten evils: every hundred years it is reduced by ten years; after another hundred years, it is again reduced by ten years, gradually diminishing in this sequence until only ten years remain, at which point it stabilizes at ten years and no longer decreases.
The maximum lifespan is eighty thousand years, and the minimum is ten years;
this is the sequence if no Buddha appears in the world.

If a Buddha does appear in the world, as long as the True Dharma remains, the lifespan of sentient beings will remain stable for a time without decreasing; however, as the True Dharma gradually declines, their lifespan will also gradually diminish.
Thus spoke the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Thus have I heard.
