Chapter Twenty-five: The Great Calamities; Section on the Calamity of Fire, Number Twenty-five.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said: "One small kalpa is called one kalpa; twenty small kalpas are also called one kalpa; forty small kalpas are also called one kalpa; sixty small kalpas are also called one kalpa; and eighty small kalpas are called one great kalpa."
How is it that one small kalpa is called a "kalpa"?

At that time, the bhikṣu Devadatta was dwelling in hell experiencing the matured fruit of retribution; the Buddha, the World-Honored One, said he would dwell there for one kalpa. Thus, one such small kalpa is termed a "kalpa."
How is it that twenty intermediate kalpas are also called one kalpa?

For example, the life span of the Brahmakāyika devas is twenty intermediate kalpas; yet the Buddha has taught that those Brahmā devas dwell for one kalpa. Thus, these twenty intermediate kalpas are also called one kalpa.
How is it that forty minor kalpas are called one kalpa?
Just as the lifespan of the Brahmakāyika devas is forty minor kalpas, and the Buddha says they dwell for one kalpa, so too these forty minor kalpas are called one kalpa.
How is it that sixty minor kalpas are called one kalpa?
Just as the lifespan of Mahābrahmā is sixty kalpas, yet the Buddha says he dwells for one kalpa, so too these sixty minor kalpas are called one kalpa.
How is it that eighty small kalpas constitute one great kalpa?

The Buddha taught that within a kalpa the world is destroyed; within a kalpa the world remains in a state of destruction; within a kalpa the world arises and is formed; and within a kalpa the world remains in a state of formation.
An *asaṃkhyeya* period of time is called a *kalpa*, during which the world is destroyed;
an *asaṃkhyeya* period of time is called a *kalpa*, during which the world remains destroyed;
an *asaṃkhyeya* period of time is called a *kalpa*, during which the world arises and is formed.
An *asaṃkhyeya* period of time is called a *kalpa*, during which a world-system arises, forms, and remains.
There are three causes for its dissolution and destruction:
first, destruction by fire; second, destruction by water; and third, destruction by wind.
Thus the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, said:
"Monks! There are three causes for the disintegration and destruction [of conditioned things]:..."
First, destruction by fire; second, destruction by water; third, destruction by wind.
Monks! There are three types of destruction at the summit:
"First, the Heaven of Supreme Pervasive Radiance; second, the Heaven of Universal Purity; third, the Heaven of Vast Fruit.
Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, said: "Bhikṣus!"
There are three types of the summit of the realm of dissolution:
first, the Heaven of Supreme Pervasive Radiance; second, the Heaven of Universal Purity; and third, the Heaven of Vast Fruit.
Why are the Heaven of Supreme Pervasive Radiance, the Heaven of Universal Purity, and the Heaven of Vast Fruit considered the three summits of the realm of dissolution?
"O Bhikṣus!
When the world is destroyed by fire, all sentient beings of the lower realms who have cultivated the second dhyāna will be reborn above in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
When the world is destroyed by water, all sentient beings of the lower realms who have cultivated the third dhyāna will be reborn above in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven."
"When the world is destroyed by the calamity of wind, all sentient beings of the lower realms cultivate the fourth dhyāna and are reborn above in the Bṛhatphala Heaven.
The Buddha said:

"Destruction by the calamity of fire occurs through the destruction of the Ābhāsvara Heaven; destruction by the calamity of water occurs through the destruction of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven; and destruction by the calamity of wind occurs through the destruction of the Bṛhatphala Heaven."
Furthermore, monks, there are two kinds of dissolution:
first, the dissolution of the world of sentient beings; second, the dissolution of the receptacle world.
"During ten intermediate kalpas, the world of sentient beings disintegrates; next, during ten intermediate kalpas, the vessel-world disintegrates.
The Buddha told them: "Bhikṣus!"

When the destruction by fire first begins, it is caused by the second dhyāna during the period of destruction by radiant light. At that time, the lifespan of all people in Jambudvīpa is eighty thousand years, and women do not marry until they reach the age of five hundred.
At that time, people suffered from only seven ailments: namely, the need for excretion and urination, cold, heat, lustful desire, hunger, and old age.

During such a period, all lands were wealthy, noble, abundant, and joyful; there were no enemies or bandits, nor even those who practiced petty theft. Villages and settlements in the prefectures, commanderies, and counties stood close together, with the crowing of roosters heard from one to the next. Although cultivation was sparse, the harvests were vast and plentiful.

At that time, these people receive little fruit from their present efforts, but they enjoy much fruit from the wholesome karma of past lives; their dwellings, vehicles, clothing, wealth, and treasures, as well as all the necessities for life, are fully provided according to their wishes.
At that time, two realms diminish and disappear:
first, the realm of ill will; second, the realm of a malicious mind.
Two realms arise and increase:
First is the realm of non-ill will; second is the realm of a mind free from malice.

At that time, people diminished and abandoned the ten unwholesome actions and practiced the ten wholesome actions. They sat peacefully in contentment without wandering in pursuit of anything, whether gathered in pavilions or resting in lodgings, in great assemblies or strolling beneath trees, they spoke thus to one another with eloquence:

"In former times, people were born into an age of turbulence (kalpa-kṣaya) due to the increase of greed for the five sensory desires. Consequently, parents and children fought with one another; brothers, sisters, friends, and kinsmen struck each other—how much more so toward strangers?"

After these people had begun to quarrel, they continued to strike one another with their hands; then they used tiles and stones, or struck with clubs; subsequently, they employed swords and staves to terrify one another, even unto killing.
"Therefore, the five sense objects give rise to various evils; for this reason, the five sense objects should be abandoned.
Thus he reviled and censured the objects of desire, explaining in various ways the faults of the five sense objects.

At that time, those people contemplated the faults and afflictions of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) and the restlessness of the lower realms; they observed the subtle and wondrous merit of the concentration without directed thought or sustained thought (*avitarka-avicāra-samādhi*) and practiced the second dhyāna. After their lives ended, they were reborn above in the Heaven of Utmost Purity and Radiance (*Śubhakṛtsna-deva*).
At that time, the devas of the desire realm transformed their bodies to resemble rhinoceroses and traveled through the world three times each day and night, proclaiming these words:
"O sons and daughters of good family!
"The meditative concentration free from applied and sustained thought is the most sublime bliss; therefore, you should practice and abide within it.

At that time, having heard these words during the first and last watches of the night, those people were filled with joy and leaped for gladness. Setting aside all other miscellaneous affairs, they gathered their minds to sit in meditation. Contemplating the faults of sensual desires and contemplating the great merit of the concentration free from applied and sustained thought, they immediately attained the second dhyāna. After their lives ended, they were reborn above in the Heaven of Utmost Pervasive Radiance.

At that time, there was a person whose constant occupation was to delight others; whether by singing or dancing, leaping and tossing about, brandishing swords or performing with weapons, beating drums or blowing flutes, chanting watches or offering praises, or adorning the bodies of others.
Such people as these composed songs and verses, transmitting them thus:

"In the past, when people were born into this world of defilement (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), because their craving for the five sensory desires increased, parents and children fought with one another; brothers, sisters, friends, and kinsmen struck each other—how much more so, then, others?"

After these people had engaged in disputes, they continued to gesture and dance at one another; some used stones or tiles, while others struck with sticks. This escalated to the use of swords and staves, leading to mutual intimidation and even killing.
"Therefore, the five sense objects give rise to all manner of evils; for this reason, the five sense objects ought to be abandoned.
Thus he reviled and censured the dust of desire, explaining in various ways the faults of the five sense objects.

At that time, those people contemplated the faults and afflictions of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) and the turbulence of the lower realms; observing the subtle merit of the meditative concentration free from applied and sustained thought (*avitarka-avicāra-samādhi*), they cultivated the second dhyāna. After their lives ended, they were reborn above in the Heaven of Supreme Pervasive Radiance (*Śubhakṛtsna-deva*).
At that time, the devas descended from the Heaven of Universal Radiance and, moving through the world while concealing their forms, proclaimed these words:
"O sons and daughters of good family!
"The meditative concentration free from applied and sustained thought is wondrously blissful and tranquil; therefore, you all should practice and abide therein.

At that time, during the early and late watches of the night, the people heard these words from the voice of the devas. Overjoyed and leaping for gladness, they gave rise to a mind of faith and delight. All the inhabitants of households, villages, towns, districts, provinces, and even great kingdoms, aroused a mind of diligence; they contemplated the faults of the sensual desires of the lower realm and contemplated the merits of the second dhyāna. By practicing the second dhyāna, after their lives ended, they were reborn above in the Heaven of Utmost Pervasive Radiance.

At that time, there was a renunciant non-Buddhist who taught and converted all those living in households, villages, towns, districts, and even great kingdoms, causing them all to leave the household life. Surrounded by countless followers, he traveled in succession throughout the land, preaching in accordance with what had been stated above:

"In the past, when people were born into this world of kalpa-turbidity, because their craving for the five sensory desires increased, parents and children fought and quarreled with one another; brothers, sisters, friends, and kinsmen struck each other—how much more so, then, toward strangers?"

At that time, after people had engaged in quarrels and disputes, they would dance against one another; some used stones or tiles, others used clubs to strike, and it progressed to the point where they used swords and staves to terrify and even kill each other.
"Therefore, the five objects of sensory desire give rise to various evils; for this reason, the five objects of sensory desire should be abandoned.
Thus he reviled and censured the objects of desire, clearly explaining the faults of the five sensory realms.

At that time, those people contemplated the faults and afflictions of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) and the turbulence of the lower realms; they observed the subtle merit of the meditative concentration free from applied and sustained thought (*avitarka-avicāra-samādhi*) and practiced the second dhyāna. After their lives ended, they were reborn above in the Heaven of Utmost Pervasive Radiance (*Abhāsvara*).
At that time, the sentient beings within the hells thought to themselves:
"In the past, we committed various kinds of unwholesome and evil deeds; for this reason, we have now come here to undergo suffering."
Because of this intention, they do not give rise to thoughts of anger or resentment toward the hell-wardens.

At that time, the sentient beings in the hells—being free from the element of malice and the mental state of affliction—naturally develop and increase their wholesome minds. Due to the ripening of virtuous karma from their past lives, they relinquish their lifespan in hell and are reborn among human beings.
Having been born as a human, he contemplated the faults and afflictions of sensual desires and observed the merits of the second dhyāna;
he cultivated the second dhyāna and, after his life ended, was reborn above in the Heaven of Supreme Pervasive Radiance (Abhāsvara).
At that time, there were sentient beings who had fallen into hell and served as hell-wardens, who thought to themselves:
"We have come to be born here because of our own evil karma; these sinners, too, have come to undergo suffering here because of their evil karma."
"How could I now bring harm to other sentient beings?
Thus, he gives rise to the realm of non-anger and the realm of a mind free from malice, whereby wholesome states of mind naturally grow, increase, and reach fulfillment.
Due to the ripening of virtuous karma from a previous life, after relinquishing his lifespan, he was reborn among human beings.

Having been born among humans, he contemplated the faults and afflictions of the five sensory objects (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) and observed the merits of the second dhyāna; by practicing the second dhyāna, after relinquishing his lifespan, he was reborn above in the Heaven of Supreme Pervasive Radiance (*Abhāsvara*).

At that time, there were aquatic beings—tortoises, crocodiles, fish, turtles, and their like—who all gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness and did not devour one another. They ate only water-moss, grass, and soil; they would take for food only those who died naturally. They would rather die of hunger than desire to harm others for their own sustenance, abiding in a realm free from anger and a realm free from the intent to oppress.
At that time, he gave rise to various wholesome minds and a mind of loving-kindness.
Due to the ripening of virtuous karma from his past lives, after relinquishing his life, he was reborn among human beings.

Having been born among humans, he contemplates the faults and afflictions of the five sensory objects as well as the turbulence of the lower realms; observing the subtle merits of the meditative concentration free from applied and sustained thought, he cultivates the second dhyāna, and after his life has ended, he is reborn above in the Heaven of Supreme Pervasive Light.

Furthermore, there are land-dwelling sentient beings—such as lions, tigers, wolves, jackals, leopards, cats, and wildcats—who all give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and do not devour one another. When hungry, they eat tender grass; when thirsty, they drink clear springs. They will only eat the flesh of those that have died naturally; they would rather starve to death than kill others for their own sustenance. Thus, they possess a realm free from malice and a realm of mind free from oppression and affliction.

At that time, they give rise to various wholesome thoughts and a heart of loving-kindness; due to the wholesome karma of their subsequent retribution from past lives, after relinquishing their life-span, they are reborn among human beings.

Having been born among humans, he contemplates the faults of the five sensory objects (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) and the turbulence of the lower realms; observing the subtle merit of the concentration without directed thought and evaluation (*avitarka-avicāra-samādhi*), he cultivates the second dhyāna. After his life-span ends, he is reborn above in the Heaven of Ultimate Pervasive Radiance (*Abhāsvara*).

"All those in the realm of hungry ghosts (preta) will conceive mutual affection and be able to generate wholesome roots, just as previously described; after they relinquish their life-span, they shall be reborn among human beings."

Having been born among humans, he contemplates the faults of the five sensory objects, observes the concentration free from applied and sustained thought, and cultivates the second dhyāna; after his life has ended, he is reborn above in the Heaven of Supreme Pervasive Radiance.
It is the same for those in the realm of asuras.

"At that time, among the people of Aparagoyānī, there were those who had cultivated the second dhyāna in that land; having attained the second dhyāna there, they were reborn above it in the Abhāsvara Heaven."
If those who come to be born in Jambudvīpa attain the second dhyāna, they will likewise ascend to be born in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
As for the people of Pūrvavideha, some may cultivate the second dhyāna there and ascend from that place to the second dhyāna heaven;
others, if they come to Jambudvīpa to cultivate the second dhyāna, will likewise ascend from here to the second dhyāna heaven.

When the people of Uttarakuru in the north relinquish their life-span, they are reborn above in the six heavens of the desire realm; or, while in the celestial realms, they cultivate the second dhyāna and are reborn in the second dhyāna heaven; or, descending from the six heavens of the desire realm to Jambudvīpa, they cultivate the second dhyāna and are likewise reborn in the Abhāsvara Heaven.

At that time, the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmakāyika Heaven, and the Brahmapurohita Heaven—some of whom had practiced the second dhyāna within these heavens and, upon the expiration of their life-span, were reborn in the Abhāsvara Heaven;
or some who had come from the celestial realms to be born in Jambudvīpa to practice the second dhyāna, and likewise ascended to be reborn in the Abhāsvara Heaven.

"Monks! At that time, all the hells will be entirely empty; the realm of animals will also be entirely empty; the realm of hungry ghosts will likewise be entirely empty; and the realm of asuras will also be entirely empty.
Aparagoyānī, Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, and Uttarakuru will all likewise be entirely empty."

The Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmā-purohita Heaven, and the Brahmakāyika Heaven were all empty and void;
at that time, all sentient beings within the entire thousandfold world-system had completely vanished, and only the Great Brahmā King remained.
Through such causes and conditions and in such a sequence, all worlds of sentient beings were entirely dispersed and exhausted.
During that time, ten small kalpas had already passed.
“Monks! At that time, the destruction of the second vessel-world begins to follow, involving the dissolution by the four great elements and the dissolution by fire.
During this period, for a very long duration of time, the heavens do not send down rain; not even a single drop falls.”

After a long period without rain, the shrubs, trees, medicinal herbs, and all seeds within Jambudvīpa will simultaneously wither and dry up; they will be consumed by fire in succession until nothing remains to grow again.

"Monks! All conditioned phenomena are thus impermanent, thus unstable; they are not a place of rest, being brief, subject to change, and prone to destruction. They cannot provide rescue, nor are they a true refuge or a place of shelter."
"Monks! For this reason, conditioned phenomena are utterly repulsive; one should become dispassionate toward them and should abandon them. Monks!"
After a very long time, there comes a moment when a second sun appears in the world, its heat and brilliance twice as great as that of the original sun.
Because of this sun, all the ponds, lakes, and small rivers in Jambudvīpa completely dry up and no longer exist.
"Monks! All conditioned phenomena are thus impermanent, as previously explained in detail, up to and including the instruction that they should be relinquished. Monks!"
Furthermore, after a very long time has passed, there comes a time when a third sun rises in succession; its heat and brilliance are twice that of the second sun.
Because of this sun, the deep and great rivers and lakes within Jambudvīpa all dry up and vanish without remainder.
"Monks! All conditioned phenomena are thus impermanent; as described above, they should even be relinquished. Monks!"
After a very long time, on the fourth day, another sun appeared; its heat and brilliance were twice those of the third sun.

Because of this sun, the Lake Anavatapta, the Lake Mandākinī, the rivers between the seven groves, and the four great rivers—these and other such places where the waters were greatest, deepest, and flowed most swiftly toward the ocean—all became completely parched and dried up, leaving nothing behind.
"Monks! All conditioned phenomena are thus impermanent, as described in detail above, up to and including: 'they should be relinquished. Monks!"
After a very long time, the fifth sun emerges in succession; its heat and brilliance are twice that of the fourth sun.

Because of this sun, the inner and outer oceans decrease by one hundred *yojanas*; then they decrease by two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, and even up to a thousand *yojanas* as the seawater is consumed. Next, they decrease by two thousand, three thousand, four thousand, and even up to ten thousand; then by twenty thousand, and so on up to sixty thousand *yojanas*, until the entire element of water is diminished.
"Monks! At such a time, the remaining water of the great ocean will be seven *tāla* trees deep, or six, or five, or four, or three, or two, or one *tāla* tree deep."
"Monks! There will come a time when the remaining water of the great ocean is seven fathoms deep; in this manner it shall gradually decrease until it is only one fathom deep. Monks!"
At that time, monks, the remaining water of the ocean will reach only as far as the human neck, or the armpits, or the chest, the waist, the navel, the knees, the shins, or the ankles. Monks!
There will come a time when the remaining seawater does not even submerge the joints of one's fingers.
Monks! All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are thus impermanent, as previously described in detail, up to and including the instruction that they should be relinquished.
"Monks! After a very long time has passed, on the sixth day, another sun rises; its heat and brilliance are twice those of the fifth day.
Because of this sun, the great earth of the world, the inner and outer oceans, and Sumeru, the king of mountains, first emit smoke, and masses of smoke spread to cover them entirely."
For example, when a potter’s kiln first emits smoke, it is shrouded by a mass of smoke;
likewise, the great earth, the great oceans, and Mount Sumeru were shrouded by a mass of smoke during the sixth sun.
"Monks! All conditioned phenomena are thus impermanent, as has been explained in detail above, up to: 'they should be relinquished. Monks!"
After a long period of time, on the seventh day, another sun appeared; its heat and brilliance were twice that of the sixth sun.

Because of this sun, the world-system, the great earth, the inner and outer oceans, and Sumeru, the king of mountains, all burst into flames. Simultaneously, everything blazed forth until they became one single mass of fire, which remained burning for a long duration without being extinguished.

"Monks! This King of Mountains, Sumeru, is consumed by a great fire until it becomes a single mass of flame. It burns for a long duration, and its summit—whether a hundred yojanas square, or two hundred, three hundred, even up to a thousand yojanas—completely crumbles and shatters; it falls away and is reduced to ashes in the same manner."

At that time, all fires within the four external great elements spontaneously ignite; the world and the heavens burn and heat until they become a single mass of fire, and by the force of this heat, the water-wheel below is drawn upward.
For example, just as a copper basin heated by fire will completely absorb the water when placed in shallow water;
so too does the entire world and the great earth, having become of the nature of fire, absorb the water wheel below.
For example, when ghee or oil is consumed by fire, it is entirely extinguished without leaving any ash or residue;

likewise, when this great earth, the inner and outer oceans, and Sumeru, the king of mountains, all break out into flames and blaze forth simultaneously, becoming a single mass of fire that consumes everything, such that not even charcoal or ash remains—it is just so.
At that time, the earth element subsides entirely, and both the water and wind elements are likewise consumed by fire.
The flames rise upward from the water element, reaching as far as the abode of Mahābrahmā.
At that time, Mahābrahmā relinquished his lifespan and his dwelling place, ascending to be born in the Abhāsvara Heaven.

At that time, the ground of Mahābrahmā’s palace was vast, circular, and lovely with its radiance; those who beheld it could never tire of looking, for its color was pure white, subtle, and immaculate, yet it was all consumed by fire at once and no longer remained.

The ground where the Brahma King dwells is originally and naturally so; thus, it remains extinguished by fire and other elements for such a long time, and likewise, the entire external vessel-world remains dispersed and destroyed for such a long time.

After twenty intermediate kalpas had passed, another twenty intermediate kalpas followed; during this time, the location of the thousandfold world system remained empty and devoid of anything, like a dark cavern, with no covering above, remaining vacant for twenty intermediate kalpas.
The Buddha said, “Monks!
At that time, the world again begins to arise and form; such is the natural law of this world.”

When the world first began to arise, if there were sentient beings who had already cultivated karma capable of inducing the retribution of Mahābrahmā, they would, after casting off their previous retribution, enter the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Due to the conjunction of the four great elements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the ground of Mahābrahmā’s palace arose spontaneously; its pure white radiance eclipsed all other places, its physical form was perfect such that one could gaze upon it without weariness, and it was a place of cherished delight where no one yet dwelt.

These sentient beings have previously created karma capable of inducing a desirable and sublime dwelling place; because of that past karma, they induce the four great elements and the derived matter of the form realm. Due to that past karma and the four great elements of the form realm, the palaces are then formed.
“The four great elements of the form realm serve as both cause and condition for this palace; the karma created in past lives serves merely as a dominant condition.
The Buddha said, “Monk!”
In this manner, the abode of the Great Brahmā King arises and is established through causes and conditions; it is originally so by the nature of phenomena, arising through causes and conditions.
This dwelling place of the Brahmā King is as vast as one four-continent world system.
At that time, while in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the Brahmā King beheld this place and gave rise to a mind of desire and attachment, thinking:
"I shall now sit here.
As soon as that attachment arose, he was reborn therein.
Dwelling here alone for ten full intermediate kalpas, taking joy as food and abiding in reliance upon joy, he possesses a mind-made body that is naturally luminous and dwells with sovereign ease.
After ten kalpas had passed, this Brahmā King gave rise to thoughts of desire and attachment, and thoughts of unease, and he reflected thus:
"I wish that other sentient beings would come to dwell together with me."

At that time, once the Brahma King had made this vow, the beings of the second dhyāna realm, their karma exhausted and their life-span ended, passed away and were reborn there to become of the same class as the Brahmā.
These beings, seeing that this Great Brahmā had originally lived alone, formed this attachment:
"In the past, when we ascended to be born here, we saw this person sitting upright and dwelling alone; now, descending from above, we see him still dwelling alone, no different from before."
Furthermore, they give rise to this attachment:

"This person is Brahmā, the creator and progenitor, the most honored and primordial; all that is done by sentient beings is accomplished through this person; possessing sovereign spiritual power, he is the foremost father of those already born and those yet to be born."
"We were born from him this very day. How is it so?
From the past until now, we have seen him here, having been born alone."
At that time, the Brahmā King thought to himself:

"I am the Great Brahmā, the creator and the progenitor, the most honored and primordial being. All that sentient beings do is accomplished through me; my spiritual power is sovereign. Of those already born and those yet to be born, I am their father; all the worlds are born from my transformation."
Why is this so? Because in the past, I gave rise to such a thought:
"May other sentient beings come to dwell with me."
"In accordance with my wishful mind, he has now been reborn.
I was already here and saw him being reborn.

This Great Brahmā King, among other sentient beings, possesses an extremely long lifespan, the most excellent physical form and color, great renown, great supernormal powers, and great majestic virtue.
The lifespans of all other Brahmā assemblies are shorter, and they fall short in physical form, complexion, renown, supernatural powers, and majestic virtue.
The ground where the Great Brahmā King dwells is completely filled, in successive layers, by all the Brahmā assemblies.

When the world was about to arise through the natural law of its own nature, due to the four great elements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) thereof, a Brahmā palace and its ground appeared spontaneously and alone; that matter was pure white, subtle, and immaculate, with lovely radiance such that those who beheld it could never tire, yet no beings resided there.

These sentient beings have previously created karma capable of inducing a desirable and sublime dwelling place; due to that past karma, they induce the four great elements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the derived matter produced from those elements. Based on that past karma and the four great elements of the form realm, the palaces are immediately formed.
“The four great elements of the form realm (rūpadhātu) serve as both cause and condition for this palace; the karma created in previous lives serves merely as a dominant condition.
The Buddha said, “Bhikṣu!”

Thus, this solitary Brahmā palace arises and is established through causes and conditions; it is originally so by the nature of phenomena, arising through causes and conditions, and this solitary abode of Brahmā becomes completely filled through this successive sequence.

By the very nature of things, as the Brahmās, when the world was due to arise, through the primary elements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the derived matter produced from those elements, the palaces and grounds of the Brahmakāyika devas spontaneously appeared. Their color was pure white, subtle and immaculate; their radiance was lovely, such that beholders could never tire of looking at them, yet they remained uninhabited.

These sentient beings have previously created karma capable of inducing a desirable and sublime dwelling place; due to that past karma, they induce the four great elements of the form realm and the derivative matter produced by those elements. By means of that past karma and the four great elements of the form realm, the palace is then formed.

“The four great elements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) serve as both cause and condition for this palace; the karma created in previous lives serves merely as a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
The Buddha said: “Monks!”
Thus, this abode of the Brahmakāyika devas arises and is established through causes and conditions; it is originally so by the nature of phenomena, arising through causes and conditions.
This dwelling place of the Brahmakāyika devas is completely filled, in succession, by all the Brahmakāyika devas.

When the world was about to arise through the natural law of its inherent nature, due to the four great elements of the desire realm and the matter derived from those four great elements, the palaces and abodes of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven spontaneously manifested, composed of the four jewels—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. Their radiance was lovely and pleasing to behold, never tiring the observer, yet no beings yet dwelt therein.

These sentient beings have previously created karma capable of bringing about a desirable and sublime dwelling place; by virtue of that past karma, they are able to bring about the four great elements of the desire realm and the derivative matter produced from those elements. Furthermore, through that past karma and the four great elements of the desire realm, the palace is then formed.
“The four great elements of the desire realm are both the cause and the condition for this palace; the karma created in past lives serves merely as the dominant condition.
The Buddha said, “Bhikṣu!”
In this way, the palaces of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, as well as their arising and formation through causes and conditions, are fundamentally and naturally produced by causes and conditions.
In these abodes of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, all the devas are filled in succession.

It is the natural law of the nature of the devas that when the world is due to arise, the palaces and grounds of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven spontaneously manifest, produced from the four great elements of the desire realm and the matter derived from those four elements. They are composed of the four jewels—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—and their radiance is so lovely that those who behold them never tire; yet, at this stage, no beings dwell therein.

These sentient beings have previously created karma that can bring about a desirable and sublime dwelling place; because of that past karma, they are able to bring about the four great elements of the desire realm and the derived matter produced by those elements. Furthermore, due to that past karma and the four great elements of the desire realm, the palace is immediately formed.
"The four great elements of the desire realm are both the cause and the condition for this palace; the karma created in past lives serves merely as the dominant condition.
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣu!"

Thus, in the realm of the Nirmāṇarati devas, there are causes and conditions through which it arises and is established; fundamentally, it is so by the nature of dharmas, arising through causes and conditions.
This dwelling place of the Nirmāṇarati devas is completely filled with all the devas in successive order.

When the world was due to arise according to the natural law of its own nature (*dharmatā*), through the desire-realm (*kāmadhātu*) four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the matter derived from them (*upādāya-rūpa*), the Tuṣita heaven palace and its site spontaneously manifested, composed of the four jewels—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—lovely in radiance such that observers could never tire of beholding it; yet, no beings resided there.

These sentient beings have previously performed karma capable of inducing a desirable and sublime dwelling place; by virtue of that past karma, they induce the four great elements and the derivative matter of the desire realm, and through that past karma as well as the four great elements of the desire realm, the palace is then formed.
"The four great elements of the desire realm are both the cause and the condition for this palace; the karma created in past lives serves merely as the dominant condition.
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣu!"
Thus, the palaces and grounds of the Tuṣita Heaven arise and are established through causes and conditions; they have always been so by the nature of phenomena, arising from causes and conditions.
This dwelling place of the Tuṣita Heaven is completely filled with all the devas in successive order.

When the world is due to arise according to its inherent nature (*dharmatā*), through the desire-realm (*kāmadhātu*) four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the matter derived from them (*upādāya-rūpa*), the palaces and celestial abodes of the Yāma Heaven spontaneously manifest. They are composed of the four jewels—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—and their radiance is so lovely that observers never tire of beholding them; yet, at that time, no beings dwell therein.

These sentient beings have previously created karma capable of inducing a desirable and sublime dwelling place; by virtue of that past karma, they induce the four great elements and the derivative matter of the desire realm, and further, through that past karma and the four great elements of the desire realm, the palace is immediately formed.
"The four great elements of the desire realm are both the cause and the condition for this palace; the karma created in past lives serves merely as the dominant condition.
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣu!"

Thus, in the realm of the Yāma devas, there are causes and conditions through which it arises and is established; from the very beginning, by the nature of phenomena, it arises through causes and conditions.
This dwelling place of the Yāmas is completely filled with all the devas in successive order.

At that time, the Yāma devas recalled the world of former times, just as a person who has awakened from sleep recalls events in a dream, or as one who has attained supernatural powers recalls events of past lives;
the recollection of the former world by these Yāma devas was likewise so.
At that time, the various devas had this thought:
"We should now go down to inspect the lower realms.
Having formed this thought, they said to one another:
"Let us go together to see that place," the other devas replied,
"We shall go with you now."
At that time, the various devas each formed groups and filled the area as they conducted their inspection, all saying:

"In days of yore, there was Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, at this location; here was the city of the Sudarśana Heaven; here was the Nanda Jewel Pond; here was the Nanda Jewel Garden; here were the Citra Pond and the Citra-ratha Garden; here was the Durmukha Pond and the Durmukha Garden; here was the Citra-puṣpa Pond and the Citra-puṣpa Garden; and here was the realm of the Pārijātaka tree."

The water is four hundred and eighty thousand yojanas deep, twelve billion three hundred and forty-five yojanas wide, and thirty-six billion one thousand three hundred and fifty yojanas in circumference; it remains at this measure and does not extend further.

Upon this water-circle, there is a distinct earth-element called "Great Taste" (*mahārasa*), which arises at the beginning of the kalpa. Day by day and night by night, it gradually thickens and becomes solid, just as when boiled milk cools and congeals, a layer of thick cream forms on top; such was the initial arising of the earth-element of Great Taste.

This earth element increases repeatedly until it reaches its limit and fulfills its full extent; it is ultimately perfected with a thickness of two hundred and forty-four thousand *yojanas*, a breadth of twelve billion three hundred and forty-five thousand *yojanas*, and a circumference of thirty-six billion one thousand three hundred and fifty *yojanas*. It abides at this measure and does not increase further.

The lower limit of this earth for one hundred and sixty million [yojanas] is composed entirely of pure gold; the remaining eighty million above are composed of a mixture of the seven elements: gold, silver, copper, iron, and so forth.

At that time, the earth element becomes supple according to the requirements, just like mud, milk porridge, fresh butter, or dough; this suppleness of the earth according to the requirements is likewise so.
In the center of this earth-wheel, through the dominant condition of the karma of sentient beings,
winds blow from the four directions to excavate the inner seas and raise Mount Sumeru. There are winds that transport soil, winds that accumulate it,
winds that shape it into the square form of Sumeru, and winds that create the four peaks of Sumeru and open the moats of the city of Sudarśana.
He constructed the city of Sudarśana; he created Lake Nanda and the Nandana Garden,
Lake Caitraratha and the Caitraratha Garden, Lake Saṃtarpaka and its garden, Lake Kūṭaśālmalī and its garden,
Lake Citraratha and its garden, the Pārijāta tree and the Kovidāra Garden, the Yugaṃdhara Ocean, and the Yugamdhara Mountains.
Mount Yugaṃdhara, Mount Īṣādhara, Mount Khadiraka, Mount Sudarśana,
Mount Aśvakarṇa, Mount Vinataka, Mount Nimindhara, and the four continents;
from the intervening lands and islands, the oceans were excavated, and Mount Cakravāḍa was raised.
Such are the trees and the Jambūvana Grove; herein formerly was the Jambū-ratna stone where the Bhagavān resided;
herein formerly was the Sudharmā Hall; herein formerly was the great inner ocean;
herein were Mount Yugandhara and the Yugandhara Sea; and herein was Mount Īṣādhara.
And as for the Īṣādhara Ocean, within it are Mount Khadiraka and the Khadiraka Sea;
within it are Mount Sudarśana and the Sudarśana Sea; there is Mount Aśvakarṇa and the Aśvakarṇa Sea;
within it are Mount Vinataka and the Vinataka Sea; within it is Mount Nimindhara and...
In the Nimiṃdha Sea, there are four continents, intermediate islands, and the outer great ocean;
within this sea is Mount Jāmbūvada.

“The bodies of these Yāma-devas are the largest and their flight is most swift; because of this rapid movement, they stir up a wind-circle, and by means of this wind-circle, it becomes the foundation for the Nārāyaṇa wind-circle.”

This wind repeatedly rises and grows until it reaches its destined limit and fulfills its destined fullness, reaching a total completion. It is nine hundred and sixty million yojanas thick, twelve billion three hundred and forty-five million yojanas wide, and thirty-six billion one hundred and three thousand five hundred yojanas in circumference; it remains at this measure and does not grow any further.

This wind is so firm and resilient that no object can penetrate it; even if a person possessed the strength of Nārāyaṇa and brandished a vajra staff against this wind-circle, the staff would shatter while the wind-circle remains unharmed.

Next, in the space above the wind-circle, rain falls in drops as large as buildings, or like axle-trees, or like carriage yokes, without ceasing day or night for countless thousands of years, like the pouring of a river.
Surrounding this mass of the water element is a wind called "Upholding," which rises day and night constantly to prevent the water from dispersing.

Thus, as long as the predominance of the water element does not cease, this water repeatedly rises and grows until that which was to be reached has been reached, and that which was to be filled has been filled, reaching total completion.
"The arising and formation of the world is brought about by the power of wind, which is induced by past karma.
Furthermore, other winds arise in a circular rotation, forming Aparagoyānī and Pūrvavideha;
yet other winds, extending in the four directions and four intermediate corners, form Uttarakuru."
Furthermore, there is another wind shaped like half a lute that forms Jambudvīpa in the south.
If the wind rises to form mountains in a straight vertical succession, the mountains will have a summit.
If the wind arises either vertically or horizontally, the resulting mountain formations will be either level or towering.
Furthermore, there are winds that arise such that they blow swiftly on one side and slowly on the other; the resulting mountains thus have one side concave and the other side level and straight.
When the winds arise and strike each other, penetrating deeply before emerging again, the resulting mountain formations come to possess cliffs and caves.
If the winds strike each other and penetrate deeply without emerging from the bottom, the interior of the mountain becomes hollow.
By means of this wind, the earth of the four continents arises and is formed; it is sometimes deep and sometimes towering.

In some places it appears eight thousand *yojanas* high, in some places it is forty thousand *yojanas* deep, in other places it is forty thousand *yojanas* high and twenty thousand *yojanas* deep, and in yet other places it is twenty thousand *yojanas* high.
Ten yojanas deep, ten thousand yojanas deep; furthermore, there are other places one thousand yojanas high and five thousand yojanas deep,
or again, places five thousand yojanas high and two thousand five hundred yojanas deep,
or again, places two thousand five hundred yojanas high and one thousand two hundred and fifty yojanas deep.
Ten yojanas; or again, in some places it is one thousand two hundred and fifty yojanas high and six hundred and twenty-five yojanas deep,
or again, six hundred and twenty-five yojanas high and three hundred and twelve and a half yojanas deep.
By these causes and conditions, the entire vessel-world (bhājana-loka) arises and is fully formed.
At that time, two kinds of elements arise and increase, namely the earth element and the fire element.
The wind element arises and blows, and the fire element steams and refines the earth element.
The wind element constantly arises, blowing upon all things to make them solid and firm.
Once they have become solid and firm, all varieties of precious jewels manifest.

Once it had manifested, the heavens sent down sweet rain in drops as large as buildings, gradually becoming finer like wheels and even as thick as chariot axles, or like gushing springs for countless thousands of years. It filled the moats of the city of Sudarśana, the Nanda Lake, the Bahuputraka Lake, the Pāruṣyaka Lake, the Caitraratha Lake, and the inner great ocean; as well as the Yugandhara Sea, Īṣādhara Sea, Khadiraka Sea, Sudarśana Sea, Aśvakarṇa Sea, Vinataka Sea, Nimindhara Sea, the intermediate lands between the four continents, and the outer great ocean.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, the waters completely fill all worlds.
Thereupon, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and the Cāturmahārājika Heaven relinquish their celestial retributions and take birth therein.
Furthermore, there are devas whose lives have ended and whose merit is exhausted, who fall from the higher heavens to be born among humans within the four continents.

At that time, these people take joy and pleasure as their food and dwell in reliance upon joy and pleasure; they possess mind-made bodies produced by transformation, are naturally radiant, abide in peace and happiness, and travel through the air.

At that time, the sun and moon had not yet appeared in the world; the stars had not yet emerged, and day and night were not distinguished. Years, seasons, and the eight festivals could not be differentiated. There was no distinction between male and female, nor were there fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters, husbands, wives, or children. There were neither slaves nor masters; all enjoyed themselves with unimpeded freedom and joy. No surnames or personal names existed, and they were all collectively called "sentient beings."

At that time, the water element gradually diminished and flowed toward its lower course; meanwhile, the great ocean alternately rose and fell. Where the waters receded, the earth’s fertility emerged, possessing great sweetness and great flavor, growing to cover the ground and endowed with desirable color, fragrance, texture, and taste.
Like fine honey, free from bitterness, astringency, or pungency, the great flavor of the earth’s fertility was likewise.
At that time, a great fragrance filled the air. Then there was a man who, smelling this scent, gave rise to a mind of desire and attachment.
Having given rise to this desirous mind, he pinched off a piece of the great flavor, smelled it, and tasted it; knowing it to be as sweet as fine honey, he took a lump and ate it.
Seeing that the food was delicious and insatiable, others imitated them by eating it in mouthfuls.

At that time, once these people had consumed the *pṛthivī-rasa*, their bodies gradually became solid and heavy; from then on, they were no longer able to fly through the air as before, and the lovely radiance of their bodies consequently vanished.
Once the light had vanished, darkness arose once more, for such is the natural law.
When these four continents were thus shrouded in darkness, the two orbs of the sun and moon appeared in the world.
Once the sun and moon have appeared, the lunar mansions and constellations appear in succession.
Once the stars have appeared, day and night are distinguished.
Once day and night are distinguished, the periods of the half-month and the month become manifest.
Once the half-months and months have appeared, the four seasons, the eight festivals, and the years are all fully established.
In this manner, over a long period of time, the world arises and comes into being.
After such a long time, sixty minor kalpas had finally passed.
At that time, sentient beings consumed this essence of the earth and dwelt upon it for a very long period.
Among those sentient beings, those who consume more of the essence have ugly appearances, little majestic power, and little supernormal power.
Among them, those who consume less of the essence have lovely forms and complexions, possess majestic power, and exercise mastery over supernormal powers.

Due to these causes and conditions, all sentient beings differ in the excellence or inferiority of their physical forms; from this excellence or inferiority arises a mind of victory and defeat, and because of this mind, they speak thus:
"I am now superior to you; you do not equal me."
At that time, unwholesome dharmas first began to circulate in the world.
Because they calculated for victory and defeat, the color and fragrance of the "earth-essence" (pṛthivī-rasa) were lost from that point on.
Then, the people gathered together in assembly, and overcome by grief, distress, and suffering, they raised their voices and wept:
"Alas! A wicked dharma has appeared in the world.
Because of physical form, one becomes arrogant and disparages others; due to this wicked dharma, I have lost my superior flavor and my inconceivable colors, fragrances, and textures."
At that time, having eaten the remaining delicious flavors, those people thought to themselves:
"Alas! This resembles the 'taste of the earth' (pṛthivī-rasa) that we used to eat in the past."
Recalling this with grief and distress, these words have now been entirely forgotten; there is no one left who remembers or speaks of them.
Once that flavor was lost, another flavor appeared called "earth-skin" (*pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*), whose color, fragrance, texture, and taste were all sweet and delicious, like fine honey.
At that time, all the people came to eat, and by means of this food and drink, they were able to subsist for a long period.

However, because those people there were greedy for flavor, they ate much of the earth’s crust; consequently, their physical forms became ugly, their majestic power diminished, and their supernormal powers became scarce.
Among those sentient beings, those who consume little of the savory essence possess lovely forms and complexions, bodies endowed with majestic virtue, and sovereign spiritual powers.

Due to these causes and conditions, all sentient beings differ in the excellence or inferiority of their physical forms; based on this disparity, they give rise to thoughts of victory and defeat, and because of such thoughts, they speak thus:
"I now surpass you; you do not equal me."
"Because of these evil dharmas, they subsequently spread throughout the world.
Due to their preoccupation with calculating victory and defeat, the color and fragrance of the earth's surface were lost from that point on.
— *Lishi Apitan Lun* (Abhidharmakośa-śāstra), Fascicle Ten.
